translation: I gave the children sweets.
note: Both non-subject participants surface as bare NPs with no case morphology; the verb ku=kore indexes only the 1SG agent. Recipient vs theme is recoverable from the semantics of kore 'give' and from constituent order, not from case marking.

translation: my elder brother
note: The possessor relation is doubly marked on the head noun: ku= is the first-singular possessor prefix and -ihi is the affiliative (possessed) suffix. An independent possessor NP, when it appears, is caseless and appositive, not genitive-marked.

translation: to ponder deeply
note: Nine syllables, eight bound morphemes in a single verb word: two applicative prefixes (e-, ko-), reflexive (yay-), incorporated distance noun (tuyma 'far'), reflexive-possessive (si-), incorporated body-part noun (ram 'heart, mind'), verbal root (suy 'revolve'), and pluractional suffix (-pa). After Shibatani (1990 §1) as an illustration of Classical Ainu polysynthetic capacity.

text: kamuynomi=an kuni hattoho an, kor itak ani renkayne ukoytak=an kuni hattoho an.
gloss: pray=4.S COMP forbidden exist CONJ language INS freely converse=4.S COMP forbidden exist
translation: We were forbidden to offer prayer to the gods, and we were forbidden to converse freely in our own language.
place: Ainu Times 25 (contributor 野本久栄, 'Parawa utar'); Saru–Chitose composed prose
note: Composed memoir prose thematising the institutional suppression of the language: the parallel clauses frame prayer (kamuynomi) and free conversation in one's own language alike as objects of hattoho an 'there was a prohibition'. The construction X kuni hattoho an nominalizes the forbidden activity with the complementizer kuni; renkayne marks acting of one's own will, here 'freely/at will'.

text: tane oka onawtari anakne, poroserke aynu uwepeker ye eaykap pe ne kusu, tane oka hekattar utar ka aynu uwepeker erampewtek pe ne hawe ne.
gloss: now exist.PL parent-ASS TOP most aynu folktale say cannot NMLZ COP because now exist.PL child PL also aynu folktale not.know NMLZ COP REP COP
translation: Nowadays, it is said, most parents cannot tell Ainu folktales; the children now cannot know Ainu folktales either.
place: Ainu Times 60 (contributor 菅野由布子); Saru–Chitose composed prose
note: Composed modern prose from the Ainu Times newsletter (菅野由布子), thematising the very breakdown of intergenerational transmission described above. The sentence pairs the negative auxiliary eaykap 'be unable to' (ye eaykap 'cannot tell') with the negative verb erampewtek 'not know/understand', and frames the statement with the reportative evidential hawe ne, presenting it as general reported knowledge rather than the writer's direct assertion.

translation: Let's drink (together)!
note: In use by the early 1990s (Ōno 2022: §8.9). The fourth-person intransitive suffix =an encodes an inclusive agent (speaker plus addressee); ro is the sentence-final hortative particle.

translation: fish (lit. 'the thing that everyone eats')
note: The surface Saru form cep continues Common Ainu *ciʔep; Horobetsu retains the medial glottal break (ciʔep) and Sakhalin Raiciska has ceh. The morpheme breakdown ci= (fourth-person agent prefix) + e (eat) + -p (nominalizer) is reconstructed by Alonso de la Fuente (2022: §4, Table 18), corroborated by the curated morpheme database (conf. 1.0).

translation: I was sitting.
place: Chiri Yukie, kamuy yukar document 1, line 3 [yukie-kamuyyukar/003/0#3]
note: The exclusive first-person plural prefix ci= and suffix =as index a singular hero-narrator ('I was sitting'). In everyday Iburi speech these forms mark 'we (exclusive)'; their deployment as a singular narrator-voice is a convention of the Iburi/Horobetsu divine-epic tradition, contrasting with the Saru/Chitose practice of using fourth-person a=/=an for the same role.

translation: Let me tell one kamuy yukar.
note: A native performance frame uttered before beginning a kamuy yukar. The first-person ku= (not the narrative fourth-person a=) appears here because this is conversational framing around the narration rather than inside it — illustrating the boundary between the everyday first person and the hero-narrator's fourth-person voice.

translation: And then (the protagonist) went — so it goes.
place: 貝澤とぅるしの口演 ウエペケㇾ「ランコ カッケマッ」桂の木の女神 [biratori/002/002#39]
note: Attested prose-tale close in a Saru uwepeker: oraun 'and then' continues the wa-chained narration, arpa=an carries the fourth-person narrative-protagonist voice, and ruwe ne (track-POSS + COP) presents the story-world event as narrated, asserted knowledge rather than a bare assertion — the evidential framing characteristic of uwepeker prose, in contrast to the ceremonial ruwe tapan na close of prayer and ritual texts.

text: oro ta k=arpa wa, “Kokusai-gengo-nen” oruspe ku=ye ruwe ne.
gloss: there LOC 1SG=go CONJ “international-language-year” talk 1SG=say PERS COP
translation: I went there and spoke about the International Year of Languages.
place: Ainu Times 47 (contributor 横山裕之); Saru–Chitose composed prose
note: First-person narration (k= 'I go', ku=ye 'I say/tell') about the speaker's own act, yet closed with ruwe ne. Here the evidential does not mark hearsay — the speaker recounts a personal experience — but presents the event as a narrated, publicly framed account rather than a bare assertion; the personal-knowledge evidential reading (PERS) follows from the first-person subject, as analysed in the chapters on the evidential system.

translation: I heard it.
note: Illustrates the format: the morphemic line segments at person-marker (=) and affix (-) boundaries; the gloss line aligns one label per morpheme. The possessed evidential formal noun ruwe (ru-we, 'the trace of —') is discussed in the evidential chapters.

translation: You are not a good fish.

text: tanpe kusu tan mosir ka ta okay ruw-e ne
gloss: this.thing because this land surface LOC exist.PL track-POSS COP
original: Tambe gusu tam moshiri ka ta okai ruwe ne.
translation: That is why they are in this land.
Is it not eaten?
Behold! (lit. one looks)
flee to the land of Egypt
I eat (a meal).
be pregnant
note: Coda /n/ of the first syllable assimilates to the place of the following dorsal /k/, yielding surface [hoŋkor]. Contrast anpe [ampe], where coda /n/ assimilates to following labial /p/.

translation: person; human being
note: The historical Japanese transcription as アイノ reflects the back-rounded quality of /u/, which Japanese listeners perceived as near [o].

translation: standing (and then)
note: Kana transcription アㇲワ shows plain [s] before /w/, contrasting with アㇱ [aʃ] for the citation form as alone. Reported from Tamura (1996) dictionary grammar sketch via aomidori (2023-12-11).

translation: a sleeper; something asleep
note: The C-allomorph -pe selects after coda /r/, diagnosing mokor as phonemically /r/-final. Contrast poro-p below.

translation: something big; a large thing
note: The V-allomorph -p selects after the vowel-final stem poro, confirming that the stem ends in /o/, not /r/.

translation: (we/they) depart
note: Illustrates the C + =an juncture. The suffix =an does not trigger resyllabification of the preceding stop; juncture [ʔ] appears before the vowel, yielding [sapʔan] rather than *[sa.pan]. Compare the tighter-bound ku=, e=, ci= prefixes where resyllabification applies.

translation: (someone) speaks; there is speech
note: Pronounced [a.ko.rə.ʔi.tak]: the echo vowel [ə] follows coda /r/ in kor, and [ʔ] marks the compound boundary before itak. The person-prefix boundary a=–kor shows no juncture stop. The a= prefix does not trigger the accent shift that ku= and e= trigger, consistent with weaker prosodic integration.

translation: pothook (hook above the hearth for suspending pots)
note: Pronounced [suwat]. An opaque compound; the /w/ belongs to the fossilized root and does not derive from the compositional glide-epenthesis rule.

translation: pot handle (the wire bail of a pot)
note: Pronounced [suʔat]. A transparent compound of su 'pot, kettle' and at 'rope, cord'. In Shizunai the juncture [ʔ] at the su–at boundary is in contrastive distribution with the /w/ of suwat above.

translation: women's possessions
note: The underlying boundary mat|ikor resyllabifies to ma.ci.kor [ma.ʨi.kor] (CV.CV.CVC). The coda /t/ shifts to onset position and undergoes the obligatory t+i → [ʨi] palatalization. The same surface form is attested throughout the Saru corpus, e.g. usa macikor usa tamasay 'various women's treasures and bead-necklaces'.

translation: I get up.
note: Stem hopúni: σ1 = ho- (open, CV), accent on σ2 (pu-) by 原則2. Under ku=, σ1 of the phonological word becomes ku- (open, CV); σ2 is the stem's ho-; accent shifts to ho-: ku=hópuni. Paradigm from Nakagawa (2024: 52) and Shiraishi (2022: §5.1).

text: topenpe atay poka ka somo a=kore
kana: tópenpe atay póka ka somo a=koré
translation: She couldn't even be given the price of one sweet.
place: 川上まつ子, isoytak 独話2, AA研アイヌ語資料 [aa-irc/004#105]
note: The σ2 accent of koré reflects the iambic pattern of a lexicalized open-initial disyllable (σ1 ko = CV, open → 原則2). The co-existent ditransitive korpare 'give to someone' is attested alongside it in the Saru corpus.

translation: How delicious!
note: Exclamatory utterance. The whole pitch level is elevated above the declarative baseline, and the final syllable carries a lengthened rise-fall. The formal noun hum-i, possessed form of hum 'sound, feeling', functions as an exclamative complement to the finite clause kera=an 'it is delicious'. Tamura 1996: 4 (reported via Shiraishi 2022: §7) characterizes this pattern; the form keraan shows vowel sequence from kera + =an without glide insertion (Nakagawa 2024: 43).

translation: a wealthy man (of one's)
note: Productive /r/+/n/ → [nn]: the coda /r/ of kor assimilates to the following /n/ of nispa, yielding a geminate [nn] at the word boundary. Standard orthography writes ku=kor nispa.

translation: a bag (that one has)
note: Productive /r/+/t/ → [tt]: the coda /r/ of kor assimilates to the following /t/ of tar, yielding [tt]. Standard orthography writes ku=kor tar.

translation: sends it away; (ceremonially) performs the bear-spirit-sending
note: The [y] glide is epenthetic at the prefix–stem boundary. Phonemic form /i-omante/. Nominalizer takes the V-allomorph: iyomante-p, not *iyomante-pe, confirming the stem is phonemically vowel-initial.

translation: tell each other stories; tell stories together
note: The [w] glide is epenthetic at the prefix–stem boundary. Phonemic form /u-epeker/. The variant spelling uepeker (without the written glide) occurs in some orthographic traditions.

translation: I send it/them
note: Stem-initial /i/ is not weakened to [y]: *ku-ykra would create the illicit onset cluster [yk]. Surface form: [ku.ik.ra] with vowel hiatus maintained. Contrast ku-ipe → ku-ype (§5), where the stem begins with an open syllable.

translation: women's treasures and bead-necklaces
place: 川上まつ子, アイヌ語アーカイブ「ワシ神の化身と人間の娘 (1986)」[nam-archive/kawakami-minwa/09#465]
note: macikor is the surface form of the compound mat 'woman' + ikor 'treasure'; the coda /t/ of mat resyllabifies before the /i/-initial ikor and palatalizes to /c/.

translation: I go / I am going.
note: Saru/Chitose combining form: ku= elides its /u/ before the /o/-initial stem oman. Underlying /ku=oman/ → surface k=oman.

translation: I ache.
note: Before the /i/-initial stem iunin, ku= retains its vowel; the stem-initial /i/ weakens to the glide [y], giving ku=yunin (Chitose; Nakagawa 2024: 40). *kuyyunin is ungrammatical because the glide is not an underlying phoneme.

translation: The magistrate put on an attus robe and …
place: 小松哲郎, Ainu Times vol. 12 (沙流・千歳) [ainu-times/012/2#5]
note: attus is the standard Hokkaido form of the compound at-rus; the /t + r/ cluster has assimilated to /tt/. Corpus count: 24 tokens.

translation: I go out.
note: Underlying ku=omare; in the Saru and Chitose dialects the /u/ of ku= deletes before the /o/-initial stem, yielding the spoken form k=omare [koˈmaɾe]. Standard romanized orthography writes the underlying form.

translation: I eat.
note: Underlying ku=ipe; the /u/ of ku= is retained (deletion is blocked before /i/), and the stem-initial /i/ weakens to the glide [j], giving ku=ype [kuype]. The form *k=ipe is ungrammatical.

text: tane rikin wa isam pe okake ta
gloss: now ascend CONJ be.gone NMLZ after LOC
translation: Now, after (the god) had ascended and vanished,
note: rikin: the nasal-coda form of the ascent verb in non-reduplicated context. The corpus attestation confirms the form cited in the rikin~rikip alternation (§5); wa isam adds completive force.

text: caricari wa isam ru-we ne kuni a=ramu kor
gloss: be.scattered CONJ be.gone track-POSS COP COMP 4.A=think while
translation: (while she was) thinking that (things) had been scattered and vanished,
note: caricari: full CVC reduplication of cari 'be scattered'; the reduplicated form expresses distributive or pluractional scattering; wa isam adds completive force with the sense of disappearance. The syllable structure [ˈca.ri.ca.ri] follows the iambic rule applied to the reduplicated string.

translation: That mountain is high.
The wind is strong.
(she) has come over to my side
note: Nakagawa ex. 281, Chitose. The locative noun sam takes the objective prefix en= (first-singular O), contrasting with the possessive prefix ku= that would appear on an affiliative common noun. Type-2 locative nouns (kim 'mountain-ward', soy 'outside') stand at clause-head without an antecedent.

translation: my furs
place: 川上まつ子 '和人になった兄' (1986), NAM database nam-archive/kawakami-minwa/13, line 226
note: utar marks an inanimate noun (furs); the 4th-person transitive prefix a= encodes the narrative first person. Kindaichi & Chiri 1936: 31 restrict utar to animates unless personified — a genuine descriptive disagreement with Nakagawa's Saru data ‹contested›.

text: tan-pe anak su sekor a=ye p ne.
gloss: DEM-NMLZ TOP pot QUOT 4.A=say NMLZ COP
translation: This is what is called a pot.
note: Nakagawa ex. 389, Saru. The demonstrative prenominal tan fuses with pe to yield the demonstrative pronoun tanpe; the second formal noun p nominalises the quotative VP su sekor a=ye 'is called a pot', supplying the predicate complement of the copula ne.

translation: a small child
note: pon 'be small' precedes the noun without morphological change, in the same attributive position as a true prenominal; in predicate position it takes person affixes and verbal derivational morphology like any intransitive verb.

translation: Get well quickly!
note: pirka means both 'be good/healthy' and 'become good/healthy'; the bare imperative form receives the inchoative reading here. *pirka ne for 'become good' is ungrammatical because the copula ne cannot add an inchoative value — pirka already encodes change-of-state as an intransitive verb.

translation: my/his boat
note: Alienable possession: the possessed noun cip 'boat' stays in the concept form; the possessor prefix a= (4th person, here functioning as a generic 'my/his') attaches to the possession verb kor.

translation: my hand
note: Inalienable possession: the affiliative suffix -he attaches to the root teke, and the 1SG possessive prefix ku= marks the possessor. The concept form *ku=tek with a direct prefix is ungrammatical in this possessive sense.

translation: a woman's hand (attributive, not possessed)
note: Attributive juxtaposition, construction (3): menoko 'woman' specifies the attribute of tek 'hand' but is not its possessor in the grammatical sense. No person prefix can substitute for menoko here: *ku=tek is ungrammatical as a possessive.

translation: I stood on top of it.
note: The long form kasi (ka + -si, extendable to kasike(he)) of Type-1 locative ka heads the clause alone; the basic form *ka could not appear here without a preceding antecedent NP. The fourth-person suffix =an carries narrative-first-person reference.

translation: It has come to settle beside me.
note: Objective prefix en= (1SG.O) attaches directly to the Type-1 locative sam 'beside'. The allative particle un follows, as sam is ⟨place⟩. Contrast the nominative/possessive prefix ku= that would appear on a common-noun affiliative.

text: pet oske oma wa ray na
gloss: river inside enter CONJ die FIN
translation: It entered the river and died.
note: Type-1 locative oske 'inside (hollow space)' immediately follows its antecedent pet 'river', as required for the basic form. The basic form cannot head a clause alone.

translation: When I went to the mountain…
note: Type-2 locative kim 'mountain-ward' heads the clause in basic form with no antecedent. The common noun nupuri 'mountain' is not ⟨place⟩ and requires nupuri or ta to express the same location.

text: huci na ipe yakne pirka p
gloss: grandmother FIN eat COND be.good NMLZ
translation: Grandmother, it would be good if you ate.
note: p after the vowel-final predicate pirka 'be good'. The clause ipe yakne pirka 'if one eats, (it) is good' is nominalised as a content complement.

translation: One should sit quietly.
note: pe after the consonant-final clitic =an (4th-person intransitive). The nominalised clause is predicated with the copula ne.

translation: as for the ones I raised …
note: Nakagawa ex. 230. p heads a relative clause with a missing object (the raised entities); anakne marks the nominalized clause as a contrastive topic.

text: sirkunne hi ka ku=eramuskari-no ku=mokor wa ku=an
translation: I slept on without even knowing that it had grown dark.
note: Satō §22 ex. 1. hi nominalises the clause sirkunne 'it became dark'; the resulting NP is the complement of eramuskari 'not know'. The antecedent clause has no missing argument, confirming the content-complement function.

text: nanu memke usi ku=oman wa ek ruwe ne
gloss: face shave place 1SG.S=go CONJ come.back track-POSS COP
translation: I went to the place where one shaves — a barber's.
note: Nakagawa ex. 330 (Kushiro dialect, citing Yaegashi 2001: 13). usi nominalises the VP nanu memke 'shave one's face', producing an NP denoting a place; the evidential ruwe ne closes the matrix clause.

translation: When (I) went to the mountains…
note: arpa 'go' is intransitive; the fourth-person subject is marked by the S suffix =an following the stem. The type-2 locative noun kim 'mountain-ward' directly heads the locative phrase with the case particle ta.

translation: That mountain is high.
note: Shibatani ex. 13b. The property predicate ri 'be tall, be high' heads the predicate with zero marking for 3rd person. No copula intervenes between the subject NP and the property predicate.

translation: As for those (children) I raised…
note: respa 'rear, raise' is transitive; ku= marks the 1SG.A subject. The object is a relativized clause headed by the formal noun p, whose internal gap is the relativized third-person object — which is why no O affix appears on the verb.

translation: I gave the children sweets.
note: kore 'give' is a three-place verb. Both the recipient hekattar 'children' and the theme topenpe 'sweets' are third person and surface as bare noun phrases; only the 1SG.A subject is indexed by ku=. Were the recipient first or second person, an O affix for that participant would appear on the verb.

translation: I am a poor woman.
note: Constructed illustration (cf. Nakagawa 2024: 118; Bugaeva ed. 2022, ch. 14: 474). The copula ne takes the A-type ku= prefix for 1SG; the predicate nominal wen menoko 'poor woman' receives no person index.

text: sonno ku=pewre or ta ku=nu yukar ne ru-we ne
gloss: truly 1SG.S=be.young inside LOC 1SG.A=hear yukar COP track-POSS COP
translation: That is truly a yukar I heard back when I was young.
note: Nakagawa ex. 1. The property verb pewre 'be young' takes the first-singular intransitive prefix ku= in the same slot as the action verb nu 'hear'; no morphological difference marks one as stative and the other as active.

translation: That mountain is high.
note: Shibatani ex. 13b. The property verb ri 'be tall/high' predicates the third-person subject nupuri 'mountain' with zero person marking and no copula.

translation: The wind is strong.
note: Shibatani ex. 13c.

translation: Get well quickly!
note: Shibatani (1990: 19). The bare property verb pirka 'be good / be healthy' receives an inchoative reading under the imperative frame. No dedicated inchoative form exists; the reading 'become good/healthy' is forced by context.

text: oka=an ayne tane asinuma ka poro=an
translation: As we lived on, I too had now quite grown up.
note: poro=an is inchoative ('become big, grow up') here, while the same bare form denotes a state elsewhere — the stative–inchoative duality in running narrative. The 4SG pronoun asinuma 'I' (the narrator as protagonist) hosts the particle ka 'also'.

text: hinak wa arki wen cikap-po utar
gloss: where from come.PL bad bird-DIM ASS
translation: the bad little birds that came from somewhere
place: Kawakami Matsuko 川上まつ子, uwepeker 民話15, ILCAA Ainu materials [aa-irc/022#23]

translation: spreading out the small fish
place: Kawakami Matsuko 川上まつ子, uwepeker 民話14, ILCAA Ainu materials [aa-irc/020#61]

translation: even small birds flocking together
place: Kanenari Matsu 金成マツ, 六人の山子, 千葉大学報告書 [chiba-325/25#19]

translation: young men (Saru: unambiguously DIM reading)
place: Kawakami Matsuko 川上まつ子, isoytak 独話1, ILCAA Ainu materials [aa-irc/003#26]

translation: his distinguished elder brother (modifier and noun are separate words)
note: Syntactic phrase: the possessive affix a= precedes yupi alone; poro is an independent attributive verb.

translation: his/one's great elder brother (compound, lexicalized as a title)
note: Compound: the possessive affix a= precedes the entire compound poro-yupi, which behaves as a single morphological word.

translation: his wife's companions / his wives (two words: affiliative on the head mac)
note: Phrase: affiliative suffix -i attaches to mac (the concept-form stem of mat 'woman, wife'), and utar 'people/companions' is a separate syntactic head.

translation: his wives (compound: affiliative on the outermost edge)
note: Compound: mat appears in its concept form inside the compound; the affiliative -i attaches to the right edge of the whole matutar unit.

translation: eyelid
note: sik 'eye' and kap 'skin, bark' are both in concept form; their immediate concatenation yields the compound 'eyelid'.

translation: crab (lit. 'the one whose claw is long')
note: ami is the affiliative form of am 'claw'; the compound names the crab by a characteristic body feature. Type ⑤: N.POSS + 1-arg-V.

translation: thief (lit. 'the one whose hand reaches far')
note: teke is the affiliative form of tek 'hand'. The compound lexicalizes the thief as someone whose reach is long. Type ⑤: N.POSS + 1-arg-V.

translation: hawk (lit. 'one that catches birds')
note: cikap 'bird' in concept form is the implicit object of the transitive verb koyki 'catch, seize'; the compound names the hawk by its characteristic predatory action. Type ⑥: N + 2-arg-V.

translation: head of household, houseowner
note: N-kor-kur compound type; confirmed as a single phonological word by accent data (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-09): accent falls on the second syllable of the whole compound.

text: huci na ipe yakne pirka p
gloss: grandmother FIN eat COND good NMLZ
translation: Grandmother, it would be nice if you ate more!
note: Satō §22.1. The clause ipe yakne pirka ends in a vowel-final form; the nominalizer surfaces as p. The construction expresses an unfulfilled wish.

translation: One ought to sit quietly.
note: Satō §22.1. The verb rok=an ends in a nasal; the nominalizer surfaces as pe. The construction carries a normative or prescriptive nuance.

translation: food
note: Patient-nominal type. The subject slot is filled by the indefinite fourth-person agent a= and the patient slot is closed by -p; the result is a stable common noun with no open argument gap. The morphemic analysis is the standard decomposition; the surface form is aep.

translation: those whom I raised
note: Nakagawa ex. 230. Here p heads a relative clause with an accessible object gap (the raised persons); this is the syntactic use. The lexicalized aep differs by having no gap and a conventionalized meaning. Both shapes are morphologically identical; the distinction is arity and degree of reanalysis.

translation: It is the thing to put on the fire!
note: Nakagawa ex. 1165. Both argument slots of e=o are filled via person morphology; p closes the zero-arity predication with a patient reading. The directive force is contextual, not contributed by p itself.

translation: a Saru person
note: Nakagawa §5.2.6. Place name + allative particle un + class-noun head kur; the pattern is productive across place names.

text: nanu memke usi ku=oman wa ek ruwe ne
gloss: face shave place 1SG.S=go CONJ come track-POSS COP
translation: I went (and came back) to the face-shaving place.
note: Nakagawa ex. 330, citing Yaegashi 2001: 13. The VP nanu memke 'shave the face' is nominalized by usi to produce 'the face-shaving place (barber's)', which then heads the goal argument of the motion-verb sequence ku=oman wa ek. The ruwe ne closes the matrix clause as inferential evidential.

translation: a stone / the stone / stones
note: The bare transnumeral form; no morphological distinction between singular and plural readings.

translation: small birds
note: Bare-NP host: cikappo is a noun; utar follows directly without a finite predicate. Nakagawa ex. 333.

translation: (one's) furs
place: Kawakami Matsuko, 'Sisam ni nare ta oyaji' (1986); National Ainu Museum archive [nam-archive/kawakami-minwa/13]
note: utar on the inanimate host rus 'fur/pelt' — corpus evidence against the animacy restriction. Corresponds to Nakagawa 2024: 259 ex. 334.

text: hinak wa arki wen cikap-po utar
gloss: where from come.PL bad bird-DIM ASS
translation: the bad little birds that had come from somewhere
place: Kawakami Matsuko, 'uwepeker minwa 15'; ILCAA Ainu materials [aa-irc/022]
note: utar follows the diminutive-marked noun cikappo 'small bird' as an animate host.

translation: many children came
note: hekattar is the lexicalized fusion of hekaci + utar. The suppletive plural verb arki cross-indexes a plural subject. Kindaichi & Chiri §37.

translation: my relatives / my family
note: utari is the affiliative form of utar 'relatives/group'; ku=kor is the alienable-possession construction. The first-person referent is not included in the group (Nakagawa 2024: 251).

translation: even though they are young men
place: Kawakami Matsuko, 'uwepeker minwa 7'; ILCAA Ainu materials [aa-irc/005]
note: utari in a collective predication: 'young men (as a group)'. Extract from a larger sentence; ne is the copula.

translation: inside that good house
note: Constructed to show the full template: demonstrative (position 1), property verb (position 3), head noun (position 5), locative noun or 'place/inside' + case particle ta (position 6). Positions 2 and 4 are empty.

translation: Is this house yours?
note: The proximal demonstrative tan precedes the head noun cise 'house'. Used here to illustrate the NP tan cise; the evidential frame ruwe and the polar-question reduction are treated in the ruwe-ne-inferential chapter.

translation: two boats
five men
a small child
note: The property verb pon 'be small' modifies hekaci 'child' with no morphological change. In predicative function the same pon takes a subject person index.

translation: bad little birds
note: The property verb wen modifies a head that is itself a diminutive compound (cikap 'bird' + -po DIM) followed by the plural formal noun utar. The full sentence hinak wa arki wen cikappo utar, 'the bad little birds that came from somewhere', also shows a relative-clause modifier (hinak wa arki) at position 4 preceding wen.

translation: The people who were walking came.
note: The VP apkas 'walk' (zero-marked third person) modifies the head utar 'people'. The main-clause verb arki is the suppletive plural of ek 'come'. No relative marker appears between the modifying VP and its head.

translation: on top of the luggage
note: The head noun sike 'luggage' is in affiliative form sikehe. The locative noun kasi (long form of ka 'on top of') follows it, and the case particle ta closes the postpositional phrase. The common noun sike does not satisfy ⟨place⟩ by itself; kasi provides the locative head.

translation: my/one's boat
note: Alienable construction: the transitive-subject person prefix (here fourth-person a=, which in narrative contexts typically encodes the speaker) attaches to kor 'have'; the possessed noun cip is in concept form. Any transitive-subject prefix may substitute for a= to encode a different possessor.

translation: my hand
note: Inalienable construction: the 1SG transitive-subject prefix ku= and the affiliative suffix -he combine on the possessed noun teke 'hand'. Body parts require the inalienable construction.

text: ku=kor seta hure toan kur kor cape retar
gloss: 1SG.A=have dog be.red DIST.DEM person have cat be.white
translation: My dog is red; that person's cat is white.
note: Minimal alienable pair: 1SG subject prefix ku= (first kor) vs. overt third-person possessor NP toan kur 'that person' (second kor). Both seta 'dog' and cape 'cat' remain in the concept form.

text: wa kotan kor kur a=ne wa an=an
gloss: CONJ village have person 4.A=COP CONJ exist=4.S
translation: I was the village chief.
note: Narrator uses narrative fourth person (a=, =an) for first-person reference throughout the text. kotan kor kur marks social dominion rather than transferable ownership of the village.

text: ku=kema-ha ka arka ku=tek-ehe ka arka
translation: My leg hurts too, and my hand hurts too.
note: kema 'leg' is vowel-final (type I) and takes the affiliative suffix -ha; tek 'hand' is type III-2 and takes -ehe. Both carry the 1SG possessive prefix ku=. The possessed body-part NP is the single argument of the intransitive verb arka 'hurt'.

translation: This is my son's (bow).
note: Inalienable (affiliative) construction for the trap-bow. ku-wehe is the affiliative of ku 'bow'; poho is the affiliative of po 'son'. The possessor a=poho 'my son' is itself in the affiliative form.

text: tan ku a=po-ho kor ku ne
translation: This is a bow that my son has.
note: Alienable (kor) construction for the same referent. The concept form ku appears twice: as the topic NP and as the gapped object of kor. Nakagawa uses the pair to show that the construction choice is construal-sensitive, not fixed by the referent.

text: ku=kema-ha ka arka ku=teke-he ka arka
translation: My leg hurts too; my hand hurts too.
note: Both body-part nouns take the 1SG possessive prefix ku= and the affiliative suffix. The intransitive predicate arka takes each body-part personal form as its subject; the verb itself carries no person-marking (third-person zero on the body-part NP).

text: ku=teke-he piro hi ta ku=kor totto noya ham uk wa
gloss: 1SG.POSS=hand-POSS be.wounded NMLZ LOC 1SG.A=have mother wormwood leaf take CONJ
translation: When my hand was wounded, my mother would take wormwood leaves and …
note: The body-part noun tekehe takes the 1SG possessive prefix (affiliative construction); the kinship term totto 'mother/breast' takes ku=kor (alienable construction). The two constructions co-occur within one sentence.

text: makan uske ta a=teke-he ani makan uske ta
gloss: somehow place LOC 4.A=hand-POSS INS somehow place LOC
translation: Somehow [the elder brother] took hold of my hand and …
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker folktale 11, ILCAA Ainu materials (aa-irc/013), sent. 11
note: In oral-narrative convention the fourth-person prefix a= identifies the narrator as the possessor of tekehe 'hand'.

translation: that elder brother's younger sister
note: Nakagawa ex. 259, Saru. Two kinship personal forms stack: a=yupihi 'my/the elder brother' (4th-person A-prefix, Type ③-1 long affiliative -ihi) and turesihi 'his younger sister' (zero 3rd-person prefix, same affiliative class). The second personal form presupposes the first as its possessor via the zero prefix.

text: nekon ne wa a=yup-ihi an=sa-ha hawe-he ka isam ruwe ene an hi an
gloss: why COP CONJ 4.A=elder.brother-POSS 4.A=elder.sister-POSS voice-POSS even be.absent track-POSS thus exist NMLZ exist
translation: How is it that neither my elder brother's nor elder sister's voice is to be heard?
place: Oda Suteno, uwepeker 'Moyuk (part 1)', ILCAA Ainu materials (aa-irc/017), sent. 52
note: hawehe is the long affiliative of haw 'voice' (Type ②: haw-e + -he); it serves here as the subject of the negative existential isam. Both kinship personal forms yupihi and saha carry affiliative suffixes stacked in the same clause. an= is a Shizunai dialectal variant of the 4th-person A-prefix a=. The clause-final ruwe ene an hi an is an indirect evidential frame; the trace-noun ruwe here is the same affiliative of ru discussed in the Formation section above.

text: ku=kema-ha ka arka ku=tek-ehe ka arka
kana: ku=kemaha ka arka, ku=tekehe ka arka.
translation: My leg hurts too; my hand hurts too.
note: kema-ha: type ①, V₁=/a/, long affiliative. tek-ehe: type ③-2, V₁=/e/, long affiliative. Both with 1SG.A possessor. The same sentence contrasts two different suffix classes.

translation: There is no voice from his elder brother or elder sister.
place: 織田ステノ, uwepeker 民話 Moyuk（前半）, AA研アイヌ語資料 (静内) [aa-irc/017#52]
note: haw-ehe: type ②, glide-final /w/, long affiliative -ehe. a=yupihi and an=saha are ③-1 kinship affiliatives; an= is the dialectal variant of 4th-person A prefix a=.

translation: I have an elder brother; I have an elder sister.
note: Classic story-opening family introduction (Huber 2025: 251, ex. 16). yup-i: ③-1 short affiliative (yup + -i). sa-ha: ① long affiliative (sa + -ha), showing type ① for comparison.

text: ku=tek-ehe piro hi ta ku=kor totto noya ham uk wa
gloss: 1SG.A=hand-POSS get.injured NMLZ LOC 1SG.A=have mother mugwort leaf take CONJ
kana: ku=tekehe píro hi ta, ku=kor totto noya ham uk wa …
translation: When my hand was injured, my mother gathered mugwort leaves …
place: 横山裕之, noya, アイヌタイムズ [ainu-times/024/1#20]
note: tek-ehe: type ③-2, V₁=/e/, long affiliative. ku=kor totto 'my mother' takes the alienable kor construction, illustrating the affiliative vs kor split on the same line.

text: ku=kema-ha ka arka ku=tek-ehe ka arka
translation: My leg hurts, and my hand hurts too.
note: Two 1SG-possessed body-part nouns, each as the intransitive subject of arka 'be.sore'. kema 'leg/foot' is type-① (vowel-final stem) with the long affiliative suffix -ha; tek 'hand' is type-③-2 with affiliative -ehe.

translation: the Wajin's village
note: The third-person (zero) prefix on the possessed noun is phonologically null; the affiliative suffix -u (short form of kotan 'village', type-③-3) is the sole overt possessive morpheme on the head. The possessor noun sisam 'non-Ainu, Wajin' is juxtaposed with no case marker.

translation: The descendants of Lord Ikuresuye will prosper.
note: The possessor phrase Ikuresuye nispa 'Lord Ikuresuye' is juxtaposed before the affiliative head santekehe 'descendants' (santek + affiliative -ehe). Third-person zero prefix leaves the possessive agreement slot phonologically silent; the affiliative suffix is the sole marker of the possessive relation on the head noun.

translation: my elder brother's younger sister
place: Nakagawa ex. 259; embedded in the clause nea a=tura a=yupihi turesihi, ne Iskar emko wa a=tura okkaypo a=eutannere
note: The 4th-person prefix a= on yupihi indexes the narrator's elder brother; the following turesihi carries a zero (3rd-person) prefix whose referent is that elder brother. Each noun enters the affiliative construction independently: yup 'elder brother' with affiliative -ihi (type-③-1); tures 'younger sister' with affiliative -ihi (type-③-1).

text: ku=kor seta hure toan kur kor cape retar
gloss: 1SG.A=have dog be.red that person have cat be.white
translation: My dog is red; that person's cat is white.
note: A minimal alienable pair: 1SG possessor ku=kor vs the zero-prefix kor (3rd-person possessor). Both seta 'dog' and cape 'cat' are non-possessible alienable nouns and cannot carry a person prefix directly.

translation: My foot hurts, too.
note: Body-part affiliative kemaha (①-type: kema + -ha) as free clause argument of the intransitive predicate arka 'hurt'. The person prefix ku= marks the possessor on the noun directly — the base construction that feeds body-part NI.

translation: We became infirm in our hands.
note: The body-part tek 'hand' takes its short affiliative suffix -e (type ③-2: tek→teke) and is incorporated into pase 'be heavy'. The 4th-person intransitive subject =an surfaces as the subject of the derived verb, not as a prefix on the body-part noun. The reading is 'our/the-relevant-persons' hands became heavy/infirm': possessor raised to subject.

translation: The wave lifted me.
note: Base transitive: koy (wave, A) yanke (lift) en= (me, O). After koy is incorporated, en= is promoted to intransitive subject; the 1SG.S form ku= surfaces on the derived unaccusative koy-yanke. Satō (2012: 8, cited in Kobayashi 2025: 167).

translation: The leaf is blown by the wind.
note: Kobayashi 2025: ex. 4. rera 'wind' is incorporated into paru 'blow/fan'; the former object konam 'leaf' surfaces as the 3rd-person (zero) intransitive subject of the derived unaccusative rera-paru.

translation: a barber shop
literal: a place where one does someone's head
note: Tamura (1996: 247), cited in Bugaeva et al. (2021: 53, ex. 16). The antipassive i- absorbs the possessor of sapa 'head', allowing bare incorporation without a person prefix on the noun. The possessor is unspecified and non-coreferential with any surface argument.

translation: (someone) cuts a/someone's throat
note: Bugaeva et al. (2021: 53, ex. 17), citing Okuda (1999). The possessor of rekut 'throat' is unspecified; i- licenses possessor-free incorporation of the body-part noun into the transitive tuye 'cut'.

translation: Sis!
note: Nakagawa ex. 263. Chitose direct address to elder sister using the specialised address affiliative sapo. The reference form ku=saha is not used vocatively.

translation: Elder brother!
note: Nakagawa ex. 264. Direct address to elder brother; the reference affiliative ku=yupihi is not used as a vocative.

text: a=ona-ha an a=unu-hu an hine oka=an
translation: My father was there, my mother was there, and we lived.
note: Nakagawa ex. 261. Standard Saru story-opening formula; the 4th-person A-prefix a= functions as the logophoric narrator's first person. Both ona→onaha and unu→unuhu are affiliative-construction terms; the concept-form terms mici/hapo do not appear in this referential slot.

text: nekon ne wa a=yupi-hi an=sa-ha haw-ehe ka isam ruwe ne
gloss: how COP CONJ 4.A=elder.brother-POSS 4.A=elder.sister-POSS voice-POSS also not.exist track-POSS COP
translation: How is it that my elder brother's and my elder sister's voice is not heard?
place: Oda Steno, ILCAA Ainu materials, Shizunai [aa-irc/017#52]; source: 織田ステノ, uwepeker 'Moyuk (zenhan)'
note: Three affiliative nouns — a=yupihi (elder brother), an=saha (elder sister; an= is the Shizunai dialectal variant of the 4th-person A-prefix a=), and hawehe (voice, long affiliative of haw 'voice') — stacked in one clause. The 4th-person prefixes function as logophoric narrator first person. The embedded ruwe ne closes the indirect-question frame.

translation: I have an elder brother and I have an elder sister.
note: Huber (2025) ex. 16; BE-type predicative possession with kinship affiliatives. The 4th-person a= is the logophoric narrator first person.

text: ku=teke-he piro hi ta ku=kor totto noya ham uk wa
gloss: 1SG.A=hand-POSS be.injured NMLZ LOC 1SG.A=have mother mugwort leaf take CONJ
translation: When my hand was injured, my mother took mugwort leaves and …
place: Yokoyama Hiroyuki, Ainu Times no. 024/1 #20; source: 横山裕之, アイヌタイムズ (沙流・千歳)
note: ku=tekehe is affiliative-construction body-part possession; ku=kor totto is concept-construction kin possession. In this Chitose-influenced idiolect hapo means 'father', so totto 'breast' has been recruited as 'mother' and takes the kor construction.

translation: (I) will clean up, so…
note: Nakagawa ex. 321. The verbal index k= (reduced form of ku= before a vowel) already marks the 1SG agent; kani adds the emphatic 'I (not someone else)'. The clause continues; kusu ne na closes the coordinating frame.

translation: I know.
note: Kindaichi & Chiri §78. The full form kuani rather than contracted Saru kani reflects the older or literary register of the source. ku= is the complete 1SG.A index; kuani is strictly additive.

text: eani anak=ne onne kur neno e=yaynu hi
translation: Do you think like an old man?
note: The following sentence in the source — kani anakne mokor akkari sus kusu pet or un k=arpa rusuy 'I'd rather go swimming in the river' — completes the contrast pair. Both pronouns carry anak=ne to mark the opposed topics. The pragmatics of topic fronting are developed in the chapter on topic-marking-anakne.

translation: …(they) looked at me too.
note: Nakagawa ex. 324, Saru. The fourth-person object i= indexes the narrator as the entity looked at. The scalar particle ka 'even/also' attaches to the pronoun asinuma; without the pronoun there is no NP host for ka. The full range of fourth-person object i= uses is treated in indefinite-fourth-person-paradigm.

text: asinuma anak=ne iwor so ka a=e-hoyupu wa
kana: asinuma anakne iwor so ka a=ehoyupu wa
translation: As for myself, I flew about over the hunting ground…
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker 民話8 (その1), ILCAA Ainu materials (沙流) [aa-irc/006#52]
note: The fourth-person pronoun asinuma serves as the first-person narrative self throughout this text. The topic marker anak=ne cannot attach to a verbal affix and requires the free pronoun as host. The ka here is the postposition 'over/on top of' (path marker with the applicative e-), not the scalar focus particle.

translation: That house (in sight, nearby) is good.
note: Illustrative. taan signals the referent is within the speaker's sphere but not immediately at hand, the closest HA equivalent to Japanese sono. Compare tan cise 'this house (right here)' and toan cise 'that house over there'.

translation: Who is that person?
note: From アコㇿイタㇰ ch. 2. The question word hunna 'who' is the h-series form of Saru and Chitose; eastern and northern dialects have the n-series instead: toan kur nen ta an (see the chapter on interrogative pro-forms). The toan kur frame illustrates the demonstrative as the carrier of third-person deictic reference.

translation: …when (he) went, that woman (the one already introduced)…
place: 川上まつ子 uwepeker 民話 11, AA研アイヌ語資料 [aa-irc/013#94]
note: Fragment from a Saru narrative. The form nea picks up a female character introduced earlier; no scene-pointing interpretation is possible in the narrative context. This discourse-tracking use accounts for the form's high corpus frequency.

text: tan-pe anak su sekor a=ye p ne
gloss: DEM.PROX-NMLZ TOP pot QUOT 4.A=say NMLZ COP
kana: tanpe anak su sekor a=ye p ne
translation: This is what is called a pot.
note: Nakagawa ex. 389. The demonstrative pronoun tanpe heads the topic NP; the predicate is the quotative frame sekor a=ye p 'what (one) calls', nominalised by p, closed by the copula ne.

translation: I am here.
note: Constructed. The proximal locative root te takes the case particle ta. te cannot head an NP (*te menoko 'this woman' is ungrammatical) and never yields a prenominal form.

text: nupuri epunkine kamuy hunna ne ya
gloss: mountain each kamuy who COP FIN
translation: Who should be the kamuy to guard each mountain peak?
place: 川上まつ子 'uwepeker 民話16', AA研アイヌ語資料, aa-irc/023#178
note: hunna 'who' as a copular predicate with ne COP and the question particle ya.

text: hemanta ne kusu ene po easir
gloss: what COP PURP like.this somewhat grow.well
translation: Why has (he) grown so well like this!
place: 川上まつ子 'uwepeker 民話7', AA研アイヌ語資料, aa-irc/005#62
note: hemanta ne kusu 'why' (lit. 'what-COP-because'). Three periphrases coexist with no clear distributional difference: hemanta kusu, hemanta ne, hemanta ne kusu (Nakagawa 2024: 412).

translation: Who is that person?
place: アコㇿイタㇰ 第2章, akor-itak/002#17
note: Western (Saru) h-series form: hunna 'who'.

translation: Who is that person?
place: アコㇿイタㇰ 第2章, akor-itak/002#18
note: Eastern/northern n-series form: nen 'who'; ta locative marks the predicative slot. The Japanese gloss is identical to the Saru version above.

translation: Anything (I) do is a bother.
note: nep (Saru indefinite 'something') + =ka (focus 'even') gives the free-choice reading 'anything'. Nakagawa ex. 901.

text: cikap utar hunak un paye wa isam ru-we an
gloss: bird companions where ALLAT go.PL CONJ be.absent track-POSS exist
translation: Where could the birds have gone?
place: 成田英敏, アイヌタイムズ, ainu-times/055/0#20
note: hunak un 'where to' in situ, in the goal position of paye 'go (pl.)'. The evidential question frame ru-we an? marks the sentence as a content question. The Horobetsu author uses h-series hunak un rather than the expected ney un, illustrating the permeability of the h/n boundary in modern usage ‹corpus-suggested›.

translation: Where did that thing go?
place: 横山裕之 'cakcak kamuy oruspe', アイヌタイムズ, ainu-times/033/2#10
note: hunak un 'where to' in situ within an embedded question; ne hemanta functions as an anaphoric pro-noun 'that thing/what-is-it'.

translation: It is beside you.

text: orwano ku=cise or ta ku=an kor
translation: Then, while I was in my house, …
note: The relational noun or follows the host noun cise 'house'; the possessor ku= marks the host noun, not or itself. The case particle ta attaches to or in the 〈場所〉 slot.

text: ne kenas or peka ekimne=an kor
gloss: DEM forest place PERL hunt=4.S while
translation: while going through that forest to hunt
place: Kawagami Matsuko, AA-ken Ainu materials, uwepeker 民話7, doc. aa-irc/005, line 140
note: or peka 'through the area of' uses the perlative particle; the fused otta form only arises with ta, not with peka or un.

text: atuy or un cip ani paye=an
gloss: sea place ALLAT boat INS go=4.S
translation: going to the sea by boat
place: Hiraga Sadamo, 'Urayushiunkur', Biratori Ainu oral literature, doc. biratori/010/003, line 124
note: or un 'to the place of (i.e. toward) the sea'; the instrumental postpositional adverb ani follows. The full clause is orowano atuy or un cip ani paye=an ranke p ne.

translation: climbed onto the tree
note: Nakagawa ex. 419. ka ta 'on top of / onto' marks the locative goal on the tree. Contrast cikuni kasi un 'toward the treetop' (allative) in the immediately following example (Nakagawa 2024: 299), where the affiliative kasi appears before the allative particle un.

translation: The boat is on the river.
note: Satō 第5課 (Chitose). pet ka ta 'on (the surface of) the river'; ka here profiles contact with the water surface.

text: nean cise soy ta paye=as ki na
gloss: DEM house outside LOC go=1PL.EXCL.S do FIN
translation: went outside that house
note: cise soy ta 'at the outside of the house'. The form =as is the first-person-plural-exclusive intransitive suffix; the Japanese source gloss uses singular first person, reflecting the narrative first-person reading that Ishikari shares with the fourth-person narrative use of Saru (see person-marking-architecture).

translation: I am at my (own) place.
note: Constructed to illustrate direct first-person possession of the relational noun or. The prefix ku= marks the possessor on or; ku=an is the first-person-singular intransitive subject form of the existential an.

translation: The boat is on the river.
note: pet-ka = river-surface (the locative noun ka 'top/surface' heads the ⟨place⟩ phrase). Locative ta marks existence at a location.

translation: Today I arrived at Ukurmem.
note: Locative ta marks the endpoint of arrival, identical in form to existence-location ta.

translation: They came from the mountains.

text: atuy or un cip ani paye=an p ne
gloss: sea place ALLAT boat INS go=4.S NMLZ COP
translation: (She) always went to the sea by boat.
place: Hiraga Sadamo, 'Urayushiunhur', Biratori Ainu oral literature
note: atuy or un = 'to the sea' (allative); cip ani = 'by boat' (instrumental postpositional adverb ani).

text: ne kenas or peka ekimne=an kor
gloss: DEM forest place PERL hunt=4.S while
translation: While hunting through that forest, …
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker folktale 7, ILCAA Ainu materials (aa-irc/005)
note: ne kenas or peka = 'through that forest area'; peka here covers the whole region, not a linear route. Simultaneous kor 'while' links the clause.

translation: (It) transformed into a human.
(He/she) went along the road.
note: ru 'road' is a common noun, not a locative noun; kari therefore does not require the intervening or that peka would demand.

text: ruyka kari saramanto kari soyne=an akusu
gloss: bridge PERL skylight PERL go.outside=4.S when
translation: Going out through the bridge and the skylight, …
note: Both ruyka 'bridge' and saramanto 'skylight' are common nouns; kari licenses them directly without or.

translation: I want to go as far as Tokyo.
I went away from the mountain.
I went to the sea.
(He/she) accompanied (them) over/through the mountains.
note: kim peka = 'over the mountain area'; a=tura = 4A=accompany. The motion direction (away, toward) is understood from context; the postposition specifies the terrain traversed.

translation: on the thirteenth (day)
place: 萱野志朗, アイヌタイムズ (沙流・千歳)
note: re-p ikasma wan = 13 (3 + exceed + 10). The noun to 'day' and locative ta follow the numeral phrase. Here the numeral-noun form rep occurs as a free numeral expression rather than in apposition to a counted noun.

translation: twenty-nine years old
place: 平石清隆, アイヌタイムズ (沙流・千歳)
note: sinepesan (9) + ikasma (exceed) + hotne (20) = 29. The noun pa 'year/spring' is repeated after each numeral component in this age expression.

text: asikne-hotne-n asir cise or ta uekarpa
gloss: five-twenty-HUM.NMLZ new house inside LOC gather
kana: asikne-hotnen asir cise or ta uekarpa
translation: A hundred people gathered in the new house.
place: 萱野志朗, アイヌタイムズ (沙流・千歳)
note: asikne-hotne-n = asikne (5) × hotne (20) = 100; the human numeral-noun suffix -n marks the referents as persons. The locative noun or 'place-of' precedes the case particle ta.

translation: thirty (lit. ten short of forty)
note: Subtractive odd decade: wan (10) + e- (toward/short of) + tuhotne (2×20=40). The prefix e- is formally identical to the applied-object prefix treated elsewhere in the grammar; its numeral function is directional — marking the following even decade as the target quantity.

translation: A young man came.
note: The prenominal sine precedes the noun okkaypo directly. No postposition or classifier intervenes.

text: toonta pon kamuy re-p an ma
gloss: there small bear three-NMLZ exist FIN
kana: toonta pon kamuy rep an ma
translation: There are three young bear cubs over there.
note: The numeral noun rep (re-p, 'three-thing') follows the head noun kamuy in apposition. The prenominal construction *re kamuy rep would be redundant; the head noun takes the prenominal form alone (re kamuy 'three bears') or the postposed numeral-noun alone (kamuy rep 'bears, three').

translation: Three of us lived.
note: The numeral noun re-n (three-human) predicates the count via copula ne; the conjunctive wa links to the following existential plural oka=an. The translative copula ne appears here in a count predication, distinct from its use as an anaphoric demonstrative.

translation: (I) was called out to many times
note: iwan suy: the cardinal 6 is used with the force of 'many/several'. This use is restricted to fixed collocations; a compositional 'six times' reading is also possible in context.

translation: A youth came, …
note: Prenominal sine immediately before the head noun okkaypo. Satō 2008: 257, Chitose; the sentence continues.

translation: one cup
note: Nakagawa 2024: 464. The numeral noun sinep is post-nominal. The inverted order *sinep tuki is ungrammatical: the numeral noun cannot precede its head (Nakagawa 2024: 465).

text: toonta pon kamuy re-p an ma
gloss: there small bear three-CL exist FIN
translation: There are three bear cubs over there.
note: Satō 2008: 256, Chitose. The numeral noun rep follows the modified NP pon kamuy 'small/young bear'.

text: aoka sine-p ka a=tuye somo ki
translation: We did not cut even one (of them).
note: sinep heads the NP with the focus particle ka 'even'; no overt noun antecedent.

text: asiknehotne-n asir cise or ta uekarpa
gloss: five.twenty-HUM new house inside LOC gather
translation: A hundred people (5×20) gathered in the new house.
note: Kayano Shirō (萱野志朗), Ainu Times (アイヌタイムズ) vol. 3 no. 2; Saru/Chitose dialect. asiknehotne = 5×20 = 100 (see vigesimal chapter); the person-counting suffix -n attaches to the compound.

translation: We were three and lived (together).
note: Nakagawa 2024: 300–301, exx. 431–433. ren ne is a predicative phrase 'being three (persons)'; wa links it to the main predicate oka=an 'we existed'. The 4th-person forms index the narrator + others.

translation: (They) called out many times, …
note: Nakagawa 2024: 469, ex. 1080. iwan functions as 'many' in fixed expressions; suy follows as the mensural element. See also the quantifier section below.

translation: alone, by oneself
note: Refsing 1986: 117, ex. 105 (Shizunai). sinen ne contracts to sinenne; the translative copula ne gives the meaning 'being one person'.

translation: Divide it in two.
note: Refsing 1986: 117, ex. 104. tup ne 'being two things' functions as an adverbial predicate specifying how the action is carried out.

translation: my three uncles
note: Nakagawa 2024: 464. The 4th-person possessive prefix a= marks the narrator's kin; ren 'three (persons)' follows in the appositional slot.

translation: One person is good at it.
note: Refsing 1986: 116. sinen is the sole argument of the intransitive predicate askay; no head noun is present.

translation: Take one chopstick.
note: Community-discussed form (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-12-12, proposed): the noun–numeral.noun–verb sequence is described as at least as common in Hokkaido Ainu as in Japanese. Consistent with the appositional numeral syntax documented in Refsing (1986: 116) and the appositional-possession pattern in Bugaeva (2021).

text: inkar=an akus e=an ru-we a=nukar hi kusu
translation: When I looked, since I saw that you were there, ...
note: The intransitive inkar takes the S-suffix =an; the transitive nukar takes the A-prefix a=. The same side-switch is the template's first ordering diagnostic.

translation: I gave the children sweets.
note: Both non-subject arguments are bare third-person noun phrases; only the 1SG.A subject is indexed.

translation: The boy caught fish yesterday.
note: Ijäs, Lesson 3. A two-argument transitive frame with two bare noun phrases and an unmarked third-person verb.

text: mean cuk ne pe merayke=an ka somo ki no
gloss: be.cold.weather autumn COP NMLZ feel.cold=4.S even NEG do ADV
translation: It was a cold autumn, but I did not feel cold.
note: Zero-place mean indexes nothing; the experiential intransitive merayke indexes its subject with =an.

translation: Four rich men came.
note: A numeral-quantified plural subject takes the singular stem ek; the numeral-to-number relation is variable across dialects and speakers.

text: inkar=an akus e=an ru-we a=nukar hi kusu
translation: When I looked, since I saw that you were there, ...
note: The intransitive inkar takes the fourth-person S suffix =an; the transitive nukar takes the fourth-person A prefix a=. The possessed formal noun ru-we nominalizes e=an as the object of a=nukar.

translation: The boy caught fish yesterday.
note: Ijäs, Lesson 3. A two-place transitive frame with two bare noun phrases and a segmentally unmarked third-person verb.

text: mean cuk ne pe merayke=an ka somo ki no
gloss: be.cold.weather autumn COP NMLZ feel.cold=4.S even NEG do ADV
translation: It was a cold autumn, but I did not feel cold.
note: The ambient v0 predicate mean carries no person index; the felt-temperature vi merayke takes the fourth-person S suffix =an, both in one sentence.

translation: I am a man.
note: The copula is two-place but indexes only its subject, and with transitive-type marking; an object index such as *en=ne is excluded.

translation: I gave the children sweets.
note: Both non-subject arguments are bare third-person noun phrases; only the 1SG.A subject is indexed. topenpe ku=kore and hekattar ku=kore are identical in form, the を/に contrast belonging to the Japanese translation.

translation: I sank into the snow and rolled.
note: The place expression upas tum is the bare object of oma; the following intransitive karkarse takes the fourth-person S suffix =an.

translation: Do you all understand?
note: The transitive plural stem eramuoka (singular eramuan) here agrees with the plural subject, an exceptional subject-sensitive transitive plural noted by Nakagawa.

text: kiwkode paye=an wa ne yakun wakkata=an ka eaykap kusu
gloss: express.train go.PL=4.S CONJ COP if draw.water=4.S even be.unable because
translation: If we go by express train, we cannot even draw water.
note: The intransitive plural stem paye takes the fourth-person S suffix =an, here a plural first-person reference; the plurality sits on the single argument S.

text: a=onáha a=unúhu a=ronnu pa wa ora
translation: My father and my mother were killed, and then …
note: Two affected objects select the transitive plural stem ronnu; the indefinite a= gives the agentless reading. The trailing pa is the postverbal plural clitic of the next section.

translation: Do you all understand?
note: The plural stem eramuoka is selected by the plural subject index eci=, one of the rare transitive pairs whose number locus is the subject.

translation: My elder brother got up.
note: The derived intransitive hopuni is the singular member, with a singular S.

translation: My elder brothers also got up.
note: The plural stem hopunpa agrees with the plural S yuputari.

text: rus patek a=mi wa hotke=an pa
translation: We wore only fur and slept.
note: pa follows the fully inflected hotke=an, after the person suffix =an, and so sits outside the person index, unlike the Type-C suffix -pa.

text: a=utárihi hokure poronno túnas suke pa wa ipe pa kironnu pa
gloss: 4.POSS=companions come.on a.lot quickly cook PL CONJ eat PL be.full PL
translation: My companions, hurry, cook plenty, eat, and eat your fill.
note: Three pa clitics follow non-suppleting predicates across a directive addressed to plural companions; pa supplies the participant plurality the stems do not carry.

translation: The Oroks came.
note: The Sakhalin plural stem ariki is over-marked by hci, doubling the plural exponence the southern Hokkaido system carries on the stem alone.

text: hokure hokure ape sam ta arki yan
gloss: come.on come.on fire side LOC come.PL IMP.POL
translation: Please come, come near the fire.
note: The polite imperative yan selects the plural stem arki; the plural morphology belongs to the directive register, not to a plural addressee.

translation: Three houses are standing.
note: The numeral re 'three' specifies a plural subject, yet both the posture stem as and the existential stem an are singular.

text: iwan a=yupi an iwan a=saha an
translation: I had six elder brothers and six elder sisters.
note: Even iwan 'six', the culturally salient large number, occurs with singular an, against any simple 'low numeral selects singular' threshold.

text: nep a=nukar ka somo ki korka
translation: Although I did not see anything,
note: Nakagawa ex. 833. The lexical verb nukar bears the fourth-person A prefix; ki carries no person index. The indefinite nep receives its negative reading inside the scope of the negator.

translation: Even if you do not take revenge,
note: Nakagawa ex. 834. The same frame without ka; the intransitive predicate keeps its 2PL.S prefix while ki remains unindexed.

text: kira=an ka apkas=an ka eaykap no cis patek a=ki kor
gloss: flee=4.S even walk=4.S even cannot ADV cry only 4.A=do while
translation: Unable to flee or to walk, doing nothing but cry,
note: The light predicate cis patek a=ki 'do only crying' shows ki with an overt event complement; the fourth-person A prefix appears on ki.

text: e=itak haw-e ku=nu hi renkayne itasaytak ku=ki kusu ne na
gloss: 2SG.S=speak voice-POSS 1SG.A=hear NMLZ following reply 1SG.A=do PURP COP FIN
translation: I will listen to what you say and answer accordingly.
note: The event nominal itasaytak 'reply' is made predicative by ku=ki and combines with the future-intentional kusu ne; haw-e is glossed as a possessed noun.

text: ku=caranke ka somo ki no ku=hosipi
translation: I went home without complaining.
note: The negated action predicate is closed by ki before no links it to the following clause. The clause-linkage system is treated in detail in the clause-linkage overview.

text: sinep ka a=isamka ka somo ki ru-we ne kusu
gloss: one even 4.A=lose even NEG do track-POSS COP because
translation: Since I did not lose even a single one,
note: Nakagawa ex. 779. The negated support frame a=isamka ka somo ki is embedded below ru-we ne; negation falls inside the evidential while the copular frame scopes over the whole proposition. The particle kusu links the evidential frame as a reason clause.

translation: I am a man.
note: Nakagawa ex. 23. The first-person prefix is the transitive-subject form; the predicate nominal okkayo is not indexed as an object.

text: mean cuk ne pe merayke=an ka somo ki no
gloss: be.cold.weather autumn COP NMLZ feel.cold=4.S even NEG do ADV
translation: It was a cold autumn, but I did not feel cold.
note: The first clause uses ne in a predicate-nominal frame over the zero-place weather predicate mean; the second uses the support-verb negation merayke=an ka somo ki closed by no.

translation: It is not cloudy.
note: Ijäs negates the existential niskur an 'there are clouds' with the ka somo ki periphrasis; ki supplies the verb position because somo cannot head a clause on its own. Constructed pedagogical example.

text: me-an cuk ne pe me-rayke=an ka somo ki no
gloss: coldness-exist autumn COP NMLZ coldness-kill=4.S even NEG do CONJ
translation: It was a cold autumn, but I did not feel cold.
note: The zero-place climate predicate me-an carries no person index. The one-place felt-state predicate me-rayke carries the fourth-person S suffix =an. Both contain the coldness root me-, but they belong to different argument classes.

translation: I am a man.
note: The subject carries the prefixal transitive-subject form ku=; no object index appears. Nakagawa contrasts this with the ungrammatical *en=ne in the same passage.

translation: When I looked, I saw that you were there.
note: The vi stem inkar carries the fourth-person S suffix =an. The vt stem nukar carries the fourth-person A prefix a=. Both index the same narrative first person, but their different morphological position reveals the grammatical transitivity distinction.

translation: I sank into the snow and rolled.
note: The locative-object verb oma takes the bare place expression upas tum as its object; no case marker intervenes. The conjunctive particle wa links the clause to the following intransitive karkarse, which carries the fourth-person S suffix =an.

translation: The boy caught fish yesterday.
note: Ijäs Lesson 3. A constructed two-place transitive frame; subject and object are third-person and carry no segmental person marker. The example is pedagogical and is not corpus-attested.

translation: Get well quickly!
note: Shibatani cites the form in his discussion of property predicates as verbs; tunas-no derives the manner modifier from the descriptive intransitive stem tunas, and pirka carries its inchoative 'become well' reading.

translation: slowly
note: Ijäs's Lesson 3 teaching example, illustrating the regular descriptive-stem-to-adverb derivation.

text: a=ona-ha somo mokor no kamuyoritak kor an
gloss: 4.POSS=father-POSS NEG sleep ADV pray CONJ exist
translation: My father was praying to the gods without sleeping.
note: No adverbializes the negated intransitive predicate somo mokor, making it the attendant circumstance under which the progressive predicate kamuyoritak kor an holds.

text: ku=caranke ka somo ki no ku=hosipi
translation: I went home without complaining.
note: The negative support frame ka somo ki, including the scalar particle ka, is adverbialised as a unit by no. The following predicate ku=hosipi retains its own first-person subject index.

text: iteke ukoyki no tup ne ukosaraye yan
gloss: PROH quarrel ADV two COP share POL
translation: Divide it in two and share it without quarrelling!
note: Shizunai. No adverbialises the prohibitive predicate iteke ukoyki; the polite imperative yan closes the main predicate.

text: orwano ku=cise or ta ku=an kor
translation: Then, while I was in my house, …
note: No pronoun appears; the intransitive existential ku=an indexes its 1SG.S subject. The possessor ku=cise carries the homophonous first-person prefix in the nominal domain.

text: aynu itak k=eramuan wa kusu icen k=eunkeray wa pirka pirka
gloss: Ainu language 1SG.A=understand CONJ because money 1SG.A=receive CONJ good good
translation: Because I had learnt Ainu, I was able to receive money, which was very good.
note: The reduced 1SG.A prefix k= is the form ku= takes before a vowel.

text: kuruma an wa ci=o tek arki=as
translation: There was a car, and we boarded it and came.
note: One clause chain indexes the same exclusive group as A by the prefix ci= on the transitive o and as S by the suffix =as on the intransitive plural arki.

text: wen kamuy a=maketa wa a=rayke ru-we ne
translation: The evil kamuy was defeated and killed.
note: The prefix a= indexes an indefinite transitive subject and defocuses the agent; the patient stays the object of the transitive verbs.

translation: Take pity on me and give me lodging.
note: The fourth-person object i= recurs three times; with a= for A and =an for S, one person distinguishes all three roles, the tripartite pattern of the table above.

text: nep ka eci=kasuy pe an ya
translation: Is there anything I can help you with?
note: The single exponent eci= encodes the 1SG.A→2SG.O combination; no separate ku= or e= appears.

translation: I gave the children sweets.
note: Both non-subject participants are third person and surface as bare noun phrases; only the 1SG.A subject is indexed.

translation: Where have you come from?
place: Nakagawa ex. 140, woman to an adult man
note: The honorific addressee is a single person, yet the fourth-person S suffix =an appears on the plural stem arki.

text: orwano ku=cise or ta ku=an kor
translation: Then, while I was in my house, …
note: The intransitive existential ku=an indexes 1SG.S. The nominal ku=cise carries the homophonous first-person prefix in the possessive domain (glossed POSS here); nominal possession belongs to the chapter on the possessed form.

text: aynu itak k=eramuan wa kusu icen k=eunkeray wa pirka pirka
gloss: Ainu language 1SG.A=understand CONJ because money 1SG.A=receive CONJ good good
translation: Because I had learnt Ainu, I was able to receive money, which was very good.
note: Both transitive verbs show k=, the reduced allomorph of 1SG.A ku= before the vowel-initial stems eramuan and eunkeray.

translation: I go back.
note: Constructed following Ijäs Lesson 2, which uses this verb type to introduce 1SG.S on an intransitive. Ijäs writes ku-hosipi.

translation: Please protect me.
note: The imperative force supplies a second-person subject; both instances of en= mark the 1SG participant as the object/recipient.

text: nep kameaske ene ne yakkay en=kasuy kun pe an cik pirka hike
gloss: what monster thus COP even 1SG.O=help should NMLZ exist if good although
translation: It would be good if any monster were to help me.
note: The prefix en= indexes the speaker as the object of kasuy 'help'; the agent is left to context.

translation: You gave me sweets.
note: Constructed following Ijäs. The translation supplies a 2SG subject from context; in Saru/Chitose the verb shows only en=, which covers both 3→1SG and 2→1SG readings. The phenomenon is attested in Nakagawa 2024: 170, 173 and Satō 2008: 146–147.

text: sinen ne e=oman wa e=ray yakun
translation: If you go alone and die, …
note: Both intransitive verbs carry e= as 2SG.S; no object is present.

translation: You drink water in the morning.
note: Constructed following Ijäs Lesson 3. The prefix e= indexes a 2SG transitive subject; the third-person object wakka receives no index.

text: nep ka eci=kasuy pe an ya
translation: Is there anything I can help you with?
note: The single exponent eci= encodes the 1SG.A→2SG.O combination; no separate ku= or e= appears.

text: kuruma an wa ci=o tek arki=as
translation: There was a car, and we boarded it and came.
note: ci= indexes the exclusive group as A of the transitive o; =as indexes the same group as S of the intransitive plural arki.

translation: although we were given 350 yen, …
place: Kawakami Matsuko, isoytak monologue 2, AA Institute Ainu materials [aa-irc/004#109]
note: The prefix sequence a=un= stacks a fourth-person (indefinite/impersonal) A and a first-plural-exclusive O on a single transitive stem.

translation: Let you and me go too!
note: The hortative construction includes the addressee; the fourth-person S suffix =an appears on the plural stem paye, not the exclusive =as.

translation: When I passed through, they ran beneath me.
place: Chiri Yukie, kamuy yukar document 1, line 12 [yukie-kamuyyukar/001/0#12]
note: In a single divine-narrator clause, ci= indexes the narrator as A of the transitive kus 'pass through', and un= indexes the same singular narrator as possessor of the positional noun corpoke 'below' — the children run beneath the flying owl. Both exclusive exponents serve kamuy-yukar self-reference in the sense of Nakagawa's claim; the verse-medial awa is the conjunctive 'and/then'. Note the possessor is not the subject of the running clause, so no reflexive si- is required.

text: re cup utur ta ar suy an henshû-kaigi or ta unukar=as hi ramma ci=tere wa okay=as
gloss: three month between LOC one again exist editing-meeting place LOC meet=1PL.EXCL.S when always 1PL.EXCL.A=wait CONJ exist.PL=1PL.EXCL.S
translation: We always look forward to the monthly editorial meeting where we gather.
note: Attested from the Ainu Times newspaper. All three exclusive exponents appear in one sentence: ci= indexes the group as A of the transitive tere 'wait'; =as indexes the group as S of the intransitive unukar 'meet' and of the plural existential okay. The Japanese loan henshû-kaigi 'editing meeting' is a single compound noun.

text: sinen ne e=oman wa e=ray yakun
translation: If you go alone and die, ...
note: Both intransitive verbs oman and ray carry e= because the addressee is singular; the role is the same (2SG.S) in both clauses.

text: eci=paye tek nean cise oro eci=epa cik anakne
gloss: 2PL.S=go.PL CONJ that house LOC 2PL.A=reach COND TOP
translation: When you (plural) go and reach that house, ...
note: eci= marks 2PL.S on the intransitive paye in the first clause and 2PL.A on the transitive epa in the second: one form across two distinct syntactic roles within one sentence.

text: nep ka eci=kasuy pe an ya
translation: Is there anything I can help you with?
note: Nakagawa identifies eci= as the 1SG.A→2SG.O portmanteau. No separate ku= or e= appears; the single prefix satisfies both the agent and object indexing requirements of the transitive predicate kasuy.

translation: You go.
note: Constructed from Ijäs Lesson 2. Her pedagogical hyphen notation (e-arpa) is normalized here to the personal-index boundary =.

translation: I give this to you.
note: Constructed from Ijäs Lesson 5, presenting a 1SG-agent-plus-2SG-object construction. The reference paradigm generalises eci= to all four 1→2 number combinations. As a ditransitive, kore indexes the recipient (2nd person) in the object slot; the thing given (tanpe) is a bare noun phrase.

translation: Please protect me.
note: An imperative clause with an implicit second-person subject; both instances of en= index the narrator as the object of 'protect' and 'give' respectively.

text: nep kameaske ene ne yakkay en=kasuy kun pe an cik pirka hike
gloss: what monster thus COP even 1SG.O=help should NMLZ exist if good although
translation: It would be good if any monster were to help me.
note: en= indexes the speaker as the object of kasuy 'help'; the transitive subject is not specified by an overt prefix.

translation: Although they gave us 350 yen, …
note: The prefix a= marks an indefinite fourth-person transitive subject; un= indexes the exclusive first-plural group as the recipient-object of kore 'give'.

translation: She gave you the book.
note: Constructed following Ijäs Lesson 5. With e= read as 2SG.O, the transitive subject is a zero-indexed third person; the same e=kore is equally grammatical with e= as 2SG.A ('you gave the book (to her)').

text: sunku tono mat i=kaopiwki wa i=kore
translation: Help me and take care of me, wife of the lord of Sunku.
note: Both i= prefixes index the oral-narrative protagonist as the object; kaopiwki 'help' and kore 'give' are linked by the conjunctive wa. This clause is an address within the narrative.

translation: I was named Ikuresuye.
note: The possessive a= on the noun rehe 'name' and the transitive-subject a= on the verb réko 'call/name' are independent instances of the fourth-person prefix; i= indexes the oral-narrative protagonist as the object of the naming action.

translation: I saw a raccoon dog.
note: Constructed following Ijäs Lesson 5. The third-person object has no overt index; only the 1SG.A prefix ku= appears on the verb.

translation: Let you and me go too!
note: The addressee-inclusive hortative uses the plural stem paye with =an following as S.

text: rus patek a=mi wa hotke=an pa
translation: We wore only fur and slept.
note: The transitive mi 'wear' takes the prefix a=; the intransitive hotke 'sleep' takes the suffix =an. The plural auxiliary pa follows outside the person index.

text: nenpoka iki=an pa wa siknu=an wa
gloss: somehow do=4.S PL CONJ survive=4.S CONJ
translation: Somehow we managed and survived, and …
note: The plural auxiliary pa follows iki=an, external to the fourth-person S suffix =an.

translation: because we were like siblings …
note: The stem-forming suffix -pa precedes =an; the ordering is reversed relative to the auxiliary pa in the preceding example.

text: wen kamuy a=maketa wa a=rayke ru-we ne
translation: The evil kamuy was defeated and killed.
note: The patient wen kamuy stays in the object role across two transitive predicates; a= supplies an unspecified human agent.

text: kamuy or wa a=epunkine wa kamuy or wa a=kasuy wa
gloss: god place from 4.A=protect CONJ god place from 4.A=help CONJ
translation: being protected by the gods and helped by the gods, …
note: The source phrase kamuy or wa names the agent-like participant; the verbs carry fourth-person A and the patient is not promoted to grammatical subject.

translation: One hears the breeze.
note: Constructed from Ijäs Lesson 7, where a=nu illustrates the generic-human A value; maw 'breeze' fills the object slot.

text: tapan kina a=e p ne toan kina somo a=e p ne
gloss: this plant 4.A=eat NMLZ COP that plant NEG 4.A=eat NMLZ COP
translation: This plant is one that people eat; that plant is one that people do not eat.
note: The head p is the thing eaten; a= supplies the unspecified human eater.

translation: Take pity on me and give me lodging.
note: The repeated i= is fourth-person O, indexing the narrator/protagonist as object and recipient across three transitive predicates.

translation: I was named Ikuresuye.
note: The naming formula combines fourth-person possessive a= on rehe 'name', fourth-person A on the predicate, and fourth-person O i= for the narrator/protagonist.

translation: Where have you come from?
place: Nakagawa ex. 140, woman addressing an adult man
note: A single addressee is indexed by =an on the plural motion stem arki; the plural stem reflects honorific register.

text: ratcitara hosipi=an yakka a=uni un tunasno hosipi=an pe ne kusu
gloss: slowly return=4.S although 4.POSS=home to quickly return=4.S NMLZ COP because
translation: Although I returned slowly, because I was able to return quickly to my home, …
note: A singular narrator uses =an on both intransitive predicates and the possessive prefix a= on uni 'home'; the singular stem hosipi confirms singular-narrator morphology in Saru.

translation: Where have you come from?
place: Nakagawa ex. 140; a woman addressing an adult man
note: The addressee is a single person; the fourth-person S suffix =an appears on the plural motion stem arki rather than the singular ek. The evidential frame ru-we an closes the question.

translation: Please come here.
note: Ijäs pedagogical example. The plural stem arki and the final particle yan form a polite request without deploying fourth-person morphology; it is a parallel addressee-politeness resource, not an instance of the honorific paradigm described above. Ijäs further notes that attaching nispa and katkemat to personal names as titles is not uniformly attested in traditional usage; such address conventions belong to contact and revitalization contexts rather than to the inherited verbal honorification system.

text: ratcitara hosipi=an yakka a=uni un tunasno hosipi=an pe ne kusu
gloss: slowly return=4.S though 4.POSS=home to quickly return=4.S NMLZ COP because
translation: Although I returned slowly, because I was able to return home quickly, …
note: The intransitive stem hosipi takes the fourth-person S suffix =an; a= functions as the narrator's possessive prefix on uni 'home'. Saru and Chitose allow a singular stem with a singular fourth-person narrator.

translation: I was named Ikuresuye.
note: a= on rehe is the narrator's possessive prefix; on reko it is an indefinite-agent prefix (someone named); i= indexes the narrator as the named object. The co-occurrence of fourth-person A as agent-defocuser and fourth-person O as narrator-object on one predicate yields a passive-like Japanese reading (私はイクレスイェと名付けられた).

translation: Take pity on me and give me lodging.
note: The object prefix i= recurs across three transitive predicates, indexing the narrator as the entity pitied, sheltered, and given to. The homophonous detransitivising prefix i- of the antipassive construction is morphologically and functionally distinct.

text: a=ye wa anun katkemat a=nure sekor a=ye acapo hawean kor
gloss: 4.A=say CONJ other lady 4.A=tell QUOT 4.A=say uncle say while
translation: "I will tell it and let another lady hear it," the uncle said.
note: Both predicates of the embedded quotation (a=ye, a=nure) carry fourth-person a= as the reported uncle's self-reference; Nakagawa notes that the actual first-person utterance would have used ku=ye and ku=nure. The narrator's own framing verb a=ye is fourth-person for the separate reason that it is the narrator's story-world first person.

text: aynu itak k=eramuan wa kusu icen k=eunkeray wa pirka pirka
gloss: Ainu language 1SG.A=understand CONJ because money 1SG.A=receive CONJ good good
translation: Because I had learnt Ainu, I was able to receive money, which was very good.
note: ku= reduces to k= before a vowel-initial stem. Both transitive predicates place the A index in the left personal layer.

text: wen kamuy a=maketa wa a=rayke ru-we ne
translation: The evil kamuy was defeated and killed.
