note: The prefix a= indexes an indefinite transitive subject; the patient is not subject-promoted. Both predicates place the 4th-person A prefix in the left personal layer.

text: kuruma an wa ci=o tek arki=as
translation: There was a car, and we boarded it and came.
note: The same exclusive group is A on the transitive o, marked by the prefix ci=, and S on the intransitive plural arki, marked by the suffix =as — both positions filled within a single clause chain.

translation: You too, let us go!
note: The 4th-person S suffix =an attaches to the intransitive plural stem paye. In this inclusive/hortative use the addressee is part of the referent; the hortative particle ro follows the fully inflected verb.

text: nenpoka iki=an pa wa siknu=an wa
gloss: somehow do=4.S PL CONJ live=4.S CONJ
translation: Somehow we managed to do it, and went on living.
note: The outer auxiliary pa follows the fully person-inflected form iki=an. It is outside the right personal layer.

translation: We lived like siblings.
note: The stem-forming plural suffix -pa precedes the person suffix =an, inside the right personal layer. The contrast with the preceding example places stem -pa inside and auxiliary pa outside.

translation: I gave the children sweets.
note: Both non-subject participants are third-person bare noun phrases; only the 1SG.A subject is indexed. The ceiling prevents a separate object index for either recipient or theme.

text: tane iperusuy ka =an sinki ka =an kor
gloss: now hungry even 4.S tired even 4.S while
translation: Now, being hungry and also tired, …
note: The particle ka intervenes between each intransitive stem and its =an, demonstrating the separability that distinguishes =an from the full prefixes and that Nakagawa cites for its clitic characterisation.

translation: I return.
note: Constructed following Ijäs lesson 2. She writes ku-hosipi; this grammar uses = for the personal-index boundary. The form shows 1SG.S on an intransitive stem in the left personal layer.

translation: You drink water in the morning.
note: Constructed following Ijäs lesson 3. The object is third person with no overt index; e= occupies the left personal layer as 2SG.A. She writes e-ku.

text: kuruma an wa ci=o tek arki=as
translation: There was a car, and we boarded it and came.
note: The intransitive arki is the plural suppletive of ek 'come'; it co-occurs with the 1PL.EXCL S suffix =as. The same group is indexed as A on the transitive o 'board' by the prefix ci=.

translation: We walk.
note: Constructed teaching form from Ijäs L9; illustrates outer pa following the 1PL.EXCL S affix on an intransitive verb in Saru-type dialects.

text: nenpoka iki=an pa wa siknu=an wa
gloss: somehow do=4.S PL CONJ live=4.S CONJ
translation: Somehow we managed and survived, and…
note: Outer pa follows the fourth-person S suffix =an.

translation: We were like siblings.
note: Stem-forming -pa precedes the fourth-person S suffix =an, confirming root-level attachment.

text: rus patek a=mi wa hotke=an pa
translation: We wore only furs and slept.
place: Kawakami Matsuko, ILCAA Ainu materials, uwepeker 7
note: Fourth-person transitive a=mi (wear) followed by intransitive hotke=an (sleep); outer pa follows the person-inflected form of the second predicate.

translation: Let's go together, you and I.
note: The plural suppletive paye co-occurs with =an; the reference is inherently multiple (speaker + addressee).

translation: Where have you come from?
place: Nakagawa ex. 140, woman addressing an adult man
note: One person is addressed; the fourth-person S suffix =an appears on the plural suppletive stem arki.

translation: When we slept first, …
note: Shizunai ci follows the fourth-person S suffix =an in the outer-plural slot, parallel to Saru outer pa.

translation: You people must have gone too.
note: The Sakhalin plural element -hci/-hcin appears with a second-person plural subject, not a third-person one, undermining its analysis as third-person plural agreement. Hokkaido dialects lack productive =hci; the corresponding function is served by outer pa (Saru/Chitose/Ishikari) or outer ci (Shizunai).

text: mean cuk ne pe merayke=an ka somo ki no
gloss: be.cold autumn COP thing feel.cold=4.S FOC NEG do ADV
translation: It was a cold autumn, but I did not feel cold.
note: The ambient predicate mean 'be cold (of weather)' is zero-place and indexes no participant. The experiential predicate merayke 'feel cold' is one-place; its affected experiencer carries the fourth-person S suffix =an, the same form an agentive fourth-person subject would carry.

text: rir-tursere=an kor mom=an ru-we ene an hi ne hine
gloss: wave-roll=4.S while flow=4.S track-POSS thus exist NMLZ COP CONJ
kana: rittursere=an kor mom=an ruwe ene an hi ne hine
translation: I was rolled by the waves and drifted along, and so …
note: Surface rittursere is segmented as rir-tursere following Nakagawa's analysis of the incorporated wave element. Both patientive intransitives carry =an, not the object form i=.

text: Sapporo or un ku=arpa ka somo ki; ku=sesek humi!
gloss: Sapporo ALLAT LOC 1SG=go also NEG COP; 1SG=be.hot INTERJ!
translation: I won't go to Sapporo; I'm hot!
note: A 1SG agentive intransitive (arpa, controllable 'go') and a 1SG experiential intransitive (sesek, uncontrollable 'be hot') both index the subject with the same ku=. The identical person form is exactly what the claim above predicts: the 1SG row does not distinguish control.

text: sinrit or ta arpa=an ka somo ki ruwe ne
gloss: ancestors place LOC go=4.S FOC NEG do INFR COP
translation: I did not go to my ancestors.
place: 貝澤とぅるしの口演 ウエペケㇾ「アオナハ ウェンカムイ オロワ アウㇰ」[biratori/004/004#79]
note: Attested uwepeker by Kaizawa Turushino (Biratori 1969). The agentive motion verb arpa 'go' carries the fourth-person S suffix =an — the narrator-protagonist convention of uwepeker narration — exactly the S-form the experiential merayke and patientive rittursere examples above carry. No overt subject NP appears; sinrit or ta 'to (the place of) the ancestors' is the goal phrase, and the clause is negated by the ka somo ki frame.

text: tane anak apto as patek ki ruwe ne
gloss: now TOP rain fall only do INFR COP
translation: Now it only rains.
note: The weather predicate apto as 'rain falls' is zero-place: the verb as carries no person index. The noun apto 'rain' is an overt NP but does not trigger S-indexing. patek 'only' scopes over the predicate; ki 'do/be the case' is the light-verb support; ruwe ne is the inferential evidential closing frame.

text: kuruma an wa ci=o tek arki=as
translation: There was a car, and we boarded it and came.
note: The exclusive group is marked as A by the prefix ci= on the transitive o 'board' and as S by the suffix =as on the intransitive plural arki 'come'; the object counterpart un= is not triggered in this chain.

translation: Take pity on me and give me lodging.
note: The fourth-person O prefix i= indexes the narrative protagonist three times; with a= for A and =an for S, all three roles are kept formally distinct within the same paradigm row.

text: nep ka eci=kasuy pe an ya
translation: Is there anything I can help you with?
note: The single prefix eci= encodes 1SG.A acting on 2SG.O; no separate first- and second-person indexes co-occur. The form is homophonous with the plain 2PL index in A, S, and O.

translation: Where have you come from?
place: Nakagawa ex. 140, woman addressing an adult man
note: The addressee is a single person, yet the fourth-person S suffix =an selects the plural stem arki. The plural signals honorific elevation rather than number of referents.

text: wen kamuy a=maketa wa a=rayke ru-we ne
translation: The evil kamuy was defeated and killed.
note: The fourth-person prefix a= fills the A position and defocuses the agent; the lexical patient remains the object of both transitive verbs. The passive-flavoured English translation reflects agent-defocusing, not a voice alternation in the Ainu.

translation: The dog sees the fish.
note: Constructed following Ijäs's pedagogical model (L2–L3); both arguments are third person and no personal index appears on the verb. Nakagawa's analysis requires no third-person affix here; Satō's analysis posits a zero affix for each third-person role.

translation: I gave the children sweets.
note: The 1SG.A subject is indexed; both non-subject participants are third person and appear as bare noun phrases with no object index. Satō's analysis posits a zero third-person object for the recipient; Nakagawa's analysis requires no zero.

translation: The boy caught fish yesterday.
note: Ijäs Lesson 3 introduces the two-argument transitive frame with constructed sentences of this type; the third-person subject and object are segmentally unmarked.

translation: The girl played.
Mother made the girl play.
note: The base subject matkaci ‘girl’ is the object of the derived causative.

translation: He cut a standing tree with a sword.
note: The instrument emus ‘sword’ is the applied object licensed by e-, which raises tuye ‘cut’ from a two-place to a three-place verb.

text: i-ri=an wa or-o wa sini=an na
gloss: ANTIP-skin=4.S CONJ place-POSS from rest=4.S FIN
translation: I will skin the catch and then rest.
place: Shizunai Board of Education 1991–1995, O0130054_6; Handbook ex. 24b
note: The intransitive S suffix =an shows that i-ri ‘do skinning’ is intransitive; the patient ‘catch’ is left out of the argument frame.

text: nea nispa utar u-koyki kor oka siri a=nukar
gloss: that rich.man PL RECP-attack while exist.PL appearance 4.A=see
translation: I saw those rich men fighting each other.

text: aynu kam ka upas ka ta ci-cari
gloss: human flesh even snow even LOC RES-scatter
translation: Human flesh and snow too lay scattered on the ground.
A person was bitten by a dog.
note: The dog appears in an or wa ‘from’ phrase; the indefinite transitive subject a= stays on the verb and the patient aynu ‘person’ stays the object.

text: pet or ta ran=an wa suy cep-koyki=an rok ayne
gloss: river place LOC descend.SG=4.S CONJ again fish-catch=4.S PL.PRF then
translation: I went down to the river and caught fish again, and at last …
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker 13; ILCAA materials aa-irc/016#14
note: The intransitive suffix =an on cep-koyki proves that the incorporated cep ‘fish’ has detransitivized koyki ‘catch’; the whole noun-verb sequence is one word.

translation: We keep swaying our hearts afar over various rumours.
literal: we sway our hearts about ourselves far over various rumours
place: after Chiri 1936: 169; Shibatani ex. 131 / Bugaeva ex. 1
note: One transitive root suy-pa ‘sway (PL)’ carries an incorporated object, an adverbial, an outer reflexive proper, an inner reflexive-possessive si- before ram ‘heart’, and two applicatives; the whole reads ‘we wonder about various rumours’.

translation: The girl played.
Mother made the girl play.
note: The base intransitive subject matkaci becomes the causee object; hapo is the new causer subject. The -te allomorph follows the consonant-final stem sinot.

translation: Mother made me play.
note: The first-person argument shifts from the subjective index ku= to the objective en=, diagnosing the arity increase from vi to vt.

text: un=ipe-re wa i=kore kur un=osura noyne sioran
translation: The person who had fed us then abandoned us, it seemed.
place: Hamada Takashi, 'pon cape asiknep'; Ainu Times no. 24, p. 3 (ainu-times/024/3#3), extract
note: un= is 1PL.EXCL object (us); ipe-re shows -re after the vowel-final stem ipe 'eat a meal'. The verb heads a relative clause (kur un=ipe-re 'the person who fed us'). sioran = siri + an, visual-evidential existential.

text: i=teke uk hine i=ahun-te ruwe ne akus
translation: He took my hand and brought me inside.
note: ahun-te with a volitional human causee, cross-referenced by the logophoric 4th-person prefix i=. Contrast ahun-ke (Nakagawa ex. 196), used when the causee is non-volitional cargo. The -te allomorph follows the consonant-final stem ahun.

translation: I went down.
note: Intransitive base; the fourth-person S suffix =an confirms intransitive status.

translation: I lowered it.
note: Transitive counterpart of ran via the motion-verb forming suffix -ke. The 1SG.A prefix ku= marks the verb as transitive. The suffix -ke here selects non-agentive, inanimate objects; agentive human causees take the productive -te (compare Nakagawa 2024: 202–203, exx. 196–197 on ahun-ke vs ahun-te).

translation: I went up.
note: Intransitive base; =an is the fourth-person S suffix.

translation: I raised it.
note: Transitive counterpart via -ka. The 1SG.A prefix ku= marks transitive status.

translation: I pretended not to know about it.
note: Satō ex. 6, approximately p. 36 (the OCR of Satō 2007 carries no per-page running heads; the location is approximate within the pp. 31–39 article). The APPL prefix ko- supplies the semantic object (the thing one pretends not to know); si- is the reflexive object of the causativized stem, hence REFL; -ka is the causative suffix. The following wa k=an reports the resulting state.

translation: I called someone.
note: The transitivizer -kar adds an object slot to the intransitive hotuye 'shout'. The 1SG.A prefix ku= marks the derived verb as transitive.

translation: I play.
Mother made me play.
note: The base subject ku= (1SG.A) reappears as the causee en= (1SG.O) of the causative; hapo 'mother' is the new causer, indexed by zero (third-person A is not marked).

translation: I made you cut the grapevines.
note: Attested form in context: ki kusu hat punkar a=e=tuy-e-re wa. The theme 'grapevines' (hat punkar) is a bare NP with no index on the verb; only the causer and causee are cross-referenced.

translation: I caused you to give (something to someone).
note: The form kor-e-re 'cause to give' (have-CAUS-CAUS) is attested in Bugaeva (2014: 142–143); this constructed illustration shows the person-indexing pattern: the outer causer takes a= (fourth person, narrative first person) and the immediate causee-giver takes e= (2SG.O), while the recipient and the theme given have no index on the verb.

text: a=omarere akusu sonno ka oripak pe ne kusu
gloss: 4.A=put.in-CAUS-CAUS CONJ really FOC be.polite NMLZ COP because
translation: I had [her] put [it] away, and since she is truly a courteous person —
place: Kaizawa Turushino, uwepeker 'Kikipo Cicipor Ukoysoytak Hi Anu' [biratori/005/008#82]
note: a=omarere is the productive double causative oma 'be inside' → omare 'put X in Y' → omare-re 'cause/have someone put X in Y'. The outer causer is a= (fourth person, narrative first person); no other person index appears on the verb. akusu is the discovery linker ('upon which'); the clause is causal (kusu 'because').

text: tuyma no new ka a=korar ka korayniwkes
gloss: far even COMP also 4=marry.off also feel.cannot.do
translation: I felt I couldn't have her married off far away.
place: Biratori oral lit., 木村きみ narration
note: korar (kor-ar, 'marry off') is the indefinite causative: the causer a= (4th-person, logophoric, referring to the narrator) is indexed on the verb, but the causee — the woman married off — is neither expressed nor cross-referenced, recoverable only from discourse. This is the structural signature of -ar.

translation: I had it heard / I reported (it) to [them].
place: 貝澤 とぅるしの narration (biratori/004/002#80)
note: nuyar (nu-yar) keeps the two-place frame of nu 'hear something': the causer a= (4th-person, logophoric) is indexed on the verb, while the recipient of the message is supplied by the eun adjunct and the causee (the hearer) is neither expressed nor cross-referenced — the structural signature of the indefinite causative.

text: a=en=kopisi p anakne opitta ku=ye wa ku=nu-yar
translation: Everything I was asked I told in full — I made it all known.
note: ku=nu-yar retains the two-place transitivity of nu 'hear something'; the content made known is the sole object and no causee argument is present.

translation: Let's have (them) eat.
note: After Tamura 2000[1988]: 214. The intransitive S suffix =an on ipe-yar confirms that the derived verb remains intransitive; the eating party is implied by context but not indexed on the verb.

text: hokure a=macihi oripakno pirkano suke wa ipeyar.
gloss: come.on 4.A=poss.wife humbly well cook CONJ eat-CAUS
translation: Quickly, my wife — cook properly and neatly, and feed [them].
place: 平賀さだも, uwepeker ‘ウラユシウㇺㇰ’ [biratori/010/003#145]
note: One of the ~2 attested ipeyar tokens. ipe-yar carries no person index: the party fed (the guest being hosted) is neither expressed nor cross-referenced on the verb, recoverable only from the hospitality context. The wife, who is to prepare the meal, is named as a=macihi (possessive fourth-person indexing) but is likewise not cross-referenced by the verb — the structural signature of the indefinite causative in a permissive-polite register.

translation: He cut a standing tree with a sword.
note: The instrument emus 'sword' is the applied object promoted by e-; tuye 'cut' moves from a two-place transitive to a three-place ditransitive.

translation: I flew up toward the sky.
note: ko- promotes the goal kanto kotor 'sky surface' to object position; hopuni 'fly up (vi)' becomes ko-hopuni 'fly up toward (vt)'.

translation: War came to the village.
note: o- applied object = a place (village, contextually supplied); o- is paraphrasable by ta/un 'to (a place)'.

translation: War came to [my] sister.
note: ko- applied object = a person (the sister); ko- is required for animate goals.

translation: I chopped it together with the weeds, together with the soil, and then …
note: mun 'weeds' and toy 'earth' are incorporated applied objects with comitative reading; the actual patient (the monster's flesh) is contextually implicit.

translation: He cut the standing tree with a sword.
note: The instrument emus 'sword' is the applied object licensed by e-, which raises tuye from a two-place to a three-place verb. Both objects — tree and sword — are core arguments marked by person affixes in a three-person frame.

translation: One can walk on one's own feet.
note: The fourth-person prefix a= marks both the possessed noun (a=kemaha 'one's foot/leg') and the agent of the derived transitive (a=e-apkas 'one walks by means of'). The foot is the instrument applied object, paraphrasable as kemaha ani apkas.

translation: go to dig lily-bulbs
note: Verbal phrase. The applied object turepta encodes the purpose of the motion, paraphrasable as turepta kusu arpa 'go for the purpose of digging lily-bulbs'. Both Manner and Path roles (each 2%) derive exclusively from intransitive bases.

translation: to be at the lake's edge
note: The place noun to teksama 'lake edge' is the locative applied object; paraphrasable as to teksama ta an 'be at the lake's edge'. The base an 'be, exist' is intransitive; e- makes it transitive with the location as its sole object.

translation: You had better run under me.
note: The postpositional noun corpokke 'under' carries the fourth-person object prefix i= — the speaker is a character quoted inside a folktale, Nakagawa's quotation-speaker use of the fourth person — yielding i=corpokke 'under me' as the path applied object. The outer second-person agent prefix e= precedes the applicative e- and the root hoyupu 'run' in the single verb word e=e-hoyupu.

translation: worry about something
note: The applied object nep 'what/something' is the content of the worry. No adpositional paraphrase exists; e- is the sole grammatical strategy for licensing this object.

text: tokaci wa ek pewre kur monrayke e-i-kasuy
gloss: Tokachi from come young man work APPL-ANTIP-help
translation: A young man who came from Tokachi helped with the work.
note: The antipassive i- absorbs the unspecified beneficiaries of kasuy 'help'; e- then re-applicativizes the resulting intransitive, taking monrayke 'work' as the Content applied object. The relative clause tokaci wa ek pewre kur 'young man who came from Tokachi' modifies the subject.

translation: I flew up toward the sky.
note: Base hopuni 'fly up' is intransitive; ko-hopuni is transitive with the Goal kanto kotor 'sky-vicinity' as applied object. The fourth-person A prefix a= marks the transitive subject.

translation: I returned to my castle.
note: The Goal applied object is a=kor casi 'my castle'; base hosipi 'return home' is intransitive, ko-hosipi transitive.

text: petkorkamuy kamuy katkemat a=ko-yay-irayke hi a=ye a
translation: saying that one gave thanks to the river goddess
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker 9; ILCAA materials aa-irc/009#289
note: The ko- applied object is petkorkamuy kamuy katkemat 'the river-deity divine woman'; yay-irayke 'show gratitude (reflexive of irayke)' is the base from which ko- derives the Addressee-licensed transitive.

translation: I chopped it up together with garbage, then together with earth, and …
note: The comitative applied objects mun 'garbage' and toy 'earth' are incorporated between the person prefix and ko-; each incorporated form is transitive (4.A prefix a=), confirming the arity increase from the intransitive base tata.

translation: War came to my village.
note: o- applied object is a place noun (the village, contextually understood); o-ek is transitive.

translation: War came against my sister.
note: ko- applied object is a person (the sister, contextually understood); ko-ek is transitive.

translation: I am angry at (someone).
note: ko- applicativizes i-ruska 'be angry (intransitive after antipassive)', adding a person-goal as the new object; 1SG.A prefix ku= confirms transitivity. See also the antipassive chapter.

translation: I narrate to (someone) about (something).
note: e- adds the content/topic (first applied object), ko- adds the addressee/listener (second applied object); with the 1SG.A prefix ku= and both applied objects as free NPs, the verb is three-place.

translation: War came to [the village].
note: The place goal (the village, contextually implicit) is the applied object licensed by o-; ek 'come' shifts from intransitive to transitive. The contrast is Nakagawa ex. 193, tumi ko-ek 'war came to [one's] sister', where the animate goal requires ko-.

translation: I went to the river.
note: The place goal pet 'river' is a bare noun in direct-object position — no postposition — because o- has licensed it as a core object. The postpositional paraphrase is pet ta arpa or pet or un arpa. The prefixal 1SG.A index ku= proves the derived transitivity; compare the intransitive base ku=arpa-as (with suffixal S =as), where no place object is licensed.

text: e=oarpa kuni p ne kusu taptap a=e=kar na
gloss: 2SG.A=APPL-go PURP NMLZ COP CONJ like.this 4.A=2SG.O=do FIN
translation: Since you are going, I shall do thus and so for you.
place: 平賀さだも, uwepeker ‘ケソランㇷ゚ カムイ イレス’ [biratori/007/002#361]
note: The prefixal 2SG.A index e= on oarpa is direct attested evidence for the derived transitivity of o-arpa. The place goal is not overtly expressed: oarpa is used as the lexicalized transitive 'go (to the place in question)', the destination being recoverable from the discourse (the addressee is being equipped for departure). The main clause a=e=kar shows the 4th-person logophoric agent preceding the 2SG object index. Contrast the next example, where the goal kamuy or is overt.

text: kamuy or oarpa hine ora nea menoko a=kor wa
gloss: god place APPL-go CONJ CONJ DEM woman 4.A=have CONJ
translation: He went to the place of the kamuy (heaven), and then took that (human) woman as his wife.
note: The place goal kamuy or 'the place of the kamuy' is the applied object licensed by o- on arpa; the postposition or co-occurs with the applicative, confirming that o- promotes the locative adjunct to core-object status. The fourth-person agent a= on kor marks an unspecified agent in the narrative.

translation: and put [them] into that [water] …
place: Kanzaki Masayoshi, 'Nisew', Ainu Times no. 66, line 19
note: The locative demonstrative wor 'there/that place' is the direct object of the verb o 'put into'; the fourth-person transitive agent a= marks an unspecified agent. The context is extracting bitterness from plant ingredients by submerging them in water. The verb root o here contrasts with the applicative prefix o-, which would derive a new transitive from an intransitive base.

translation: tell stories to someone about something
note: e- contributes the Content participant; ko- contributes the Addressee. Both applied objects are unmarked bare NPs cross-referenced by a single O-index. Nakagawa 2024: 211 gives e-yay-e-isoytak, with reflexive yay- filling the ko-slot.

translation: We keep wondering about various rumours.
literal: we sway our hearts afar and toward ourselves over various rumours
place: after Chiri 1936: 169; Shibatani ex. 131 / Bugaeva ex. 1
note: Root suy-pa 'sway (PL)' carries e- and ko- (both applicative), yay- and si- (both reflexive), the adverbial tuyma 'far', and the incorporated object ram 'heart'. The valency and template bookkeeping in Xr:valency-voice-overview holds at every step.

translation: eat meagre meals
note: ipe 'food' is incorporated as the e-object (Content); yay- fills the ko-object slot (Addressee = reflexive self). The resulting verb is transitive with a single indexed object.

translation: chopping along with the grass, chopping along with the soil, and then …
note: mun 'grass/weeds' and toy 'soil' are comitative objects first promoted by ko-, then incorporated. The implied patient (the demon's flesh) is cross-referenced by a=. Each verb-word is the output of the applicative-then-incorporation feeding sequence.

translation: I bit the fish together with its bones.
note: Stage 1: pone 'bone' is an oblique held by the comitative postposition tura 'with'. It cannot incorporate.

translation: I bit the fish together with its bones.
note: Stage 2: ko- promotes pone to core object, dropping tura; pone is now an unmarked argument of the three-place verb.

translation: I bone-bit the fish.
note: Stage 3: pone incorporates into the verb word, landing outside ko- but inside the person index a=. The Mirror Principle is satisfied: ko- (morphologically inner, syntactically prior) sits between pone (morphologically outer, syntactically later) and the root kuykuy.

translation: the sword with which [someone] cut the standing tree
note: The head noun emus 'sword' is interpreted as the e-object (instrument) of the relative clause. A null gap occupies the applied-object position within the clause; emus appears outside as the head. The construction is possible because e- has promoted emus from the Instrument oblique tier to the Direct Object tier.

text: tokaci wa ek pewre kur monrayke e-i-kasuy
gloss: Tokachi from come young man work APPL-ANTIP-help
translation: A young man from Tokachi helped with the work.
note: i-kasuy 'do helping' (antipassive, intransitive) is re-applicativized by e- (purpose 'with work'); monrayke 'work' becomes the applied e-object, restoring transitivity. This e-object is accessible to incorporation or relativization via the standard feeding logic.

text: i-ri=an wa or-o wa sini=an na
gloss: ANTIP-skin=4.S CONJ place-POSS from rest=4.S FIN
translation: I will skin the catch and then rest.
place: Shizunai Board of Education 1991–1995, O0130054_6; Handbook ex. 24b
note: The intransitive suffix =an on i-ri confirms that the antipassive has intransitivized ri 'skin sth'; the Patient — the catch — is outside the argument frame. Both clause-final =an tokens carry fourth-person S reference.

text: ene wa poka a=reka hi ka isam menoko i-huraye kor an na
gloss: thus CONJ even 4.A=praise NMLZ even not.exist woman ANTIP-wash while exist FIN
translation: A woman of incomparable beauty was doing the laundry.
note: The antipassive i-huraye 'do the washing' is intransitive; the specific object (laundry) is inferrable from context but suppressed from the argument frame. The embedding clause ene wa poka a=reka hi ka isam means literally 'there is no way to praise her' — the conventional formula for incomparable beauty.

translation: Since I had heard (the story) thus, in this very way,
note: Attested narrative evidence for the intransitive diagnostic: the antipassive i-nu 'hear, listen' takes the suffixal fourth-person S index =an (logophoric first-person here), not a prefixal A index — the Patient of the hearing is left out of the argument frame and recoverable only from discourse. The causal kusu links the heard report to the following clause.

text: ipe=as kaki, iku=as ka ki wa
gloss: eat=1PL.EXCL.S also ANTIP-drink=1PL.EXCL.S also do CONJ
translation: We ate and also drank.
place: 浜田 隆史, 'te ta anakne...', Ainu Times no. 40 (ainu-times/040/0#16)
note: The suffix =as (1PL.EXCL.S) on both ipe and i-ku confirms intransitive status. i-ku is the antipassive of ku 'drink', here in its lexicalized 'drink (alcohol)' sense. The parallel structure ipe=as … iku=as shows both antipassive derivatives taking the same intransitive S suffix in a single coordinated clause.

text: tokaci wa ek pewre kur monrayke e-i-kasuy
gloss: Tokachi from come young man matter APPL-ANTIP-help
translation: A young man who came from Tokachi helped with the work.
note: e-i-kasuy combines the content applicative e- (+1) with the antipassive i- (−1), netting zero arity change relative to the base kasuy 'help sb'. The applied object monrayke 'matter, work' specifies what the helping is directed at, while the human Patient-person remains suppressed and unindexed.

text: asinuma ka nusa sam ta yay-karkarse-re=an kor paraparak
gloss: 1SG.EMPH even altar beside LOC REFL-roll-CAUS=4.S CONJ wail
kana: asinuma ka nusa sam ta yaykarkarsere=an kor paraparak
translation: I too rolled about by the altar, wailing.
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker 民話11; ILCAA materials aa-irc/013#377
note: yay-karkarse-re 'roll oneself / roll about': yay- fills the object slot of karkarse-re 'cause to roll (something)'; the fourth-person S suffix =an on the derived intransitive confirms the detransitivization.

text: aynu ne yay-kar wa kamuy ko-sunke wa an ru-we ne
gloss: human COP REFL-make CONJ deity APPL-lie CONJ exist track-POSS COP
translation: He had taken on human form and was deceiving the deity.
place: Nakagawa corpus K8007292UP; Bugaeva & Kobayashi ex. 4b
note: yay-kar 'transform oneself': yay- fills the object slot of kar 'make', turning the transitive 'make X into Y' into an intransitive of self-directed change. an in an ruwe ne is the existential/copular verb 'be (in that state)', not a person suffix.

text: sunku anakne peka ta si-pusu wa mom pe ne
gloss: spruce TOP surface LOC ANTIC-float CONJ drift thing COP
translation: Spruce floats on the water and drifts — that is its nature.
place: Satō ex. 4; narrator 白沢ナベ, Chitose
note: si-pusu 'float of itself': buoyancy is a property of the wood, not a directed self-act. The spruce has no volition, showing that the si-/yay- distinction is not intentional vs unintentional but direct vs indirect involvement. The contrast with yay-pusu 'pop up by swimming' is Satō's primary minimal pair.

translation: I was pretending to know nothing about it.
note: ko- promotes the object-of-pretence to applied object; si- supplies the subject-coreferent object of the causativized stative, hence REFL: the unknowing-state depends on others' belief; -ka causativizes the resulting stative. ki=an (do=4.S) marks the ongoing activity as intransitive, confirming the final vi status of the complex.

text: i=nukar rok pe si-etaye wa isam
translation: On seeing me, it withdrew and was gone.
place: Oda Suteno, reyep kamuy; ILCAA materials aa-irc/027#108
note: si-etaye: withdrawal triggered by the act of being seen — an externally caused, indirect involvement of the subject in its own motion. Its yay- counterpart yay-etaye 'draw oneself out' involves no external trigger.

text: petkorkamuy kamuy katkemat a=ko-yay-irayke hi a=ye a a=ye a kor
gloss: river.deity deity woman 4.A=APPL-REFL-be.grateful NMLZ 4.A=say PFV 4.A=say PFV CONJ
kana: petkorkamuy kamuy katkemat a=koyayrayke hi a=ye a a=ye a kor
translation: Again and again giving thanks to the river-deity woman, as she was telling it …
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker 民話9; ILCAA materials aa-irc/009#289
note: Surface koyayrayke: the phonological sequence yay-irayke surfaces as yayrayke at the morpheme boundary (dialectal and orthographic variants yayirayke ~ yairayke reflect the same junction). ko- = addressee applicative; yay- = reflexive on the inner object slot.

text: sunku anakne peka ta si-pusu wa mom pe ne
gloss: Ezo.pine TOP surface LOC ANTIC-float.up CONJ flow NMLZ COP
translation: The Ezo pine floats up to the water surface and flows along by itself.
note: si-pusu 'float up spontaneously' has no agentive subject; yay-pusu would require one. The absence of an A-set prefix confirms the intransitive output.

text: i=nukar rok pe si-etaye wa isam
translation: The thing that had caught sight of me withdrew and was gone.
note: si-etaye 'withdraw, pull back' contrasts with yay-etaye 'draw oneself outward'; the withdrawal here is triggered by the narrator's presence, the canonical indirect-reflexive context. The fourth-person object prefix i= on nukar references the narrator logophorically.

text: ci=kus kor si-corpok un inkar=as ko
translation: While passing through, I gazed down below.
place: Chiri Yukie, kamuy yukar document 1, line 4 [yukie-kamuyyukar/001/0#4]
note: si- prefixes the locative positional noun corpok 'below' and supplies the subject-coreferent possessor ('my own beneath') to it, exactly the locative reflexive-possessive configuration of Satō's claim. The narrator (the owl goddess) is the sole referent indexed by the exclusive forms. Verse-final ko is the song-variant of conjunctive kor (final -r dropped in verse, Tamura s.v. ko), linking onward to the next verse.

translation: I was pretending not to know about it.
note: ko- is the applicative referencing what the subject ostensibly does not know; si- fills the object slot of the causativized stem with a subject-coreferent 'self', hence REFL; -ka is the direct-causative suffix. Together si-ranpewtek-ka yields the pretend-to reading. The final k=an is a contracted progressive existential (kor an).

translation: I lay down, stretching myself out.
note: The verb form yay-si-turi-re is attested in Nakagawa (2024: 189) to demonstrate the yay-outer / si-inner ordering; the surrounding clause is constructed. The fourth-person S suffix =an confirms that si-turi-re is intransitive. Both prefixes keep the reflexive gloss: an autocausative reading of the inner si- is conceivable but not asserted by Nakagawa's analysis.

text: nea nispa utar u-koyki kor oka sir-i a=nukar
gloss: DEM chief ASS RECP-fight CONJ exist.PL appearance-POSS 4.A=see
translation: I saw the chiefs fighting each other.
note: Bugaeva & Kobayashi 2022 ex. 11a. u-koyki is intransitive and takes no A-prefix; the clause sir-i a=nukar ('the appearance of which was seen') frames the event as a witnessed scene.

translation: teach each other
note: Indirect reciprocal: the Addressee of e-pakasnu 'teach sb sth' is reciprocalized; the Theme content remains as the surviving object. The epenthetic glide w surfaces between u- and the vowel-initial applicative e-.

text: Iskar emko ta u-tures-kor okkaypo okay pe
gloss: Ishikari upper LOC RECP-sibling-have young.man exist.PL NMLZ
translation: A young man with a sister, up the Ishikari River.
note: Nakagawa ex. 164. The singular okkaypo 'young man' is the surface subject, yet u-tures-kor carries u- because having a sibling is an inherently two-party relation. The plural existential okay reflects the broader story context.

translation: listening to each other's stories, living on
note: Excerpt from Bugaeva & Kobayashi 2022 ex. 13. In u-oruspe-nu, u- is the reciprocal possessor of incorporated oruspe ‘story’. The resulting predicate is intransitive and takes the fourth-person S suffix =an.

translation: Oh, how obedient they are indeed!
note: Bugaeva segments u-itak-nu as RECP-word-listen. The predicate expresses obedience through the conventional meaning ‘heed one another’s words’.

translation: the book containing the New Covenant
note: Historical spelling: Ashiri Aeuitaknup Oma Kambi. Tajima analyzes the title word as a=e-u-itak-nu-p. The reciprocal possessive constituent is [u-itak], incorporated into nu; -p nominalizes the complex predicate.

translation: make them fight each other
note: Object-oriented causativized reciprocal. Arity: koyki (2) + u- (−1) = 1 (vi); then u-koyki (1) + -re (+1) = 2 (vt). After Bugaeva & Kobayashi 2022 §4.2.1.

text: matkaci a=maci turano a=u-ko-kor hine oka=an wa
translation: Together with my wife, I had a daughter, and we went on living.
note: Nakagawa ex. 218. a=u-ko-kor is transitive because sociative uko- preserves the base verb kor's arity: kor has arity 2, and uko- has net arity change 0. The 4.A prefix a= (narrative first person) on the verb confirms this. Plain reciprocal u-kor 'marry each other' is intransitive because u- reduces arity from 2 to 1 and takes =an.

translation: All the spirits rejoiced together.
note: Bugaeva & Kobayashi 2022 ex. 34. uko- (= u- + ko-) combines with the reflexive yay-; the whole form is intransitive (arity: uko- = 0, then yay- = −1).

text: aynu kam ka upas ka ta ci-cari kamuyasi kam ka ci-cari kor
gloss: human flesh even snow even LOC RES-scatter evil.spirit flesh even RES-scatter while
translation: Human flesh and snow lay scattered on the ground; the evil spirit's flesh too lay scattered, and …
note: Third-person subjects are morphologically zero; the intransitive form ci-cari takes no object. Both clauses show the affected entity (flesh, snow) as sole argument — the defining property of the ci- middle.

translation: the place where blood lay scattered
note: The possessed-form variant ci-car-i in a nominalised relative clause; ci-cari and ci-car-i are morphological doublets, the latter appearing in nominalised or attributive positions.

text: he-puni=an kor somo a=nu wa kusu
translation: When [I] raised my head, [the sound] could no longer be heard.
note: The intransitive suffix =an on he-puni confirms that the body-region prefix he- has reduced the arity of puni 'lift' by one; the head-referent fills the object slot. The co-occurring a=nu is the indefinite-agent construction treated below.

translation: [I] lifted my mother's head, and then —
note: The affiliative e- 'head of' (arity 0, not the applicative e-) keeps puni transitive; the object argument a=unuhu 'mother' is the entity whose head is being raised. Contrast the intransitive he-puni above, where the subject's own head is raised.

translation: A person was bitten by a dog.
note: The dog appears in the or wa 'from' demoted-agent phrase; the indefinite transitive prefix a= occupies the A slot; the patient aynu 'person' remains the grammatical object.

text: nikekke wenkur sekor aynu or wa a=reko kor an yakka
gloss: wood-break poor.person QUOT people place from 4.A=call while exist.SG even.though
translation: Even though [he] was called 'the wood-breaking pauper' by people —
note: a=reko 'the indefinite agent calls'; aynu or wa provides the demoted agent. The object (the called person) is not cross-referenced here because it is zero-marked third person.

translation: [He] was greatly loved by a respected man.
note: The Ishikari variant an= replaces a= as the indefinite transitive prefix; the construction is otherwise identical. The patient is zero-marked (third person, object).

text: huci oro wa a=en=omap hi ku=ki rusuy
translation: I want to be loved by grandmother.
note: The patient is cross-referenced as object (en= '1SG.O') on the verb, and the nominalized clause hi is required by the desiderative. A construction with a true passive subject would take subjective marking and bare rusuy without hi — that form is ungrammatical. Satō describes the overall structure as 'a very peculiar passive' (受け身文としては極めて特殊な構造, Satō 2008: 205).

translation: Someone digs lily bulbs.
note: Transitive: a= marks an indefinite 4th-person agent; pukusa 'lily bulb' is a free NP object external to the verb.

translation: Someone digs lily bulbs.
note: After object incorporation the intransitive S suffix =an replaces the transitive A prefix a=. The noun pukusa is now inside the verb word and can no longer appear as an external NP.

text: pet or ta ran=an wa suy cep-koyki=an rok ayne
gloss: river place LOC descend.SG=4.S CONJ again fish-catch=4.S PL.PRF then
translation: I went down to the river and caught fish again, and at last …
note: The 4.S suffix =an on cep-koyki is the diagnostic: after O-NI the compound is intransitive. The compound cep-koyki 'fish-catch' occurs 144 times in the Hokkaido corpus (rank 848).

text: toy ku=hok wa or-o ta ku=cise-kar wa k=an ruwe ne wa
gloss: land 1SG.A=buy CONJ place-POSS LOC 1SG.S=house-build CONJ 1SG.S=exist track-POSS COP CONJ
translation: I bought land, built a house there, and lived on.
note: ku=cise-kar: the 1SG prefix is the sole argument index on the compound, showing that cise 'house' has been absorbed and the resulting verb is intransitive. k=an is contracted ku=an 'I exist / live'.

translation: Close the door.
place: 新井田セイノ, アイヌ語鵡川方言日本語‐アイヌ語辞典 [chiba-mukawa/0#2493]
note: Phrasal apa asi 'close the door': apa is a free NP object and asi a transitive verb, the non-incorporated alternant of the NI compound apa-asi cited by Satō (§3.1). The phrasal form recurs throughout the corpus (imperatives and elicitation); the incorporated apa-asi is the marked member of the pair, illustrating how few near-pairs exist.

translation: The weather will be fine tomorrow.
note: The absorbed sir 'weather' is the incorporated zero-argument subject; pirka 'be good' is the predicate. No person index appears because the result is a zero-place predicate; nankor expresses the inferential.

translation: My hands feel heavy (I feel I've aged).
note: tek-e is the possessed form of tek 'hand', with -e as the possession suffix (distinct from the applicative e-). The stative base is pase 'be heavy'. The possessor of the hands — the speaker — is promoted to S of the whole predicate and indexed by ku=.

translation: I was rolled by waves and drifted.
note: rir 'wave' is the incorporated former A subject of tursere 'roll/tumble'; the original O (the speaker) now surfaces as S, indexed by =an. The parallel mom=an 'drift' is a separate intransitive clause.

text: apto as kor apto-kar=an upas as kor upas-kar=an rera-kar=an
gloss: rain fall CONJ rain-strike=4.S snow fall CONJ snow-strike=4.S wind-strike=4.S
translation: I was rained on, snowed on, and struck by wind.
place: Nakagawa ex. 1121, after Chiba University Ainu oral-literature materials 2015: 190
note: apto 'rain', upas 'snow', and rera 'wind' are the incorporated former A subjects of kar 'strike/do'; =an on each compound proves the derived intransitive. The parallel phrases apto as and upas as present the same nouns as free subjects in coreferential adverbial clauses.

translation: and here I spent the night (lit. the weather brightened for me)
note: ku=sirkopeker directly attests the sir-ko-peker applicative: the weather stem sir- incorporates as the subject, ko- adds the 1SG experiencer as the promoted S, indexed by ku=. ruwe ne packages the event as established narrative fact.

text: tane sirkokunne an no iwak=an pe
gloss: now weather-APPL-dark exist ADV return=4.S NMLZ
kana: tane sirkokunne an no iwak=an pe
translation: when I returned, it was already getting dark
place: Kaizawa Turushino, Uwepeker Yuk Sik Seireka [biratori/001/002#32]
note: sirkokunne attests the sir-ko-kunne applicative in running Saru prose. The weather stem sir- incorporates; ko- adds the ambient darkening as a backgrounded predicate. The logophoric =an on iwak indexes the narrator.

translation: I bit the fish with its bones.
note: Shibatani ex. 122, stage 3 of the three-step derivation. The person prefix a= (4th person transitive agent) sits outermost, proving that pone-ko-kuykuy is a single word. The original patient nea cep 'that fish' remains as the surface transitive object.

translation: (I) chopped it with grass and chopped it with earth —
note: The ko- applicative encodes the comitative participant ('with'); the comitative postposition tura is dropped. The person prefix a= (4th person transitive agent) sits outside the noun-verb complex in each clause, confirming one-word status. The object of the chopping — the demon's flesh — is recoverable from context and left unexpressed.

translation: (I) fed them well.
note: Phrasal form; pirka-no 'well' is an adverb outside the verb word, shown by the person prefix a= sitting on ipere alone.

translation: (I) fed them well.
note: Incorporated form; -no is dropped and the person prefix a= precedes the entire adverb-verb complex, proving one-word status.

text: ku=kor yupi ney pak en=askeuk wa
translation: My elder brother always invited me, and …
note: askeuk (lit. 'hand-take') is a QI compound meaning 'invite'; the first-singular-object prefix en= sits outside the entire askeuk complex, showing that the compound stays transitive. Under true NI, the incorporated noun would intransitivize the verb and the outer index would be a subject suffix.

translation: (I) fed them well.
note: Phrasal: pirka-no 'well' is an adverb outside the verb word, and the person prefix a= sits on ipere alone.

translation: (I) fed them well.
note: Incorporated: -no is dropped and a= precedes the whole pirka-ipere sequence, so it is one word.

translation: raised me with care and raised me well
note: The paired manner verbs before one head, a verse-register doublet; the object index i= precedes each whole stem.

translation: they were raising me on good food
note: e- adds the instrument (the food) as an object; the original patient stays. Cf. Batchelor's ae-oresu 'brought up on fish'.

text: a=epirkatomteresu kor an pe a=ne ayne
translation: I was one who had been raised well and with care
note: e- (instrument, +1) over pirka (+0) + tomte (+0) + resu (+2) = a three-place verb. Only the applicative changes arity; the two manner verbs never do.

translation: The bear killed the man.
note: Shibatani ex. 23a. The verb rayke carries no overt person marker (both arguments are third person, zero-indexed). On Shibatani's reading, the first NP is agent and the second is object by linear position alone.

translation: The man killed the bear.
note: Shibatani ex. 23b. With the NPs reversed, the person is now the agent and the bear the object. Shibatani allows OSV inversion when context or semantics prevents misinterpretation.

translation: The woman I am to marry.
literal: the woman for the purpose of my having
note: Nakagawa ex. 753. The relative clause a=kor kusu ne 'that I am to have' precedes the head noun menoko 'woman'. The gap inside the relative clause corresponds to the object of the transitive verb kor. The construction yields a Rel–N order consistent with the general head-final profile.

translation: There is not a single mat either.
note: Nakagawa ex. 750. The head noun toma 'mat' and the numeral-noun sinep 'one' are separated by the focus particle ka 'also/even'; yet isam 'not exist' is a one-place intransitive, so toma and sinep must together fill the single S slot. Nakagawa analyses [[toma] ka [sinep] ka] as a discontinuous NP — a classic indicator of pragmatically free constituent structure. Community discussion notes that the N + adverbial-numeral + V order (this N ka Num V pattern) appears frequently in Ainu oral texts, perhaps more so than comparable structures in Japanese (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-12-12, proposed ‹contested›).

translation: It is not only humans.
note: Nakagawa ex. 708. The negator somo occupies the adverb slot immediately before the copula ne; it takes no person marker and cannot predicate independently. Contrast Japanese ～ではない, where the negative element is a predicative auxiliary following the complement.

translation: As for the dog, it is in good condition.
note: Constructed for illustration. The referent of seta could be agent, patient, or topical subject of predication depending on wider context; anakne marks pragmatic foreground regardless of role.

translation: I look around.
note: After Tamura 1988: 72, cited in Satō 2025: 355. No overt pronoun or NP appears; the prefix ku= alone encodes the first-singular agent.

translation: We catch fish.
note: Satō 2025: 363. The NP cep 'fish' is an optional appositive specifying the zero-marked third-person patient. The predicate a=koyki is grammatically complete without it.

text: eani anakne a=kor son e=ne ruwe ne
translation: You are indeed my son.
place: 貝澤とぅるしの口演 ウエペケㇾ「ケトゥペ カムイ イレス」[biratori/006/005#206]
note: Attested uwepeker by Kaizawa Turushino (Biratori 1969). The independent pronoun eani 'you' is fronted and topicalised by anakne, but the verbal indexes already encode both participants: a=kor 'I have' (fourth-person A prefix on kor 'have') and e=ne 'you are' (2SG.S index on the copula ne). son is 'beloved child'. The pronoun supplies the identificational emphasis of the reveal, not any reference the indexes lack. The immediately following clause (biratori/006/005#207) drops the pronoun entirely — a=poho e=ne ruwe ne 'you are my child' — the index-only baseline the pronoun contrasts against.

translation: I'll give it to the old man.
note: Satō 2025 ex. 21 (second clause). The theme — a sweet, established in the preceding clause tanpe topenpe ne na 'this is a sweet' — is null. The verb kore 'give' is three-place; valency alone guarantees the theme's interpretation. Only the human recipient ekasi 'old man' and the 1SG agent ku= are expressed.

translation: She put the cooked food into the basket.
note: Nakagawa 2022 ch.14 ex. 74 (Saru). The locative relational noun or 'place of' on saranip marks the basket as the goal (Location argument); ci a=e-p 'the cooked food' is therefore unambiguously the theme. Without or, the two NPs would be structurally indistinguishable from a third-person agent and patient.

translation: I look around.
note: Satō ex. 1 (after Tamura 1988: 72). A finite verb carrying only the first-singular subject prefix ku=. No overt subject NP is required; the clause is grammatically complete. The prefix ku= covers both S and A for 1SG; see the person-marking chapters.

translation: We catch fish.
note: The fourth-person agent prefix a= is the grammatical subject argument; the NP cep 'fish' lexically specifies the zero-indexed object. The clause is complete without cep; the overt NP narrows what is caught but does not fill a structural position.

translation: The bear killed the man.
note: Shibatani ex. 23a. Initial NP interpreted as agent; the only role indicator is linear position, since neither NP carries a case suffix and the verb rayke is zero-marked for third-person arguments.

translation: The man killed the bear.
note: Shibatani ex. 23b. With order reversed, agent-patient assignment reverses. Shibatani (1990: 22) concludes that word order plays as important a role as in English in determining grammatical function.

text: sekor a=onaha a=unuhu haweoka kor i=kimatekka hine
translation: Saying so, my father and my mother encouraged me on and then …
place: Kawakami Matsuko, ILCAA Ainu materials, Saru
note: ILCAA aa-irc/009#154. Both co-subjects (a=onaha, a=unuhu) are overt; the object of kimatekka is zero, recovered from the 4.O prefix i= (narrator as object in logophoric-narrative context). All other participants in the surrounding passage are null. The fourth-person possessive a= marks the narrator's own kin in oral narrative; see the logophoric chapter.

translation: There is not a single mat either.
note: Nakagawa ex. 750 (second clause). Full pair: sintoko utar ka opitta sinep ka isam. toma ka sinep ka isam. 'there is not a single box either; there is not a single mat either.' Nakagawa analyses [toma ka sinep ka] as one discontinuous NP filling the S slot of the intransitive isam; the arity of the verb (one place) rules out reading toma and sinep as separate arguments.

translation: It is cold.
note: Zero-place ambient predicate: the incorporated nominal me 'coldness' + existential an. No subject NP; no person index. Nakagawa's §4.2.2 lists this as the type-① 完全動詞.

translation: The weather is fine.
note: The sir- prefix incorporates the ambient-domain noun into the property verb.

translation: There is a sound; it is said (an utterance is occurring).
note: Nakagawa exx. 16–17 distinguish 0-place hawas (no subject) from 1-place hawean 'X says' (= haw- + -ean with 1sg/4-person suffix), showing the 0-place / 1-place minimal pair in the voice domain.

translation: Without even feeling cold…
note: The 1-place merayke indexes the experiencer via the fourth-person S suffix =an, as opposed to 0-place mean, which takes no index.

translation: being in the mountains …
place: 川上まつ子, uwepeker 民話8, AA研アイヌ語資料 [aa-irc/006#128]
note: The locational or ta is an oblique adjunct on the existential an; the NP iwor 'mountains' is the subject of the existential, not a second argument.

text: e=kor iwatarap apunno hon or ta anakne apunno an wa
gloss: 2SG.A=have infant gently womb inside.of LOC TOP gently exist.S CONJ
translation: your infant, peacefully in your womb …
place: 川上まつ子, uwepeker 民話13, AA研アイヌ語資料 [aa-irc/016#166]
note: Locational predication: hon or ta is the locational oblique 'in the womb', anakne is the topic marker, apunno 'gently/peacefully' an adverb, and an is the predicate head. The subject of an is the infant (e=kor iwatarap 'your infant'), which is the topic of the wider discourse.

text: tap a=ye katu Piratur sekor a=ye hawe ne
gloss: now 4.A=say way Piratur QUOT 4.A=say NMLZ COP
translation: The way it is now called is 'Piratur'.
note: Specificational copular: the nominalized clause tap a=ye katu 'the way of now saying' is the subject; the quoted name Piratur sekor a=ye hawe 'the formal-noun report of calling it Piratur' is the complement before ne. The formal noun hawe (voice-NMLZ) nominates the whole quotation as the complement.

translation: You understood? / You understood!
note: The bare formal noun hawe (voice-nominalizer) without a following copula or existential; polar question or exclamative depending on intonation and context. This is the reduced/insubordinated frame of the hawe ne declarative.

translation: Yes, I heard it.
note: The final particle un forms the affirmative-reply frame while the formal noun ruwe is retained. Compare the declarative ku=nu ruwe ne 'I (certainly) heard it' and the content-question frame ku=nu ruwe an? 'did I hear [what]?'.

text: mak ne hine nea CAWAN isam isam
gloss: how COP CONJ that bowl NEG.exist NEG.exist
translation: How can that bowl be gone, gone?
note: The negative existential isam stands as the predicate of a rhetorical question; its repetition is a discourse-emphatic pattern in oral narrative rather than a distinct construction.

translation: I am not going.
note: Constructed elliptical reply to a polar yes/no question. In non-Saru dialects, the VP is repeated without a yes/no affirmation particle; the negative particle somo is part of the predicate being affirmed, not a sentential denial-word.

translation: if I am an Ainu …
note: The copular conditional frame: the copula ne takes the 1SG transitive-subject prefix ku= and is followed by the conditional particle yakun. The whole antecedent is a dependent clause; the consequent follows in the main clause.

translation: if (he) is a chief …
note: Third-person subject: the copula ne takes no person affix (zero = 3rd person). The nominal complement nispa precedes ne in the standard V-final order.

text: toan kur arikinne wen pe ne
gloss: that person very bad thing COP
translation: That person is a very bad one.
I am (an) Ainu.
This is a dog.
You are a foreigner.
This person is / became a great chief.
note: Shibatani ex. 15c. The same form is felicitous under both the stative ('is a chief') and the inchoative ('became a chief') readings; temporal context disambiguates.

translation: boy (lit. 'a child that is a man')
mare (lit. 'a horse that is a woman')
make (it) into a horse

text: tan pe anak seta ka somo ne wa
gloss: this thing TOP dog even NEG COP CONJ
translation: This thing is not a dog, and …
I am an Ainu.
place: 横山裕之, アイヌタイムズ 51, p. 1
note: The copular clause ku=ne is nominalised by the formal noun ruwe (the possessed form of ru 'track') and the outer copula ne predicates the whole as recognized fact.

translation: There was a big house, and —
place: Kawagami Matsuko, 'uwepeker 民話11', AA研アイヌ語資料 [aa-irc/013#85]
note: Bare existential predication: a single NP subject; no second argument. The conjunctive hine continues the narrative clause chain.

text: orwano ku=cise or ta ku=an kor
translation: Then, while I was in my house, —
note: Locational predication: the oblique or ta 'at the place of' follows the location NP. The first-person intransitive prefix ku= indexes the subject on the existential stem.

translation: My grandchild lives in this village.
note: Singular subject controls singular an. The inalienable-possessed form mippoho encodes 'my grandchild'. Based on Nakagawa (2024: 146).

translation: My grandchildren live in this village.
note: Plural subject mippoutari 'my grandchildren' controls plural oka. Based on Nakagawa (2024: 146).

text: a=kor kotan ta oar sinen ne oka=an wa
gloss: 4.A=have village LOC truly one COP exist.PL=4.S CONJ
translation: I was living all alone in my village, and —
note: Singular-referent/plural-verb: the narrative first person triggers the fourth-person suffix =an, which requires plural stem oka, even though oar sinen ne 'truly alone' makes the single referent explicit. Constructed after Nakagawa (2024: 178, exx. 151–152; Shizunai and Kushiro narrators).

text: mak ne hine nea cawan isam isam
gloss: how COP CONJ that bowl not.exist not.exist
translation: Where has that bowl gone? Gone?
note: isam as the whole predicate of a content question. The repeated isam in the source text marks rhetorical emphasis.

translation: There was not even one.
place: Kanzaki Masayoshi, 'Nibutani kotan ta cip-sanke an', Ainu Times [ainu-times/003/0#21]
note: sinen ka isam 'not even one exists': the negative-polarity particle ka 'even' combines with isam to express total absence (NPI construction).

translation: I have an umbrella.
note: Canonical HAVE-type predicative possession. Community discussion confirms the same form for Saru: kasa kor 'hold an umbrella', first-person kasa ku=kor (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2025-12-31; Ref aynucorporadiscord).

translation: One has an elder brother.
note: Story-opening family introduction. The noun yupi 'elder brother' takes the affiliative suffix -i; the 4th-person possessive prefix a= on the noun encodes the story protagonist as possessor.

translation: One has a younger sister.
note: Parallel BE-type form; sa 'younger sister' takes the affiliative suffix -ha.

translation: One even has a son / child.
note: ka 'even' is the additive focus particle. The noun po 'child, son' takes the affiliative suffix -ho.

translation: having gained a soul; being in possession of a soul
place: 川上まつ子, AA研アイヌ語資料 民話21 [aa-irc/021#530]
note: Noun incorporation: ramat 'soul' incorporated into kor yields the compound ramatkor 'soul-have'. The wa an resultative marks the ongoing state of being ensouled.

translation: (one) has no necklace even
note: The transitive sak 'lack' is the suppletive negative of kor; tamasay 'necklace' is the object (lacked possession) and the possessor is third-person (zero-marked A).

translation: one who has no father
note: Nominalized negative-possession clause. sak is transitive: ona 'father' is the O argument, and the possessor is third-person (zero). pe nominalizes the whole clause.

translation: Everything was big.
place: Maruya Kazuko 丸野和子, '「Kuma」turano k=an', アイヌタイムズ 15/1 [ainu-times/015/1#5]
note: The property verb poro 'be big' is the sole predicate; the evidential frame ruwe ne closes the clause exactly as it does on action verbs.

text: sonno ku=pewre or ta ku=nu yukar ne ru-we ne
gloss: really 1SG.S=be.young place LOC 1SG.A=hear epic COP track-POSS COP
translation: It was when I was really young that I heard this epic.
note: Nakagawa ex. 1 (p. 118). The 1SG.S prefix ku= on pewre 'be young' is identical to its use on ku=an 'I exist' or ku=arpa 'I go'.

translation: That mountain is high.
note: Kindaichi & Chiri §189B. Predicative property verb with zero third-person subject marking.

text: tane pakno e=poro ru-we ne korka
translation: You have grown big, but …
place: Kawakami Matsuko 川上まつ子, uwepeker 民話18, AA研アイヌ語資料 [aa-irc/025#266]
note: The 2SG.S prefix e= marks the single argument of poro in the inchoative reading; the evidential ruwe ne predicates the growth as a recognized fact.

translation: not feeling cold, and …
note: Nakagawa ex. 15 (p. 127, 表12). The 4th-person S suffix =an indexes the subject of the experiencer predicate merayke 'feel cold'; ka somo ki frames the negation contrastively.

text: toan kur arikinne wen pe ne
gloss: that.one person very be.bad thing COP
translation: That person is a very bad one.
note: Satō ex. 4 (p. 20). The degree adverb arikinne modifies the attributive property verb wen; the whole complex wen pe serves as the nominal complement of the copula.

translation: It is slow in coming.
note: Nakagawa §3.4.3 ex. 5. The property verb moyre follows the main predicate ek 'come' and qualifies its pace; the existential an (not the copula) closes the evidential frame, as expected for a content-question-capable sentence-final form.

text: tan pe anak seta ka somo ne wa
gloss: this NMLZ TOP dog even NEG COP CONJ
translation: This is not a dog.
Because I was a small cat —
note: 浜田隆史, アイヌタイムズ [ainu-times/024/3#4]. The perfective auxiliary a follows ku=ne, locating the copular state in the past. The clause links to what follows via the purposive-causal kusu.

translation: I won't be here tomorrow.
I don't feel cold, and …
note: Nakagawa ex. 15. The post-verbal ka somo ki no frame negates the property verb merayke 'feel cold'. The 4th-person S suffix =an marks the narrative first person; contrast the 0-place meteorological verb mean 'it is cold (weather)', which has no subject index.

text: nep eci=e-sirkirap ka somo ki ru-we ne na
gloss: something 2PL.A=APPL-worry even NEG do track-POSS COP FIN
translation: You will not be troubled by anything.
place: Kaizawa Tsurushino, Biratori; Dal Corso siglum KAY: 2-2,18
note: Dal Corso ex. 128. The negation ka somo ki targets the verb sirkirap and sits inside the evidential frame; ruwe ne predicates the whole negated proposition as an established fact.

text: tapan kina a=e p ne toan kina somo a=e p ne
gloss: this plant 4.A=eat NMLZ COP that plant NEG 4.A=eat NMLZ COP
translation: This plant is one that people eat; that plant is one that people do not eat.
note: The fourth person a= gives a generic human eater; p is the object head of each clause — the thing eaten. The vowel-final e selects the short allomorph -p.

translation: the things one is carrying along
note: pe is the object of se and the subject of okay; the consonant-final okay selects the allomorph -pe.

translation: kitchen utensil
note: The applicative e- licenses the instrumental participant that p nominalizes; the plain compound sukemakiri has no such prefix.

translation: a thing to drink hot water with
note: The instrumental ani stays inside the clause; p is the generic instrument head, the object of ku 'drink'.

translation: the knife I cut fish with
note: Ijäs Lesson 11. The instrumental ani is fronted and retained; the head here is the common noun makiri, the same gap strategy that p and pe carry without a lexical head.

text: ne kusu haweoka wa cis pa p ka a=erampewtek
gloss: COP because speak.PL CONJ cry PL NMLZ even 4.A=not.understand
translation: I did not even understand why they were crying.
note: p is not an argument of speak or cry; the clause haweoka wa cis pa is complete (arity 0). p nominalizes the whole reason clause, which is then the object of a=erampewtek.

translation: One should sit quietly.
note: pe nominalizes a saturated intransitive; the predication pe ne na carries the deontic 'should' reading of Satō's content-clause use.

text: a=e=túskote kuni p ne ru-we ne na
gloss: 4.A=2SG.O=tie.up PURP NMLZ COP track-POSS COP FIN
translation: You will surely be tied up.
note: The fourth-person agent a= with the second-person object e= yields a passive-like reading; kuni p forms a future/deontic nominal, and the framing predicate ru-we ne presents it as established fact.

text: ku=kemeyki kor ku=itak hi iyotta pirka
translation: it is best to talk while sewing
note: After Tamura 2000: 126. hi takes two person-marked, fully specified clauses and nominalizes the whole as the grammatical subject of iyotta pirka 'is most good'.

text: a=ye hi ka a=kar hi ka a=eramiskari
translation: not knowing what to say or what to do
place: Oda Ito, NINJAL corpus of Ainu oral literature (Chitose) [ninjal-folklore/026#61]

translation: the place where someone built a house
note: ta (LOC) retained inside the RC signals the locative role of hi; compare the time reading below, where no postposition is present.

translation: since I was small
note: hi nominalizes the intransitive clause pon=an (arity 0); wano 'since/from' governs the nominalized clause as a temporal adverbial.

translation: there was no place to ask about it
note: Bugaeva ex. 16. nu 'hear, ask about'; eun 'toward' retained inside the RC signals the directional role; usi 'place' is the formal-noun head. The NP is the argument of isam 'not exist'.

translation: the village I live in
note: Ijäs Lesson 11. oro 'place/vicinity' (relational noun) fronts before ta (LOC). With a usi-type head no oro would be needed.

text: poro cikuni oar isam sir-i ku=nukar wa sonno ku=iruska
gloss: big tree at.all not.exist appearance-POSS 1SG.A=see CONJ truly 1SG.A=be.angry
translation: I saw that there were no big trees at all, and was truly angry.
note: sir-i = sir 'appearance/state' + possessed suffix -i. siri heads the complement of ku=nukar 'I saw'; ku=iruska follows wa (CONJ) as a second, main-clause predicate.

translation: fox
note: ci= (1PL.A) + ronnu 'kill' + -p (NMLZ = formal noun p/pe, 'thing'). The generic patient 'things we kill' has been conventionalized as the species name for fox.

translation: hearth
note: -i is the allomorph of formal noun hi after a consonant, giving the 'place' reading. ape 'fire' is incorporated; o 'enter'. Contrast aep (4.A=eat-NMLZ) 'food', where -p gives the concrete 'thing' reading of p/pe.

translation: the stick with which that woman dug uba-lilies
note: ani (INS) is retained inside the RC because ni 'stick/wood' fills the instrument role. The compound tureptani suppresses the grammatical relation; the RC must express it.

translation: the stick with which that woman dug uba-lilies
note: The instrumental ani must stay in the clause; its removal collapses the arity. The lexicalized compound tureptani 'uba-lily-digging stick' contains the same morphological material but grammatically specifies no instrumental relation.

translation: the tree at which I gathered chestnuts
note: The relational noun oro supplies the NP argument of the locative ta; cikuni 'tree' is the external head. Without oro the particle ta has no host.

translation: the men who came up to the doorway
note: arki is the suppletive plural of ek 'come'. The S (the men) is gapped; the directional adjunct cise soy pakno 'up to outside the house' stays in the clause. utar 'people' is the external head.

text: kem sawot pe tumi sawot pe
gloss: famine flee NMLZ war flee NMLZ
translation: people fleeing famine, people fleeing war
note: sawot 'flee, escape' is transitive; kem 'famine' and tumi 'war' are the retained O arguments. The A (the fleeing people) is gapped and the formal noun pe supplies the generic head 'person'. In the corpus, O-relativization is more frequent than A-relativization (Bugaeva 2015: 48).

translation: the book I read
note: Ijäs Lesson 11. The O (the book) is gapped; ku= is the 1SG agent prefix on the transitive verb nukar 'see, read'. The gap strategy is identical when the head is a bound noun rather than a common noun.

translation: children who have been taught to read
note: hekattar 'children' is the Recipient-O head; kampi 'paper/literacy' is the retained Theme. The applicative e- licenses the Recipient in the O position. The A of the three-place verb (the teacher) is not the gapped position; it is simply unrealized (generic).

translation: a thing to drink hot water with
note: The instrumental ani is retained at the clause edge. The formal noun p is the generic instrument head. The indefinite fourth-person a= gives a generic reading.

translation: the uncle my brother shot the bear with
note: turano 'together with' is the retained comitative postposition. ku=yupo 'my older brother' is the A of cotca 'shoot'; kamuy 'bear' is the O. acapo 'uncle' is the external head — the gapped comitative co-participant.

translation: there was no place to ask about it
note: eun is the retained dative postposition. usi 'place' is the formal-noun head; it fills the dative position. nu has the meaning 'ask, inquire about' here (Bugaeva 2015: 49 fn.9).

translation: the restaurant I went to
note: Ijäs Lesson 11. oro un 'to there' is the retained allative phrase. Without oro the allative un has no NP host and the sentence is ill-formed. ipeusi 'restaurant' is the external head.

translation: an insect whose legs are long
note: cikir-ihi is the possessed form of cikir 'leg'; the POSS suffix -ihi remains inside the RC and identifies the possessor as the gapped position. kikir 'insect' is the external head — the gapped possessor. tanne 'long' is the stative predicate.

text: a=ona pakno nispa isam nispa ne
translation: my father was a rich man with no equal
note: Bugaeva's discovery example. The prenominal RC [pakno nispa isam] 'to whose degree of wealth no rich man exists' is a degree-adjunct modifier on the second nispa (the head). The standard of comparison is expressed as the negated content of the RC, not as a gapped participant.

translation: the one I have; my husband
note: Classical Ainu (Itadori/Ishikari data in Shibatani 1990). The person-type suffix -kur (< kuru 'person') attaches to kor 'have' with the first-person agent prefix ku=. The result is a single morphological word.

translation: the men who came up to the doorway of the house
note: arki is the suppletive plural of ek 'come'; 3rd-person subjects have zero person-marking, so the verb appears without a prefix. utar 'people' is the formal-noun head of the headless relative clause.

text: kem sawot pe tumi sawot pe
gloss: famine flee NMLZ war flee NMLZ
translation: those who flee famine, those who flee war
note: pe heads two parallel clauses whose argument gap is the S/agent of sawot 'flee'. The thing-type nominalizer pe reads as 'person' by contextual inference; no person prefix appears because the referent is generic/3rd-person.

translation: there was no place to ask about
note: The dative/directional postposition eun 'to, about' remains inside the relative clause; usi fills the gap as the headless place-head. The fourth-person prefix a= marks a generic participant. The construction follows the same postposition-stranding pattern as an externally-headed oblique relative.

translation: the sound of a man's coming
note: Classical Ainu (Itadori/Ishikari data). The bare concept form hum 'sound' — not the possessed hum-i — takes the preceding clause as its content. Shibatani reads this as a construction intermediate between a relative clause and an evidential nominalization.

translation: a sight of a man's crying
note: Again the bare concept form sir 'appearance', not the possessed siri. Compare the evidential siri ne, where the possessed form sir-i heads the clause-final nominalization and is closed by the copula ne.

translation: (someone) felt like a good person
note: The bare hum 'sound/sensation' (not the possessed hum-i) combined with the existential as 'stand/exist'. Bugaeva reads this as an emerging GNMCC pattern in which hum classifies the type of sensation rather than heading a gapped external relative clause. Dal Corso 2020: 52 cites the same distributional contrast in his structural analysis.

translation: He/she said, 'It is good.'
note: Minimal sekor frame: an unmodified stative predicate quoted before the fourth-person matrix verb a=ye 'say'.

translation: I thought, 'He/she will come.'
note: sekor with the thought verb ramu: the fourth-person intransitive suffix =an on ek 'come' marks the referent of the thought inside the quote. The matrix ku=ramu carries the first-person speaker-agent.

translation: He/she said, 'I will return.'
note: Direct quotation under sekor: the first-person intransitive prefix ku= on hosipi 'return' is the original speaker's own form, intact inside the quote. The matrix a=ye carries the fourth-person narrator-agent.

translation: I said I would return.
note: Indirect quotation under kuni: the original first-person subject is shifted to the fourth-person intransitive suffix =an, adopting the narrator's viewpoint. kuni nominalizes the embedded clause as the nominal object of a=ye 'say'.

text: ku=matnepo tanto ek kunak ye kor an
gloss: 1SG.POSS=daughter today come COMP say CONJ exist
translation: My daughter says she will come today.
note: kunak frames the future proposition ek 'come.SG'; kor an 'while/is' marks the report as ongoing. The embedded subject of ek is the shifted fourth person (the daughter). The possessive ku=matnepo 'my daughter' is the topic of the whole utterance.

text: a ahun kuni a=ye akusu toykooripak
translation: When I told them to enter, they were very abashed.
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker 民話8 (その2) [aa-irc/007#213]
note: kuni follows the directed action ahun 'enter'; a=ye 'say/tell' is the fourth-person matrix verb. akusu marks the sequential relation to the consequent clause. The perfective a closes the speech event before the consequence.

translation: It is said that he/she came.
note: sekor hawe ne: the quotative particle sekor intervenes between the embedded clause ek 'come' and the reportative frame haw-e ne. The internal morphology haw-e shows the source noun haw 'voice' plus the possessed ending -e.

text: hekattar tura sinot=an hi ka a=onaha kopan
gloss: children COMIT play=4.S NMLZ even 4.A=father refuse
translation: My father refused even that I play with the children.
note: The embedded clause hekattar tura sinot=an has arity 0 and hi nominalizes it as a fact-complement. Nakagawa's arity count: sinot (+1) with =an (−1) = 0. hi cannot be a relative-clause head here because there is no open slot to fill.

text: a=ye hi ka a=kar hi ka a=eramiskari
translation: not knowing what to say or what to do
place: Oda Ito, アイヌ語口承文芸コーパス (NINJAL) [ninjal-folklore/026#61]
note: Two parallel hi complements coordinated with ka 'even/also': a=ye hi 'the saying-thing' and a=kar hi 'the doing-thing' both serve as objects of a=eramiskari. Each embedded clause has arity 0 (the 4th-person agent a= fills the A slot of a transitive verb).

text: ku=kemeyki kor ku=itak hi iyotta pirka
translation: Speaking while sewing is best.
note: After Tamura (2000: 126). hi nominalizes the saturated coordinated clause ku=kemeyki kor ku=itak (arity 0: each transitive verb has its A slot filled by ku=). The nominalized NP is the clausal subject of the predication iyotta pirka 'is best'.

translation: I saw the child walking.
note: sir-i (< sir 'appearance' + POSS suffix -i) nominalizes the saturated arity-0 clause hekaci apkas ('child walks': apkas +1, hekaci −1 = 0). The whole [clause sir-i] is the object of ku=nukar. Constructed to illustrate the pattern; the semantic profile of siri (ongoing, visually accessible event) is established by Satō (2008: 178).

translation: I heard the child speaking.
note: haw-e (< haw 'voice' + POSS -e) nominalizes the auditory event as the object of nu 'hear/ask about'. Constructed to illustrate the pattern; the hawe + nu pairing is established by Satō (2008: 176–177) and Nakagawa (2024: 508).

translation: I said I would return.
note: kuni nominalizes the saturated clause hosipi=an (intransitive 'return', +1 with =an −1 = 0) as the object of a=ye. The kuni complement presents the speaker's stated intention — a future event in the speaker's assertion.

translation: When I told them to enter, they were very abashed.
note: The directive use: the matrix subject (4th-person narrator) tells the addressees to enter. The complement's agent (the addressees) differs from the matrix S. akusu 'thereupon/when' links to the consequence clause.

translation: I think it would be good.
note: Constructed to illustrate the kuni + ramu pattern. pirka 'be.good' is a stative intransitive (arity +1); without an overt S it has arity +1 — but in this context the subject is pragmatically recoverable. For the complementizer reading, the argument is that the speaker's kuni-complement expresses wished or inferred content, not a specific participant gap. Compare the analysis of arity in Nakagawa (2024: 476).

text: míre kuni p ére kuni p nepki ne ki wa
gloss: clothe PURP NMLZ feed PURP NMLZ be.work COP do CONJ
translation: making things to clothe (the grandchild) and things to feed (her) her work,
note: Two parallel kuni p nominals ('thing to clothe', 'thing to feed') coordinate as the content of nepki ne ki wa 'making (it) one's work'. Each kuni p packages the action as a purposive-deontic event-nominal.

text: ku=matnepo tanto ek kunak ye kor an
gloss: 1SG.A=daughter today come COMP say while exist
translation: My daughter is saying she will come today.
note: kunak nominalizes the prospective clause ek 'come' as the content of ye 'say'. The periphrastic ye kor an ('is saying') marks ongoing speech. Person marking in the embedded clause (3rd person zero-marked ek) reflects the narrator's viewpoint, not the daughter's.

translation: I said I would return.
note: Nakagawa's own example. The fourth-person intransitive suffix =an marks the reported subject (the speaker's self-reference shifted to 4th person inside the embedded clause); kuni nominalizes the prospective VP as the object of ye.

translation: When I told them to enter, they were very abashed.
note: kuni nominalizes the directive ahun 'enter' as the content of ye 'say'; akusu links the result clause temporally.

translation: I think it would be good.
note: Constructed to illustrate the kuni complement of ramu; the pattern is established by Nakagawa 2024: 476, which lists both ye and ramu as matrix verbs for kuni.

text: míre kuni p ére kuni p nepki ne ki wa
gloss: clothe PURP NMLZ feed PURP NMLZ task COP do CONJ
translation: making things to clothe (the grandchild) and things to feed (the grandchild) her task,
note: Two parallel kuni p nominals ('thing to clothe', 'thing to feed') are predicated as the grandmother's task via nepki ne ki wa; the construction names purpose-defined objects.

text: a=e=túskote kuni p ne ru-we ne na
gloss: 4.A=2SG.O=tie.up PURP NMLZ COP track-POSS COP FIN
translation: You will surely be tied up.
note: The fourth-person agent a= with the second-person object e= yields a passive-like reading; kuni p forms the deontic nominal, ne is the copula predicated over it, and ruwe ne frames the whole as recognized fact.

text: nen poka iki wa yayetuytak kuni p ne ru-we ne na
gloss: who even do CONJ make.a.living PURP NMLZ COP track-POSS COP FIN
translation: Somehow, (the old man) will surely manage to make a living.
