note: The embedded clause nen poka iki wa yayetuytak expresses the desired future outcome; kuni p ne ruwe ne presents its coming-to-pass as deontic and epistemically certain. nen poka 'somehow / by whatever means' is an indefinite expression built on the interrogative nen 'who'.

text: sine ancikar ne wa ek=an kusu ne na
gloss: one night COP CONJ come=4.S PURP COP FIN
translation: After one night, I will come.
note: kusu ne supplies the scheduled-future reading; ek is the singular 'come' stem and =an the fourth person used as the narrative first person.

translation: I went on living, doing this day after day.
note: Both iki and the existential an carry the fourth-person =an, the diagnostic that kor an is a chain of two finite clauses; the value here is habitual.

translation: A deer is standing.
note: wa an presents the standing as the state resulting from the posture-change verb as 'stand'.

text: tane pakno a=e=tumam wa hotke=an a korka
gloss: now until 4.A=2SG.O=embrace CONJ lie.down=4.S PFV although
translation: Until now I had held you in my arms and lain down, but —
note: Nakagawa reads a here as marking the event that forms the background to the following korka clause, not simply as a past.

translation: when it turned out that I had fallen asleep,
note: aan joins perfect aspect to indirect evidentiality and after-the-fact realization; the following ru-we ne repackages the proposition as established fact.

translation: It will probably get better soon.
note: nankor follows the predicate and supplies epistemic probability.

text: aoka ka sikunu=an easkay pe ne na
gloss: we even survive=4.S be.able NMLZ COP FIN
translation: We too can survive.
note: The transitive-verb auxiliary easkay follows the person-marked intransitive verb to express ability.

translation: because I cannot go outside,
note: Negative ability is the dedicated word eaykap, not somo easkay; the scalar ka intervenes before it.

translation: You may eat it.
note: Ijäs's Lesson 10 permission frame, cited as a constructed illustration rather than a corpus token.

translation: Come on, dig it up and look!
note: The singular imperative is a chain of bare verbs; no second-person subject prefix appears.

translation: Do not come near the fire!
note: The prohibitive adverb iteki precedes the verb, which keeps the bare imperative shape.

text: ney ta ka kuruma ani mosir epitta payoka=an wa inkar=an ro
gloss: when LOC even car INS land throughout go.around=4.S CONJ look=4.S HORT
translation: Someday let us travel around the whole country by car and see it.
note: The hortative particle ro follows a clause chain with the fourth-person inclusive =an.

text: nisatta kunneywa tunas soyne=an nankor kusu
gloss: tomorrow morning early go.out=4.S probably because
translation: Tomorrow morning I will probably go out early —
note: The temporal adverb nisatta 'tomorrow' supplies the future anchor; the epistemic auxiliary nankor adds probability. The verb soyne=an 'go out' carries no future inflection.

text: nisatta onuman anakne sine ancikar ne kusu
gloss: tomorrow evening TOP one night COP FIN
translation: Tomorrow evening, it will be just one night.
note: Attested from a SAR dialect narrative. The adverb nisatta 'tomorrow' combined with onuman 'evening' supplies the future anchor without any tense inflection on the copula.

text: apeoy anak an hine ape ruyruy kor an
gloss: hearth TOP exist CONJ fire burn.vigorously while exist
translation: The hearth was there, and the fire was burning vigorously.
note: Neither the bare an 'exist' nor the kor an progressive carries a tense morpheme; the past reading comes from the narrative reference frame. Both an tokens are zero-marked third person.

text: arwen kamuy ne an=an nisa ruwe ne na
gloss: very.bad god COP exist=4.S PRF.REC INFR COP FIN
translation: He has become a terribly bad god.
note: The recent perfect nisa marks the change-of-state as just completed; the past reading ('has become') is an inference from the completion semantics, not from a tense morpheme. The verb an=an 'exist' carries no tense inflection; ruwe ne is the nominalized assertion frame.

text: an epitta paye=an kusu ne na
gloss: one throughout go=4.S PURP COP FIN
translation: I intend to travel through the night.
note: kusu ne supplies the intentive reading; the future temporal implication follows from the modal value. The verb paye=an 'go' carries no future inflection.

translation: while (he) was springing upon the deer —
note: kor an with an action verb (yukkoterke, incorporating the noun yuk 'deer'); the progressive marks the action as in progress at a narrative reference point.

text: sittokap kor pon seta turano sinot=an kor an=an ayne
gloss: noon when small dog with play=4.S while exist=4.S then
translation: at noon I would always play with the puppy, and
note: Habitual value set by the temporal clause sittokap kor 'whenever it was noon'. Both sinot and the existential an carry the fourth-person suffix =an, the pair-verb signature (§agreement below).

translation: they are chatting
note: Plural subject: oka replaces an in the auxiliary slot. This is the predicate of Nakagawa's ex. 983; the full sentence is a=onaha turano uenewsar pa kor oka 'they are chatting with my father'.

translation: What are you crying about?
note: The second-person prefix e= prefixes both ciskar 'cry' and the existential an; two independently indexed finite verbs joined by kor.

text: ek wa an pe hoppa kor
gloss: come CONJ exist NMLZ send.away CONJ
translation: taking away what had arrived, and
note: ek wa an 'has come and is now here': the resultative of the motion-change verb ek. The nominalized clause ek wa an pe 'the thing that has arrived' functions as the object of hoppa.

translation: is coming / is on the way
note: kor an with ek: the change of location is in progress, the arrival not yet complete. Nakagawa ex. 986.

translation: has arrived and is (now) here
note: wa an with ek: the motion is complete and the resultant state — being present at the destination — persists. Nakagawa ex. 987.

translation: The hare is dead.
note: Satō's constructed diagnostic (Bugaeva ex. 72f). The punctual change verb ray 'die' yields a stable result state; *isepo ray kor an is bad — death is not an ongoing process.

translation: is asleep
note: Nakagawa ex. 998. Only the resultant-state reading is available: Ainu construes sleep as the result of falling asleep, not as an ongoing activity.

translation: (I) have put it in — it is in there.
note: Object-agreement pattern (c): an indexes the object (the thing placed), not the fourth-person agent a=. The agent's action is presupposed; what the construction asserts is the object's resultant state (Nakagawa exx. 996–997).

text: tane pakno a=e=tumam wa hotke=an a korka
gloss: now until 4.A=2SG.O=embrace CONJ lie.down=4.S PFV although
translation: Until now I had held you in my arms and lain down with you, but —
note: Person marking (4.A=, =4.S) falls on the lexical verbs tumam 'embrace' and hotke 'lie down'; the auxiliary a carries no person index. The contrast particle korka signals that this clause supplies the background to a subsequent reversal — a discourse environment typical of a.

translation: They came.
note: rok replaces a when the subject is plural; the suppletive plural verb stem arki simultaneously replaces singular ek. The fourth-person suffix =an indexes the subject on the lexical verb; rok carries no person marking. Compare the singular ek=an a 'she came'.

translation: [she] walked on and on.
note: The verb-plus-auxiliary unit apkas a repeats to form the iterative; rok rok patterns identically with a plural subject. Nakagawa's attested form is onkami=an a =an a 'worshipped over and over' (Nakagawa 2024: 308, ex. 453), where =an abbreviates the repeated verb base in the second occurrence.

text: oripak kamuy poho a=ne aan ru-we ne hine
gloss: noble deity child 4.A=COP PRF.MIR track-POSS COP CONJ
translation: it turned out that I was the child of an honored deity, and …
place: Hiraga Sadamo, ウエペケㇾ ウラユシウンクㇽ [biratori/010/003#421]
note: The speaker discovers after the fact that she is the child of a deity; aan encodes indirect, retrospective access to this information. ruwe ne then packages the realized content as established fact.

translation: when it turned out that I had fallen asleep,
note: aan presents the sleep as discovered retrospectively; the following ruwe ne repackages the discovery as established knowledge.

translation: Penanpe was, surprisingly, the child of a deity.
note: The Horobetsu form awan carries the after-the-fact surprise (admirative) reading systematically noted by Chiri; the example is preserved in Yoshikawa 2018: 4. The competing segmentation [haw+an] is one of the etymological readings Yoshikawa discusses.

translation: That person appears to be going.
note: Illustrates the appearance-based continuative: sir-an replaces plain an as the existential predicate, signalling that the ongoing action is perceptible to the observer. Compare nea kur arpa kor an 'that person is going', which carries no evidential colouring.

text: supuya at kor sir-an ru-we ne anan
gloss: smoke rise CONJ appearance-exist track-POSS COP MIR
translation: Smoke was rising, it turned out!
place: Nakagawa text, Dal Corso siglum NGF:176
note: Dal Corso ex. 268. The visual-state predicate sir-an is embedded before the inferential ruwe ne, which repackages the proposition as a fact the speaker now recognizes with surprise. The stacking confirms that sir-an and ruwe ne are separate predicates with a fixed scope order: aspect/visual-state inside, inferential outside.

text: asir sapa tuye kane an hine mina kane an wa
gloss: be.new head cut CONJ exist CONJ laugh CONJ exist CONJ
translation: having cut the new head and laughing
note: The first kane an follows the change verb tuye 'cut' with a resultative reading — the new head has been cut and the state persists; the second follows the action verb mina 'laugh' with a progressive reading — laughter is ongoing. The same form covers both, unlike kor an (progressive only) and wa an (resultative only).

text: a=tura wa cepkoyki=an kan an pe a=ki kan oka=an ainne
gloss: 4.A=accompany CONJ catch.fish=4.S CONJ exist NMLZ 4.A=do CONJ exist.PL=4.S CONJ
translation: while we were fishing together
note: kan an in Tokachi progressive use: the ongoing collective action of fishing persists as a state. The nominalizer pe packages the first kan an clause; a=ki kan oka=an continues the chain with a plural subject marked by oka=an.

text: poro cise as kan an na
gloss: be.big house stand CONJ exist FIN
translation: A large house was standing there.
note: kan an in Ishikari resultative use: the posture verb as 'stand' enters kan an where Saru would use wa an, presenting the house as being in the resultant state of having stood up.

text: tane rikin wa isam pe okake ta
gloss: now ascend CONJ be.gone NMLZ after LOC
translation: Now, after (the god) had ascended and vanished,
note: rikin wa isam: the subject rises and then is absent — isam retains its lexical sense 'be absent'. pe okake ta nominalizes the wa isam clause and frames it temporally.

translation: Then they grew old and passed away.
note: The postverbal plural clitic pa marks a plural subject; wa isam closes the sequence with the lexical force of disappearance.

text: caricari wa isam ru-we ne kuni a=ramu kor
gloss: be.scattered CONJ be.gone track-POSS COP COMP 4.A=think while
translation: (while she was) thinking that (things) had been scattered and vanished,
note: wa isam is embedded inside a nominalized complement (ru-we ne) governed by ramu 'think'; kuni is the complementizer.

translation: You finished making it.
note: wa okere foregrounds completion of the action; there is no sense of loss or disappearance as in wa isam.

translation: Dawn is breaking; it is getting light.
note: kor an with a change verb in its inceptive extension: the transition to daylight is ongoing and approaching its endpoint.

translation: The buds are now about to open.
note: kor oka (plural existential) with a plural subject; the inceptive reading: the opening is under way with completion imminent.

translation: (I) worshipped again and again.
note: Reduplicated a … a with a fourth-person subject: =an attaches to the second a. Only the person marker reduplicates with a fourth-person subject, not the full stem.

translation: (They) keep going again and again.
note: ranke follows arpa 'go' and precedes kor oka=an; ranke takes no person marking. The combination marks repeated habitual going.

text: sittokap kor pon seta turano sinot=an kor an=an ayne
gloss: noon while little dog together play=4.S while exist=4.S as
translation: Every noon she would play with the puppy,
note: sittokap kor 'whenever noon (comes)' provides the frequentative temporal frame; sinot=an kor an=an is the habitual kor an construction. ayne marks the clause as background to what follows.

text: arwenkamuy ne an=an nisa ru-we ne na
gloss: truly.evil.kamuy COP exist=4.S PRF.REC track-POSS COP FIN
translation: (I) have now truly become an evil kamuy.
note: nisa follows the existential an=an and precedes the evidential ruwe ne; the recent-perfect value and the fact-evidential reinforce each other.

translation: Come on, dig it up and look!
note: Two bare-stem verbs (pusu, inkar) linked by the sequential particle wa. The absence of any second-person subject prefix is the sole formal mark of the singular imperative.

text: ku=kor kuruma o wa hosippa yan
translation: Get in my car and go home!
note: hosippa is the suppletive plural stem of hosipi 'return'; both the plural stem and the particle yan are obligatory for a plural or polite addressee. A bare *hosippa without yan is ungrammatical as a command.

translation: Please sleep well!
note: hani follows the bare imperative mokor 'sleep' and converts a direct command into a polite wish.

translation: Please don't shout.
note: hani follows yan in a prohibitive context; the sequence iteki … yan hani produces a softened negative directive to a plural or polite addressee.

translation: Please cook [it] for me.
note: Benefactive request pattern: the lexical verb takes the bare imperative shape, wa links it to kore, and the object prefix en= on kore identifies the beneficiary.

translation: Do not come near the fire!
note: The prohibitive adverb iteki precedes the verb, which retains the bare imperative shape with no second-person subject prefix.

translation: You should let them in.
note: The conditional-advice frame yak pirka na; the second-person subject prefix e= is present, in contrast to the bare-stem imperative which suppresses it.

translation: You should probably go and check on your mother.
note: With a second-person subject, nankor shades from probability into expectation or gentle suggestion; both verbs carry the second-person prefix e=.

translation: Take care not to fall!
note: The admonitive adverb ikiya precedes a person-marked verb with the 2SG.S prefix e=; the presence of the subject prefix distinguishes this from the bare-stem prohibitive iteki.

translation: Let's go.

text: ney ta ka kuruma ani mosir epitta payoka=an wa inkar=an ro
gloss: when LOC even car INS land throughout go.around=4.S CONJ look=4.S HORT
translation: Someday let us travel around the whole country by car and see it.
note: Both finite verbs carry the fourth-person suffix =an, the diagnostic of the pair-verb construction in which wa links two independent finite clauses. The hortative ro scopes over the full conjoined proposition.

translation: Shall I go? / I'll go then.
note: With a first-person rather than fourth-person subject, ro shifts from a cohortative 'let us' to a volitional 'shall I / I will', presenting the speaker's intention as a proposal open to the addressee's response.

translation: Let me carry you!
note: Chitose form. The second-person object prefix eci= is overt while the first-person agent is contextually implied. Nakagawa analyses this as a 1SG-agent, 2SG-object hortative in which the speaker proposes to act for the addressee.

translation: (Hmm,) shall I go?
note: Deliberative so with a first-person subject; the speaker reasons aloud without directing the question to another participant. Contrast the cohortative paye=an ro, where the invitation is addressed to the interlocutor.

translation: One wants to look; one has a wish to see.
note: Fourth-person (indefinite) subject: the person-agreement suffix =an attaches to the main verb inkar, and rusuy is bare. The fourth person here expresses a generic or narrator's first-person referent in the narrative context.

translation: I want to eat (it).
note: Ijäs's constructed illustration. The first-person agent ku= attaches to the transitive verb e 'eat'; rusuy is bare. The unspecified patient is understood from context. This is the simplest transitive desiderative form.

translation: I want it.
note: A nominal object precedes kor in the full clause: e.g. cep ku=kor rusuy 'I want a/the fish'. rusuy is in its auxiliary function; kor takes the normal person prefix.

translation: I want to go to/for it.
note: The applicative prefix e- introduces a goal or beneficiary argument to the intransitive motion verb arpa 'go (SG)'. Person agreement (ku= 1SG.A) attaches at the outer edge of the complex stem; rusuy is bare. The person-marking pattern is identical to the plain V rusuy frame.

translation: I do not want to see (it).
note: somo negates the V rusuy predicate as a unit. This is the expected scope position for sentential negation in the auxiliary frame: somo sits inside any outer evidential frame and takes the modal complex as its target.

translation: I could compose songs.
note: The verb root sinotca 'compose/perform songs' is incorporated into easkay; the fourth-person suffix =an attaches to the whole compound as a unit. The pattern parallels incorporated desideratives such as arpa=rusuy (Nakagawa 2024: 314–315).

text: aoka ka sikunu=an easkay pe ne na
gloss: we even survive=4.S be.able NMLZ COP FIN
translation: We too can survive.
note: The fourth-person inclusive suffix =an indexes the subject of sikunu 'survive'; easkay is person-unmarked. pe ne na nominalizes the ability clause and predicates it with the copula.

text: yaykata kina poka a=kar easkay hi neno
gloss: by.oneself greens just 4.A=gather be.able NMLZ since
translation: from when she could gather wild greens by herself
note: The fourth-person agent prefix a= marks the transitive verb kar 'gather'; easkay follows without any affix. The nominalized hi neno frames the ability event as a temporal onset point.

translation: because I cannot go outside,
note: soyne 'go outside' is intransitive; =an is the fourth-person S affix; ka eaykap is the scalar-amplified inability expression in a causal clause.

text: aynu mosir ka ta ney ta pakno an=an ka eaykap kusu
gloss: human land even LOC wherever LOC until exist=4.S even be.unable because
translation: because I cannot stay in the human realm indefinitely,
note: The main verb is an 'exist/stay' with fourth-person =an; ka eaykap expresses the inability to continue. The concessive ka ta 'even LOC' before the locative phrase and the second ka before eaykap are both scalar.

text: somo a=ahunke eaykap pe ne na
translation: There is no way one cannot let (you) in.
note: somo negates the main verb ahunke 'let in'; eaykap 'be unable' lies outside the scope of negation, yielding the reading 'cannot not let in'. The clause-final pe ne na nominalizes and predicates the proposition.

text: e=ma eaykap yakun atuy or ta e=sus ka koyaykus
gloss: 2SG.S=walk be.unable COND sea place LOC 2SG.S=swim even circ.unable
translation: If you cannot walk, you cannot even swim in the sea.
note: Ijäs Lesson 9 constructed example. eaykap covers intrinsic inability (cannot walk); koyaykus marks a circumstantial obstacle that prevents the swimming. The scalar ka reinforces koyaykus.

text: paye=an easirki p mak e=iki hawe an
gloss: go.PL=4.S must NMLZ what 2SG.A=do voice-POSS exist
translation: I have to go — what are you doing?
note: The nominalizer p closes the easirki clause. The final mak e=iki hawe an is a rhetorical question in the hawe-frame existential evidential; the fourth-person =an functions as the narrative first person.

text: wente kuni ramu kor an pe ne aan ru-we ne hine
gloss: devastate COMP think while exist NMLZ COP PRF.MIR track-POSS COP CONJ
translation: — it turned out there was something thinking to cause devastation, and …
note: kuni here is the irrealis complementizer nominalizing wente before the cognition verb ramu kor an 'is thinking'. This is the complement use; the main-clause deontic reading of kuni ne arises when no matrix verb hosts it.

translation: One ought to be there.
note: Constructed to illustrate the main-clause deontic use of kuni ne; modeled on Nakagawa 2024: 310 exx. 461–463 for the Saru dialect.

text: somo a=ahunke eaykap pe ne na e=ahunke yak pirka na
gloss: NEG 4.A=enter.SG be.unable NMLZ COP FIN 2SG.A=enter.SG if be.good FIN
translation: There is nothing stopping you from going in — you should go in.
note: The first clause establishes the possibility via double negation (somo eaykap 'it is not the case that one cannot'). The yak pirka na frame delivers the advice as a directive. The final particle na reinforces directive force.

translation: You may eat it.
note: Ijäs Lesson 10 permission frame, constructed illustration.

translation: If you are tired, you should rest.
note: Ijäs Lesson 10; yak pirka delivers advice conditional on a stated premise.

text: kotan wente kus arki kus ne aan ru-we ne wa
gloss: village devastate PURP come.PL PURP COP PRF.MIR track-POSS COP CONJ
translation: — it turned out that they had been coming to devastate the village, and …
note: kus ne here is the intentional/prospective, not the deontic near-command. The example shows the form in its narrative use, combined with the mirative aan and the inferential ruwe ne. The construction wente kus arki kus ne is a purpose-clause chain: 'coming (in order) to devastate'.

translation: You should go / you will go, then.
note: Constructed to illustrate the near-command reading of kus ne na with a second-person subject; modeled on Nakagawa 2024: 423.

translation: because he will probably come there,
note: First clause of a longer utterance; the continuation is 'let us live together for two or three years.' kusu here is the reason conjunction 'because', not part of the prospective construction kusu ne.

translation: You should go that way then.
note: Nakagawa ex. 469. With a second-person subject and final na, nankor functions as a softened directive rather than a probability statement.

text: an epitta paye=an kusu ne na
gloss: one entire go.PL=4.S PURP COP FIN
translation: I intend to go, spending a whole night.
note: paye is the plural stem of arpa 'go'; =an is the fourth-person single argument, used here as the narrative first person. kusu ne na expresses the speaker's commitment to an unrealized future action.

translation: I will go tomorrow.
note: Constructed illustration of the scheduled-future reading with an overt time adverb. The form is neutral between volitional intention and an event foreseen as certain.

translation: I am just about to go.
note: Constructed illustration of oasi with tane 'now', giving the imminent reading. Nakagawa (2024: 318, exx.500–501) documents this combination.

translation: They are about to arrive.
note: Constructed illustration of etokus; arki is the plural stem of ek 'come'.

translation: the thing called old age
note: Nakagawa ex. 464. manu predicates the nominalized clause as attributed or named: the speaker presents the concept 'old age' as a received designation rather than a directly asserted fact.

text: kotan wente kus arki kus ne aan ru-we ne wa
gloss: village ravage PURP come.PL PURP COP PRF.MIR track-POSS COP CONJ
translation: and it had turned out that they were going to come to ravage the village,
note: The inner purpose clause kotan wente kus arki 'come to ravage the village' is followed by kus ne (prospective: they intended to), then aan (admirative: the speaker realizes this after the fact), then ruwe ne (evidential: presented as established fact). wa closes the clause and chains it to the following predication.

text: tap a=ye katu Piratur sekor a=ye haw-e ne
gloss: this 4.A=say manner Piraturu QUOT 4.A=say voice-POSS COP
translation: This way of saying it is called Piraturu, so they say.
note: hawe (haw-e, 'the voice of —') nominalizes the embedded clause; ne closes it as a direct reportative evidential. The doubled a=ye sequence illustrates the quotation-plus-report structure typical of hawe ne.

translation: I drank tea — how delicious!
note: The bare formal noun hum-i as an exclamatory main clause, without ne. The insubordinated nominalized clause carries the exclamatory value alone; the copula is absent.

translation: (We) have now arrived!
note: siri ne declarative with the sentence-final particle na. The suppletive plural come-form arki (vs. singular ek) encodes number inside the nominalized clause; the evidential scopes over the whole clause including this number distinction.

translation: This potato is green.
note: An individual-level (permanent) property takes the bare concept form ru even though it is visually accessible: sir is barred from individual-level predicates in Tokachi. The existential an replaces the copula ne, as is standard in Tokachi declarative evidential clauses.

text: supuya at kor sir-an ru-we ne anan
gloss: smoke rise while appearance-exist track-POSS COP MIR
translation: Smoke was rising — it turned out!
place: Nakagawa text, Dal Corso siglum NGF: 176
note: Dal Corso ex. 268. The indirect visual siri an is embedded under the direct ruwe ne; the admirative tail anan adds the surprised-retrospective value (glossed MIR). The supporting outer form is systematically ruwe ne, never siri ne — evidence that ruwe ne functions as a higher-scope operator that ratifies another evidential's output as established fact.

translation: I came to meet you.
place: Ito Oda, Chitose; Dal Corso siglum BUG:126
note: Dal Corso ex. 21. The indefinite/fourth person =an serves as the narrative first person; ek=an ruwe ne presents the speaker's own arrival as an established fact, the reasoning-based direct value (DIR.RSN) in Dal Corso's terms.

translation: Is this house yours?
note: Whether a house ‘is one's own’ is an abstract relation, not a perceptible state; hence ruwe, not the visual siri. The bare clause-final ruwe is the polar-interrogative reduction discussed in the section on frames.

text: atuy kor kamuy a=ne hine an=an ru-we ne
gloss: sea have god 4.A=COP CONJ exist=4.S track-POSS COP
translation: I am the god who holds the sea.
note: Hirosawa ex. 16. The fourth-person transitive prefix a= marks the copula and the suffix =an the existential; a self-identification packaging discourse-new information for the addressee.

text: pananpe an penanpe an hine sir-an pe ne ru-we ne hike
gloss: Pananpe exist Penanpe exist CONJ appearance-exist thing COP track-POSS COP although
translation: There were Panampe and Penampe, and …
note: Hirosawa ex. 13; the storyteller's frame-text presents a story-world state of affairs under ruwe ne as established narrative fact.

text: mak an pe kusu e=moyre a ru-we an
gloss: how exist NMLZ because 2SG.S=be.late PFV track-POSS exist
translation: Why were you late?
place: Wateke, Saru; Dal Corso siglum TMA: 12
note: Dal Corso ex. 124. The wh-expression mak an pe kusu ‘for what reason’ opens the clause and the existential an replaces the copula; the perfective a closes the embedded predicate before ruwe.

translation: Yes, I heard it.
note: The final particle un forms the affirmative-answer frame while the formal noun is retained.

text: nep eci=e-sirkirap ka somo ki ru-we ne na
gloss: something 2PL.A=APPL-worry even NEG do track-POSS COP FIN
translation: You will not be troubled by anything.
place: Kaizawa Tsurushino, Biratori; Dal Corso siglum KAY: 2-2,18
note: Dal Corso ex. 128. Negation sits inside the evidential: somo ki denies the verb sirkirap, while ruwe ne stays outside the scope of negation and predicates the whole as recognized fact.

text: mat-kor hine oka=an ru-we ne a p
gloss: wife-have CONJ exist.PL=4.S track-POSS COP PFV NMLZ
translation: he had taken a wife, and we went on living — and yet,
place: Wateke, Saru; Dal Corso siglum TMA: 2
note: Dal Corso ex. 170 (excerpt). The perfective a follows ruwe ne in the post-evidential slot, and the nominalizer p carries the adversative ‘but’ that turns the narrative — confirming that aspect and clause-linking material attach above the evidential.

translation: This potato is green.
note: In Tokachi the bare concept form ru (not the possessed ruwe) closes the clause, and the existential an replaces the copula. An individual-level property takes ru even though it is visually accessible, because sir is barred from permanent properties.

text: supuya at kor sir-an ru-we ne anan
gloss: smoke rise while appearance-exist track-POSS COP MIR
translation: Smoke was rising, it turned out!
place: Nakagawa text, Dal Corso siglum NGF:176
note: Dal Corso ex. 268: the indirect visual siri an is layered under ruwe ne, with the admirative tail anan glossed mirative here. The supporting form is systematically ruwe ne, never siri ne.

text: pon nay ohta i-huraye ruwe-he ne
translation: She washed me in a small river.
place: Piłsudski corpus; Dal Corso siglum PLA: 227
note: Dal Corso ex. 224. The copular ruwehe ne(e) presents a fully processed, personally witnessed event — the more reliable counterpart of the existential ruwehe ʔan; the indefinite-person object i- here references the narrator. East Sakhalin keeps the possessed -he that the southern Hokkaido evidential drops (ruwe-he, not ru-we).

text: tan husko karauto an ruwe-he an manuy
gloss: this be.old box exist track-POSS exist REP
translation: There was this old box.
literal: there is a trace that this old box is there
place: Piłsudski corpus; Dal Corso siglum PLA: 200
note: Dal Corso ex. 226. The inferential is built on the existential an over a clause that itself ends in existential an; the literal ‘there is a trace of —’ stays transparent. Southern Hokkaido lacks this existential ruwehe ʔan and uses only the copular ruwe ne.

translation: I am distributing (food) to my grandfather.
note: The speaker presents her own ongoing action — the food distribution — as a directly visible situation under siri ne.

text: tane a=ko-onne sir-i ne wa tapne
kana: tane a=koónne siri ne wa tapne,
translation: And so I have aged along with it, as one can see —
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker民話8(その3); ILCAA Ainu materials aa-irc/008#6
note: siri ne asserts the visible fact of the narrator's ageing concurrent with the passage of events; the wa-clause links the observation to the following narrative beat.

text: i=resu sir-i an sekor yaynu=an kor an=an a p
gloss: 4.O=raise appearance-POSS exist QUOT 4.S=think while 4.S=exist PFV NMLZ
translation: I had been thinking that (my older sibling) was raising me, but (it turned out otherwise)…
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker民話11; ILCAA Ainu materials aa-irc/013#348
note: The siri an here carries the aspectual / indirect value: 'it seemed that he was raising me'. The sekor yaynu=an frame embeds this under the narrator's own cognitive report; the nominalized tail a p carries an adversative nuance.

text: ineap kusun a=i=eoripak wa siri ki ya ka a=eramiskari
gloss: how.very CONJ 4.A=1SG.O=respect CONJ appearance-POSS do Q even 4.A=not.know
translation: I was being respected to such an extent as I had never seen before.
place: 平賀さだも, uwepeker ‘ウラユシウンクㇽ’ [biratori/010/003#10]
note: The narrator's own experience of being honored is assessed under siri ki — the external-perspective indirect visual: the situation is presented as it appears to sight, distanced from the speaker's direct assertion. The ya ka 'whether or not' frame pairs the appearance clause with eramiskari's experiential negation ('beyond anything I have ever known').

translation: Did you go to Tokyo?
note: Kanazawa 1898 (Saru topical conversation dictionary), cited in Nakagawa 2024: 394 for the siri an interrogative frame. The existential an replaces the copula; no question word is present, and the polar reading is pragmatically available.

text: tap a=ye katu Piratur sekor a=ye haw-e ne
gloss: thus 4.A=say manner Biratori QUOT 4.A=say voice-POSS COP
translation: The way one says it is 'Biratori' (so they call it).
place: Nakagawa ex. 778; underlying source Kawamura 1985: 30, Saru
note: hawe ne predicates the naming 'Biratori' as verbally transmitted knowledge — the speaker heard this name used, rather than independently assigning it. Compare the ruwe ne version at Hirosawa (2026: 81, ex. 24), where the same naming is presented as assimilated personal knowledge, illustrating the gradient boundary between the two forms.

text: Nispa-utar nisatta ekimne sekor haw-as pe ne kusu
gloss: rich.man-PL tomorrow go.to.mountains QUOT voice-stand NMLZ COP PURP
translation: The men of standing would go to the mountains the next day (so it was rumored), and therefore …
place: Bugaeva collection (Ito Oda, Chitose 1998–2000); Dal Corso siglum BUG:377; Dal Corso ex. 272
note: hawe as in the hearsay function: no specific speaker is named. The embedded hawe as clause is nominalized with pe ne before kusu, relating the rumored event to what follows. hawe as scopes over the full reported content.

translation: He went away (so I hear / so they say).
note: Minimal declarative hawe ne: the formal noun plus copula predicates the verb phrase as verbally sourced information. Any finite verb phrase may appear before hawe ne in this position.

text: e=hosipi haw-e ne kusu tane anakne a=eyayramkar pe ne na
gloss: 2SG.S=return voice-POSS COP PURP now TOP 4.A=resign NMLZ COP FIN
translation: Because you returned (so they/you said), I will now resign myself.
place: Kawakamimatsuko, uwepeker minwa 14 (second half), ILCAA Ainu materials, aa-irc/021#271
note: hawe ne in a causal subordinate clause (hawe ne kusu 'because it is said/heard that …'). The evidential scopes over the embedded proposition; kusu then relates the reported event to the main clause.

translation: She came down (the voice said — and so the narrator presents as traditional knowledge).
place: Kayano (Kaizawa Tsurushino, Biratori); Dal Corso siglum KAY; Dal Corso ex. 273
note: Double evidential: hawe as encodes the character's indirect verbal source; ruwe ne layers the narrator's framing of the event as story-world fact. The supporting outer form is systematically ruwe ne, never siri ne — a distributional argument for ruwe ne's role as a knowledge-ratifying operator.

text: usa sisakpe a=i=y-e-re hum-i ne ya
translation: Whether I was given all sorts of delicious things to eat…
place: Wateke (Saru), Tamura audio materials; Dal Corso siglum TMA: 42
note: Dal Corso ex. 242 (DIR.FLT). A gustatory stimulus (being given food) appears under the sound/feeling-derived humi ne, illustrating the sensor-stimulus mismatch discussed at pp. 307, 311. The verb complex a=i=y-e-re is a causative benefactive ('caused to eat for 4O'); ya is a question/dubitative particle.

translation: It had completely frozen solid.
note: Chiri 1936: 192, cited via Hirosawa 2026: 66. A bodily-tactile state (freezing solid) is encoded with humi ne; the admirative tail awan carries the surprised-retrospective value. The source noun hum 'feeling' grounds the tactile domain in the same formal noun that covers sound.

translation: It felt as though anger was welling up.
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker 'Folktale 13' (Saru); AA研 aa-irc/016, sent. 122
note: The fourth-person prefix a= marks the agent in the narrative frame. The periphrasis humi ne pekor yay-nu=an 'it felt as though' is a common collocation combining the sensory evidential with the simulative pekor and the reflexive-perception verb yaynu; see the section on frames for related variants.

text: hum-as hum-i ne kunak ku=ramu kor ku=soyne a p
gloss: sound-stand sound-POSS COP COMP 1SG.A=think while 1SG.S=go.outside PFV NMLZ
kana: húmas humi ne kunak ku=ramu kor ku=soyne a p
translation: Thinking that it sounded like there was a noise, I went outside — but (nothing was there).
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker 'Folktale 8 (Part 1)' (Saru); AA研 aa-irc/006, sent. 358
note: The contracted form húmas (= hum-as 'a sound arises') provides the sensory stimulus; humi ne encodes the speaker's non-visual sensory access to that sound; kunak introduces the complement of the cognition verb ramu 'think/feel'. The nominalized tail p sets the clause as backgrounded against a disappointed expectation.

translation: I drank tea — how delicious!
note: The bare formal noun humi functions as an exclamative main clause, without the copula ne. The gustatory evaluation triggers the non-visual sensory evidential; the insubordinated frame conveys immediate spontaneous reaction.

translation: The sound of someone arriving was heard.
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker 'Folktale 8 (Part 2)' (Saru); AA研 aa-irc/007, sent. 200
note: The posture verb as replaces the copula ne: the narrator infers the person's arrival from an auditory impression rather than direct sight. The indirect humi as contrasts here with the direct humi ne that would encode the arrival as directly sensed.

text: poro cep a=ne hum-i ne hum-i as orano a=yupi-hi os ma=an wa
gloss: big fish 4.A=COP sound-POSS COP sound-POSS stand after.that 4.POSS=elder.brother-POSS follow swim=4.S CONJ
translation: It felt as though I had become a great fish, and then I swam after my elder brother.
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker 'Folktale 11' (Saru); AA研 aa-irc/013, sent. 32
note: Dal Corso 2018: 333 (ex. 275 context). The direct humi ne presents the bodily transformation as directly felt; the immediately following humi as then hedges it as also inferential, conveying that the same sensation was simultaneously vivid and uncertain. Both evidentials draw on the non-verbal sensory channel.

text: pirka menoko a=ne aan ru-we ne
translation: She turned out to be a beautiful woman!
note: Constructed after the attested pattern in Hirosawa 2026: 90 (ex. 33), Tamura audio materials 02-06: 42 (Saru). The auxiliary aan contributes the mirative reading; ruwe ne closes the proposition as established knowledge. The evidential itself is not the source of the surprise.

text: supuya at kor sir-an ru-we ne anan
gloss: smoke rise while appearance-exist track-POSS COP MIR
translation: Smoke was rising — it turned out!
place: Nakagawa text; Dal Corso siglum NGF: 176
note: Dal Corso ex. 268. The indirect visual siri an is layered under ruwe ne; anan follows the entire complex and contributes the surprise reading. The mirative is anan, not the evidential predicate it follows. On the double-evidential construction siri an ruwe ne, see §5 below.

translation: (It is established that he) did not go.
note: Negation somo ki scopes over the embedded verb paye; ruwe ne predicates the resulting negative proposition as an established fact, outside the scope of somo. The parallel pattern holds for siri ne, hawe ne, and humi ne (e.g. …somo ki siri ne).

text: kamuy ek ru-we ne wa paye=an
gloss: god come track-POSS COP CONJ go=4.S
translation: A god came, and (we) went.
note: The clause-linker wa follows ruwe ne in the post-evidential slot, showing that clause-linking material attaches outside the evidential predicate. The embedded verb ek and the person marker =an carry the clause-internal TAM and agreement; ruwe ne scopes over all of it.

translation: Though tired, (she) cooked.
note: Constructed after the adversative siri use documented in Horobetsu and in early records (Chiri 1923: 86, cited by Takahashi 2018: 108). The bare formal noun siri without a following ne functions as an adversative/concessive clause marker, a use not attested in well-described Saru. Takahashi 2018: 111 treats this as a further step in the grammaticalization of the possessed-form nominalizers.

translation: (She) reportedly came — and so it was.
note: Constructed after the Type A combinations in Dal Corso 2018: 331 (e.g. Kayano text, ran hawe as ruwe ne; Dal Corso ex. 273, siglum KAY, narrator Kaizawa Tsurushino, Biratori). The inner hawe as (indirect reportative) presents the event from a reported source; the outer ruwe ne frames it as the narrator's established fact.

text: poro cep a=ne hum-i ne hum-i as orano
gloss: big fish 4.A=COP hum-POSS COP hum-POSS stand after
translation: Feeling as though I were a great fish, and as that sensation arose —
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker, ILCAA Ainu materials (AA研アイヌ語資料) 013, line 32
note: The direct humi ne presents the speaker's immediate non-visual sensation (feeling as though one is a fish); humi as presents the arising of that same sensation from an external, indirect-sensory standpoint. The two forms cooperate: direct inner experience followed by indirect-sensory report of its occurrence. The sentence continues with a clause describing the speaker swimming after her elder brother.

translation: One did not even see its figure.
note: Nakagawa ex. 832. The simple preverbal pattern; the possessed noun noka-ha carries the additive poka ‘even’, a polarity item licensed under somo.

translation: I will not go.
place: Bugaeva ex. 73, siglum NN 28 (Nakagawa Chitose data)

text: tanto anak somo ek nankor wa
gloss: today TOP NEG come.SG probably FIN
translation: He probably will not come today.
note: The negator precedes the verb ek; the dubitative nankor and the final wa stay in their postverbal positions.

translation: It did not rain.
note: Takahashi ex. 11b, against the affirmative ruyanpe ruy ‘it rained’ (ex. 11a); the clauses differ only in somo.

text: nep a=nukar ka somo ki korka
translation: Although I did not see anything,
note: Nakagawa ex. 833. The periphrasis with ka; the indefinite nep ka ‘anything’ is licensed under the negation.

translation: Even if you do not take revenge,
note: Nakagawa ex. 834. The same periphrasis without ka; yayeymontasa is intransitive, so eci= indexes the 2PL subject.

translation: I am not angry.
note: The bracketed [ku=iruska ka] is the object-like complement that ki formally negates.

text: tan pe anak seta ka somo ne wa
gloss: this thing TOP dog even NEG COP FIN
translation: This one is not a dog.
note: Satō ex. 6. Copular ka somo ne; somo precedes the copula ne, with ka on the complement seta.

text: sinep ka a=isamka ka somo ki ru-we ne kusu
gloss: one even 4.A=lose even NEG do track-POSS COP because
translation: Since I did not lose even a single one,
note: Nakagawa ex. 779. The negated predicate a=isamka ka somo ki sits inside the evidential ru-we ne; the evidential itself is outside the scope of somo.

translation: He went to sleep without eating.
note: The parallel with the successive linker, *somo ipe wa mokor, is ungrammatical: a negated event links only with the stative no.

translation: There is not even one who can rival me.
note: The negative-polarity phrase sinep ka ‘even one’ is licensed by the negative existential isam; the object prefix i= belongs to epetturasi ‘rival, be a match for’, not to isam.

text: seta ka nep ka isam pe ne a p
gloss: dog even something even not.exist NMLZ COP PFV NMLZ
translation: There was not even a dog or anything,
note: Repeated ka ‘even’ over seta ‘dog’ and nep ‘anything’ yields the exhaustive reading under isam; the tail pe ne a p nominalizes the clause and carries the adversative ‘but’.

text: k=uni-hi okari anakne nep ka isam
translation: There is nothing around my house.
note: Satō’s negation example. The locative phrase k=uni-hi okari ‘around my house’ fixes the domain of absence, and the absent entity is the ka-indefinite nep ka, subject of isam.

text: ene an nispa maci-hi ene tamasay ka sak ru-we an hi an
gloss: such exist rich.man wife-POSS such necklace even lack track-POSS exist NMLZ exist
translation: The wife of such a wealthy man does not even have a necklace.
note: The possessor is the wife (maci-hi); the lacked entity tamasay ka ‘even a necklace’ is the object of privative sak. The tail ru-we an hi an is the situational-evidential frame, handled in the evidential chapters.

translation: I went home without my bag.
note: Ijäs’s constructed example. The lacked entity is the possessive phrase ku=kor pukuro ‘my bag’; sak chains to the main clause with the stative linker no.

translation: I cannot walk.
note: The simplest frame: apkas ‘walk’ carries the first-person subject, and eaykap follows it person-unmarked.

text: na hepera paye a=eaykap ru-we an
translation: Is it that one cannot go any further upstream?
note: a= indexes the subject of eaykap, and the embedded event paye ‘go (PL)’ is its object; ruwe an is the content-question frame of the evidential.

text: a=tekehe ka a=epuni ka eaykap pe ne kusu
gloss: 4=hand.POSS even 4.A=raise even cannot NMLZ COP because
translation: Because I could not even raise my hand,
note: The possessor prefix a= on the possessed noun tekehe is glossed by person alone; the verb epuni keeps its agentive a=, and eaykap follows the predicate after the scalar ka.

text: kira=an ka apkas=an ka eaykap no cis patek a=ki kor
gloss: flee=4.S even walk=4.S even cannot ADV cry only 4.A=do while
translation: Unable to flee or to walk, doing nothing but cry,
note: Two coordinated intransitive verbs each carry the fourth-person subject =an under one eaykap; the negated event links to what follows with no, not wa (see below).

translation: Last night I could not sleep.
note: The inability is situational — sleep would not come — which is the domain of koyaykus rather than eaykap.

text: cip a=o ka eramiskari p ne korka
gloss: boat 4.A=board even never NMLZ COP although
translation: Although I had never been in a boat,
note: The event cip a=o ‘board a boat’ is the experiential domain of eramiskari; p ne korka frames it as a concessive nominalized clause.

text: an=cise soyke ta asip=an ka eramuskare
translation: I had never even gone outside my house.
note: Eramuskare is the Ishikari variant of eramiskari in the banked source.

translation: I looked at it, but I do not understand.
note: Affirmative perception nukar contrasts directly with the cognition negative erampewtek in one clause.

translation: Even if you do not understand, I will not be angry.
note: The cognition negative erampewtek and the standard negator somo co-occur, each over its own verb.

text: sir-kunne kor soyne hi a=eramiskari aan ru-we somo ne
gloss: land-be.dark when go.out NMLZ 4.A=not.know PFV track-POSS NEG COP
translation: I had not known that he went out when night fell.
note: ruwe somo ne here is the rhetorical/convictional frame ‘was I not unaware’, i.e. emphatic ‘I really did not know’, with the lexical negative eramiskari inside it.

text: kuani anakne pu ari an cise ku=nukar eramuskare
gloss: 1SG TOP storehouse QUOT exist house 1SG.A=see never
translation: I have never seen a building called a storehouse.
note: The Tokachi variant eramuskare follows the person-marked verb ku=nukar as the experiential negative ‘have never seen’; pu ari an cise is ‘a building called a pu (storehouse)’.

translation: Someone is coming.
note: Constructed minimal pair to the attested negative in (3): nen ka is the plain existential ‘someone’ in a non-negative clause, the negative-polarity ‘no one’ only under a negator.

text: nep a=nukar ka somo ki korka
translation: Although I did not see anything,
note: Nakagawa ex. 833. The base nep takes its indefinite reading because it stands in the complement that somo ki negates; the second ka focuses that complement.

text: tanpe akkari nep ka somo e=kon rusuy
gloss: this.one beyond what even NEG 2SG.A=have want
translation: Do you not want anything more than this?
note: Kanazawa, 沙流. nep ka ‘anything’ under preverbal somo; the question expects the negative answer ‘nothing’.

translation: Is no one there?
note: Kanazawa, 沙流. nen ka under isam yields ‘no one’; the reduced clause-final ru-we marks the polar question (see the evidential frames cross-referenced below).

text: seta ka nep ka isam pe ne a p
gloss: dog even what even not.exist NMLZ COP PFV NMLZ
translation: though there were no dogs or anything,
note: Nakagawa ex. 529. Two distinct uses of ka in one clause: additive seta ka ‘dogs too’ and the indefinite nep ka ‘anything’, both under isam.

text: a=teke-he ka a=epuni ka eaykap pe ne kusu
gloss: 4.POSS=hand-POSS even 4.A=raise even cannot NMLZ COP because
translation: because I could not even raise my hand,
note: Nakagawa ex. 532. The negative-ability predicate eaykap is the licenser; ka marks scalar ‘even’ on each focused constituent.

text: nep ka menoko payeka siri henne eci=nukar
gloss: what even woman pass.by appearance NEG 2PL.A=see
translation: Did you see no sign at all that a woman had passed?
note: The negator henne licenses the same nep-plus-ka indefinite as standard somo.

text: nep kar kay omo an=ki wa okay=an
gloss: what do even NEG 4.A=do CONJ exist.PL=4.S
translation: We lived doing no work at all.
note: kay is the Shiranuka focus variant of ka, omo the Shiranuka negator; the indefinite-licensing pattern is invariant across these dialect forms.

text: nep ka pawci a=omare ka somo ki
gloss: what even poison 4.A=put.in even NEG do
translation: I did not put in any poison.
note: Nakagawa ex. 530. The first ka forms the indefinite nep ka ‘anything’; the second ka focuses the notional predicate a=omare before somo ki.

text: tan pe anak seta ka somo ne wa
gloss: this thing TOP dog even NEG COP FIN
translation: This one is not a dog.
note: Satō ex. 6. The focused predicate nominal seta ka is negated by somo before the copula ne; the same ka that builds nep ka here focuses the complement of the copula.

translation: There is not a single one that is my equal.
note: Nakagawa ex. 1025. The scalar sinep ka ‘even one’ under isam yields ‘not even one’.

translation: There is nothing at all.
note: The intensifier oar ‘completely’ reinforces nep ka under isam to ‘absolutely nothing’.

text: tu ipe somo ki re ipe somo ki no
gloss: two eat.a.meal NEG do three eat.a.meal NEG do ADV
translation: eating neither two meals nor three meals,
note: Nakagawa ex. 531. Repetition of somo ki yields exhaustive denial; the stative linker no closes the negated subordinate clause (see the subordinate-asymmetry section of the standard-negation chapter).

text: sinep ka a=isamka ka somo ki ru-we ne kusu
gloss: one even 4.A=lose even NEG do track-POSS COP because
translation: since I did not lose even a single one,
note: Nakagawa ex. 779. The scalar sinep ka and the negation somo ki sit inside the proposition over which ru-we ne predicates evidential status; the evidential is not in the scope of somo.

translation: Do not come near the fire.
From now on, never think bad thoughts.
note: Shiranuka has no separate build-time dialect label, so the example is tagged HK. The Shiranuka form etekke precedes the object wenpuri and the verb ramu.

text: eciki iruska no hopuni wa e=koucaskuma=an kusu ne na
gloss: PROH be.angry CONJ get.up CONJ 2SG.O=explain=4.S PURP COP FIN
translation: Get up without being angry, and I will explain the reason to you.
note: The Ishikari form eciki heads a no-linked negative-directive clause ‘without being angry’, which is followed by an affirmative directive continuation.

translation: Do not sleep.
place: Kanazawa 1898; NINJAL topical dictionary, ‘Sleeping and waking’
note: The bluntest form: prohibitive adverb plus a bare, person-unmarked verb.

translation: Do not play such tricks.
note: The final yan carries the polite or plural value that also marks affirmative directives.

translation: Please do not be startled in the least.
note: The polarity item ponno ka ‘even a little’ precedes the prohibitive and is licensed within its scope.

text: iteki e=esina no e=ye p ne na
translation: Say it without hiding it.
note: Both verbs keep second-person subject indexing. The no-linked first predicate gives the prohibited manner; the p ne na frame delivers the positive directive.

translation: Do not follow me.
place: Kawakami Matsuko, ILCAA Ainu materials, uwepeker 9
note: The indefinite-person object i= references the narrator; the no-clause links the prohibited action to the following discourse.

translation: You need not eat.
note: Ijäs Lesson 10. The permission frame yakka pirka is negated with somo, not with iteki; the result is a release from necessity, not a command.

text: iteki pasirota somo eci=ki nankor na
translation: You are certainly not to scold (him).
note: The notional verb pasirota ‘scold, revile’ is negated through the somo ki periphrasis, and eci=ki hosts the second-person plural index; iteki frames the whole as a directive, with the modal nankor na giving the emphatic ‘certainly not’.

translation: Be careful not to fall.
note: Reproduced in Ijäs Lesson 10. The second-person subject is indexed on the verb e=hacir, unlike the unindexed verb of a bare prohibitive.

text: a=yupi-hi i=resu hine oka=an pe ne hike
translation: My elder brother raised me, and we lived on, and …
note: Each clause around hine is finite: i=resu carries its own fourth-person object index, oka=an its fourth-person S; pe ne closes the chain on a formal-noun predicate before the further connective hike.

text: micipa ku=kar hine ohaw or k=omare
translation: I gathered honewort and put it into the soup.
note: A plain hine sequence: two finite predicates, each with first-person A indexing, listed in order with no claim of dependence.

text: hekaci suma osura wa ontaro hokus
gloss: child stone throw CONJ barrel fall.over
translation: The child threw a stone, and the barrel fell over.
note: A different-subject wa chain: the thrower is the subject of the first clause, the barrel of the second.

text: kanpi ku=sanke ru-we ne akusu itasa kanpi ek ru-we ne
gloss: letter 1SG.A=send.out track-POSS COP CONJ in.return letter come track-POSS COP
translation: I sent a letter, and a reply came.
note: Akusu attaches after a ruwe ne evidential tail: the first clause is already closed as an established fact before the discovery linker is added.

text: ku=caranke ka somo ki no ku=hosipi
translation: I went home without complaining.
note: No follows a negated action predicate; both clauses share the first-person subject, so the choice of no over wa here tracks polarity, not a change of subject.

text: e=ype rusuy haw-e ne yakun tan kaboca e
gloss: 2SG.S=eat.a.meal DES voice-POSS COP CONJ this pumpkin eat
translation: If you are saying that you are hungry, eat this pumpkin.
note: The protasis closes on the reportative tail hawe ne before yakun; the matrix is an imperative, one of the several moods yakun freely admits.

text: apto as yakka upas as yakka wakka poro yakka sonno k=ek kusne wa
gloss: rain fall CONJ snow fall CONJ water be.big CONJ truly 1SG.S=come intend FIN
translation: Even if it rains, even if it snows, even if there is a flood, I will truly come.
note: A teaching example built on a triple yakka listing; constructed, not corpus-attested. The future kusu ne appears here in its reduced one-word form kusne.

text: sisam itak ani ku=respa p ne kusu aynu itak sinep ka erampewtek pa
gloss: Japanese language INS 1SG.A=raise NMLZ COP CONJ Ainu language one even not.understand PL
translation: Because I raised them in Japanese, they do not understand even one word of Ainu.
note: Kusu marks the preceding formal-noun predicate p ne as the cause of the following clause; the matrix verb erampewtek takes the plural pa.

text: tap a=ye katu Piratur sekor a=ye haw-e ne
gloss: now 4.A=say way Piratur QUOT 4.A=say voice-POSS COP
translation: The way it is said now is to call it Piratur.
note: Sekor frames the quoted name; the fourth-person a=ye and the reportative tail hawe ne close the naming frame.

text: a=kor katkemat utar an=oskur kane kesto an konno oka=an
gloss: 4.A=have lady PL 4.A=cherish CONJ every.day exist CONJ exist.PL=4.S
translation: Cherishing our ladies, we lived on day after day.
note: Shizunai kane marks the simultaneity Saru would mark with kor, and konno the recurrent-time conditional; both differ from the Saru forms.

translation: Walking beneath it, I went along, and then…
note: wa marks the walking as manner and route of the going; ayne is the culminative particle treated in §5 below.

text: hokure pirkano e=ipere wa mimus yakne
translation: Now, feed her well so that, once she has fattened up…
note: wa links the feeding (E1, cause) to the fattening (E2, effect); the subsequent conditional yakne opens a premise on the result-state.

text: hekaci suma osura wa ontaro hokus
gloss: child stone throw CONJ barrel fall.over
translation: The child threw a stone, and the barrel fell over.
note: The thrower (child) is the A of the first clause; the barrel is the S of the second. Satō uses this example to show that wa carries no same-subject requirement.

text: sikerpeni kapu a=sospa wa siwnin pe a=uyna wa kusuri ne a=kar
gloss: Phellodendron bark 4.A=peel CONJ yellow.bark NMLZ 4.A=take CONJ medicine COP 4.A=make
translation: She peeled the bark of the Phellodendron tree, took the yellow inner bark, and made it into medicine.
place: 横山裕之, 'sikerpeni', Ainu Times no. 18/3, text 12; corpus ainu-times/018/3#12
note: A three-step wa-chain; each step is a completed result-state enabling the next. pe after siwnin nominalizes the NP; the fourth-person a= carries the narrating subject.

translation: Crying and crying, and finally…
place: 丸野和子, '"Kuma" turano k=an', Ainu Times no. 15/1, text 24 (excerpt)
note: The V a V a ayne intensifier pattern: the perfective a marks each iteration; ayne closes the protracted stretch and points to the outcome. The full sentence continues with the result clause.

translation: a hanging cup
note: racitke wa an is the attributive resultative: 'the cup that hangs / is in the state of being hung'. The construction modifies tuki as a head noun.

translation: S/he has gone.

text: a=onaha an a=unuhu an hine oka=an
translation: My father was there, my mother was there, and we lived on.
note: Nakagawa ex. 601; a stock prose-tale opening. The three items — father, mother, living — are listed in order with hine as a pure temporal enumerator, no causal claim made.

text: rikun kanto ta a=saha i=resu hine oka=an pe ne hike
gloss: above sky LOC 4.POSS=elder.sister 4.O=raise CONJ exist.PL=4.S NMLZ COP CONJ
translation: My elder sister in the sky raised me, and we lived on, and …
place: 川上まつ子「uwepeker 民話15」, AA研アイヌ語資料, aa-irc/022#0
note: The hine chain closes on oka=an pe ne hike, the standard narrative-pivot formula. The formal-noun pe and the loose-link hike then open the episode proper.

translation: After killing that small deer, …
place: 川上まつ子「isoytak 独話1」, AA研アイヌ語資料, aa-irc/003#73
note: The fourth-person agent a= completes the killing; akusu opens the clause in which the narrator discovers or experiences what follows. The continuation is not preserved in the banked fragment.

text: kanpi ku=sanke ru-we ne akusu itasa kanpi ek ru-we ne
gloss: letter 1SG.A=send.out track-POSS COP CONJ in.return letter come track-POSS COP
translation: I had sent a letter, and in return a letter came.
note: Satō ex. 16 / Satō 2009 ex. 32. The discovery linker attaches outside the ruwe ne evidential tail. The cross-linguistic asymmetry with Japanese — factual と/たら cannot follow preceding のだ, but Ainu akusu can follow ruwe ne — is discussed in §5.

translation: I looked, and nothing was there.
place: Chiri Yukie, kamuy yukar document 1, line 33 [yukie-kamuyyukar/004/0#33]
note: A Horobetsu verse text uses awa where Saru prose would use akusu, instantiating the register-and-dialect split of the table. The =as suffix indexes the singular narrator-voice in the exclusive first-person form, as established for the Horobetsu yukar convention in §oral-literature.

text: an=nu akus a=kor yupo utar hawetoko koeskari.
translation: When it was heard, my brothers' voices suddenly fell silent.
place: 織田ステノ (Oda Steno), Shizunai; uwepeker「Moyuk（前半）」, AA研アイヌ語資料, aa-irc/017#51
note: Shizunai prose uses the reduced form akus in the same discovery function as Saru akusu. The compound hawetoko koeskari 'voices fall suddenly silent' is listed as a lexical unit in Tamura's Saru dictionary (1996); here it predicates the brothers' voices. The fourth-person prefix a= marks the narrator's kin (4.POSS 'my brothers'), and akus opens the clause in which the silence is discovered.

text: sirokane otcike or sirokane makiri saya eusi wa kasi mikemike kor san hine
gloss: silver tray place silver small.knife sheath be.with CONJ surface sparkle CONJ descend CONJ
translation: The silver knife on the silver tray, with its sheath, came descending while gleaming on the surface.
note: The mikemike kor san sequence is the simultaneity construction: gleaming (ongoing) kor descending. The preceding saya eusi wa closes an attendant-state clause ('sheathed, and'); hine continues the chain.

translation: While I was dancing, s/he looked at me.
note: Different-subject kor clause: the dancer (first person, ku=) and the observer (third person, unexpressed) are distinct. After Tamura 2000: 155, adapted by Ijäs as a teaching example.

translation: (s/he) is walking
note: Paradigmatic progressive: simultaneous kor followed by the existential an. The subject is third/fourth person, zero-marked on both predicates in this canonical form.

text: a=onaha somo mokor no kamuyoritak kor an
gloss: 4.POSS=father NEG sleep CONJ pray.to.god CONJ exist
translation: Father was praying to the gods without sleep.
note: no closes the negated somo mokor clause ('without sleeping'); kor an on kamuyoritak forms the progressive 'was praying'. Both no and kor are simultaneous-type connectives, assigned by the temporal phase of their respective first predicates.

text: a=kor huci a=kor ekasi earkinne i=omap wa sirkunne kor i=ukotumam wa hotke=an
gloss: 4.A=have grandmother 4.A=have grandfather both 4.O=love CONJ become.night CONJ 4.O=hold.together CONJ sleep=4.S
translation: My grandmother and grandfather both loved me, and whenever night came they would hold me close and sleep.
note: The first two a=kor are the transitive possession verb 'have' (4th-person A prefix); sirkunne kor is the habitual conditional 'whenever it became night'. The recurrent pattern — night after night — is the core habitual reading.

text: ku=cis a ku=cis a ayne k=esikarun kor ku=cis patek ku=ki kor k=an
gloss: 1SG.S=weep PFV 1SG.S=weep PFV CONJ 1SG.S=recall CONJ 1SG.S=weep only 1SG.A=do CONJ 1SG.S=exist
translation: I cried and cried, and finally, whenever I recalled it, I was doing nothing but weep.
place: 丸野和子, 'Kuma turano k=an', Ainu Times 015/1
note: k=esikarun kor: habitual conditional 'whenever I recalled it'. ku=ki kor k=an: progressive 'was continuously doing'. Two distinct kor readings appear within the same clause chain.

text: a=kor katkemat utar an=oskur kane kesto an konno oka=an
gloss: 4.A=have lady PL 4.A=cherish CONJ every.day exist CONJ exist.PL=4.S
translation: Cherishing our ladies, we lived on day after day.
note: kane marks the simultaneity that Saru kor covers; konno marks the recurrent-time relation that Saru also assigns to kor in its conditional reading. The Shizunai system distributes these functions across two distinct particles.

text: sirkunne yakun suy ruyanpe an nankor
gloss: get.dark CONJ again storm exist probably
translation: If it gets dark, there will probably be another storm.
note: yakun with a conjectural main clause (nankor 'probably'); Satō uses this Chitose example to illustrate the absence of mood restrictions on yakun. The particle is compatible with nankor here, with an imperative elsewhere (Satō 2009: 52 ex. 28), and with a declarative in general statements.

translation: Keeping you alive is frightening.
note: Nakagawa ex. 651. yak with an evaluative-stative matrix (isitoma 'be frightening / dangerous'); the indefinite 4th-person agent a= covers an unspecified subject ('one'), and =an marks 4th-person S on the matrix predicate. The Japanese rendering 'お前を生かしておくと恐ろしい' confirms the warning-evaluation reading.

text: itak=an ciki e=nu katu ene an hi
gloss: speak=4.S CONJ 2SG.A=hear manner thus exist NMLZ
translation: As I speak, listen in the following manner.
note: Nakagawa ex. 655. ciki closes the premise clause (itak=an 'one speaks / as I speak'), and the matrix is a nominalized directive — the standard formula for opening a speech, recipe, or demonstration. The imperative force is embedded in the nominalized ene an hi 'the manner in which (you are to) listen'.

translation: When(ever) it gets dark, the birds go home.
note: Satō's illustration of the habitual-conditional kor: darkness is a recurrent condition and the birds' return a recurrent response. The associative plural utar after cikap collects the birds as a group. A formal-noun tail pe ne frequently closes the matrix of such clauses to foreground the generalization.

text: kironnu=an yakun a=i=rayke yakun a=i=rayke yakka pirka
translation: If I am full, even if they kill me — let them; it is fine.
note: Nakagawa ex. 641. The first two clauses deploy yakun for successive hypothetical premises; the third uses yakka with the evaluative pirka in the concessive-permissive reading. The indefinite 4th-person agent a= covers an unspecified actor; i= marks the 4th-person object.

translation: You may eat it.
note: Teaching illustration of the permissive yakka pirka frame, constructed after Ijäs L8 ex. 11-5. The Shizunai parallel e=kor yakka pirka 'you may keep it' (Refsing 1986: 254, ex. 448) confirms the construction across dialects.

text: nay poro p ne korka nay nutap ka hutne uske ne wa an
gloss: river big NMLZ COP CONJ river bend even narrow place COP CONJ exist
translation: The river was big, but even the bends had become narrow.
note: Nakagawa ex. 662. The first clause closes on a formal-noun predicate p ne before korka; the particle spans the expectation set by the size of the river and the counter-result of narrow meanders. The resultative wa an at the end of the matrix presents a state that has come into being.

translation: (Someone) went out to gather firewood.
note: Kusu marks the preceding activity as the purpose of the following motion verb soyne 'go out'. The fourth-person suffix =an indexes the narrator-external agent on both verbs.

text: kese a=anpa wa arpa=an rusuy kusu cip etoko a=oyki hine
gloss: behind 4.A=pursue CONJ go=4.S DES CONJ boat prow 4.A=prepare CONJ
translation: Wanting to pursue and go, (she) made the boat ready.
note: Kusu marks the desiderative clause arpa=an rusuy ('wanting to go in pursuit') as the reason for the preparation. The sequential hine links that preparation to the next event in the narrative chain.

text: sisam itak ani ku=respa p ne kusu aynu itak sinep ka erampewtek pa
gloss: Japanese language INS 1SG.A=raise NMLZ COP CONJ Ainu language one EMPH not.understand PL
translation: Because I raised them in Japanese, they do not understand a single word of Ainu.
note: The formal-noun predicate p ne nominalizes the cause clause; kusu marks it as causal. The plural marker pa on the matrix verb reflects multiple objects. The instrumental ani marks the means of upbringing.

text: e=hosipi haw-e ne kusu tane anakne a=eyayramkar pe ne na
gloss: 2SG.S=return voice-POSS COP CONJ now TOP 4.A=give.up NMLZ COP FIN
translation: Because you came back (as they say), now I give up.
note: The reportative evidential haw-e ne (voice-POSS COP: 'it is said that') precedes kusu, marking the cause proposition as known by report before kusu signals it as the reason for giving up. The matrix clause closes on a formal-noun predicate pe ne with the final particle na.

translation: Because you came, I returned.
note: Wa kusu: wa closes the first clause as a completed event; kusu marks it as the cause of the return. The same sentence with plain kusu (e=ek kusu ku=hosipi) is grammatical but leaves the purpose reading marginally open; wa kusu disambiguates in favour of cause. Constructed after Nakagawa (2024: 353) and Ijäs (2023).

translation: (She) intends to go.
note: Extracted from the quoted-speech context '…paye=an kusu ne na.' sekor hawean 'she said: I intend to go.' The copula ne bears no person index; paye=an already carries the fourth-person S suffix =an. The final particle na closes the quoted clause.

text: a=onaha somo mokor no kamuyoritak kor an
gloss: 4.POSS=father NEG sleep CONJ pray CONJ exist
translation: My father, without sleeping, was praying to the gods.
note: no follows the negated predicate somo mokor 'does not sleep'; the main-clause progressive kamuyoritak kor an 'was praying' is expressed with the simultaneity particle kor plus the existential an.

translation: Without eating, she went.
note: The canonical somo V no construction: no is the required linker after a negated action predicate. Compare the unpreferred *somo ipe wa, which is disfavoured precisely because the preceding predicate is negated.

translation: You are acting as if you can see something.
note: pekor follows the finite clause nep ka e=nukar 'you see something' and connects to the main clause e=yki 'you behave/act'. The presupposition is that nothing is actually visible — the comparison is counterfactual. Satō (2008: 56) uses this example to contrast pekor with noyne: noyne would instead report a genuine inference from evidence.

text: tane tamanko kor noyne okokokse hawe as
gloss: now egg have INFR cluck voice-POSS exist.PL
translation: Apparently having just laid an egg, it is clucking kok-kok.
note: The subject (a hen) is implicit. kor is the transitive verb 'have'; noyne is the inferential clause-linker that marks the entire first clause [tane tamanko kor] 'now having an egg' as inferred rather than directly witnessed. okokokse is onomatopoeic 'kok-kok' used as a sound verb; hawe as 'there is the voice/sound of' closes the main clause.

text: a=ona pakno nispa isam nispa ne
translation: My father was a rich man with no equal.
note: pakno marks the degree of the father's wealth as the comparison standard. The prenominal clause [a=ona pakno nispa isam] 'to whose extent/degree no rich man exists' modifies the head nispa 'rich man'. The strategy amounts to a comparative without a dedicated comparative particle: no other rich man exists to the extent/degree of my father. See the full relativization analysis in the prenominal chapter.

text: a=onaha an a=unuhu an hine oka=an
translation: My father was there, my mother was there, and we lived.
note: The fourth-person prefix a= on the possessed kinship nouns marks the protagonist's father and mother. The formula [kin-NP exist, kin-NP exist hine, oka=an] recurs across Saru uwepeker narrations as a standard framing device.

text: nea su ka itanki ka pirkano huraye hine rorunso or ta kor wa arpa hine ukao hine oka=an
gloss: DEM pot also bowl also well wash CONJ upper.seat at LOC carry CONJ go CONJ put.away CONJ exist.PL=4.S
translation: (She) washed those pots and bowls cleanly, brought them to the seat of honour, stored them away, and they lived on.
note: Three consecutive hine junctures form one narrative segment. Fourth-person prefixes on the transitives huraye 'wash' and kor 'carry' are not displayed in the source transcription; they surface phonologically in performance as reduced a=. The chain closes with the narrative existential oka=an.

text: inkar=an awa somosuykusun inkar=an kuni a=ramu rok hi
gloss: look=4.S CONJ beyond.belief look=4.S COMP 4.A=think PRF NMLZ
translation: (I) looked — at something beyond all imagining that (I) would look at — so (I) had thought.
note: Four verse lines displayed as one morphemic line. The tail verb inkar=an '(I) looked' at the end of line 1 is repeated as the head of line 3 (inkar=an kuni 'that (I) would look'), with the awa discovery connective bridging the juncture. somosuykusun 'something beyond imagining' is a lexical expression whose internal morphology is opaque in the accessible sources; the gloss follows Nakagawa's Japanese rendering まさかそのようなものを. rok is a perfect marker.

text: a=yupi-hi an hine oka=an pe ne hike
gloss: 4.POSS=elder.brother-POSS exist CONJ exist.PL=4.S NMLZ COP CONJ
translation: My elder brother was there, and we lived on — and, being that, …
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker no. 21, ILCAA Ainu materials; aa-irc/031#1
note: The pe ne hike construction recapitulates the two-clause hine-chain (elder brother existed; narrator and sibling lived on) as an established fact and pivots to the story's opening event. a=yupi-hi: fourth-person possessive prefix a= on the possessed-form noun yupi-hi 'elder brother (possessed form)'.

text: rikun kanto ta a=sa-ha i=resu hine oka=an pe ne hike
gloss: be.high heaven LOC 4.POSS=elder.sister-POSS 4.O=raise CONJ exist.PL=4.S NMLZ COP CONJ
translation: In the upper sky, my elder sister raised me, and we lived on — and, being that, …
place: Kawakami Matsuko, uwepeker no. 15, ILCAA Ainu materials; aa-irc/022#0
note: A richer opening: the locative phrase rikun kanto ta 'in the upper sky' establishes the supernatural story world; then a raising-and-living hine-chain closes on pe ne hike. The fourth-person object prefix i= on resu 'raise' indexes the narrator as the protagonist being raised by the sister.

text: kanpi ku=sanke ru-we ne akusu itasa kanpi ek ru-we ne
gloss: letter 1SG.A=send.out track-POSS COP CONJ in.return letter come track-POSS COP
translation: I sent a letter, and (then, it turned out) a reply arrived.
note: The ruwe ne tail closes the first event as an established fact before akusu pivots to the discovered consequence. In oral narrative the same sequence marks episode-level transitions, signalling the boundary between what has been established and what unfolds next.

text: mat-kor hine oka=an ru-we ne a p
gloss: wife-have CONJ exist.PL=4.S track-POSS COP PFV NMLZ
translation: He had taken a wife, and they went on living — and yet, (now something changed) …
place: Wateke, Saru; Dal Corso siglum TMA: 2
note: The hine-chain (took a wife; lived on) is nominalized into a ruwe ne predicate, then the perfective a and the connective nominal p mark a narrative turn. The p is not an argument of the following clause — it is at the connective end of the formal-noun grammaticalization cline (see the nominalization chapter). The turn coincides with a change in the narrative state of affairs.

text: tan-pe topen-pe ne na ekasi ku=kore na
gloss: DEM-NMLZ sweet-NMLZ COP FIN old.man 1SG.A=give FIN
translation: This is a sweet. I'll give it to the old man.
note: Satō ex. 21 (two sentences). The theme 'it' of the second clause is zero — no pronoun, no person index — yet its reference to the sweet of the first clause is unambiguous because kore's valency requires a theme argument.

translation: Take pity on me and give me lodging.
note: The fourth-person object prefix i= indexes the narrator-protagonist as recipient across three chained predicates. In kamuy yukar, i= here tracks the protagonist's first-person reference within the story world.

translation: She put the fish into the basket.
note: Constructed to illustrate location-noun role assignment. The NP saranip or (basket + locative noun or 'inside') is unambiguously the Goal; cep (fish) must be the theme. Without or, both NPs would be semantically eligible for either argument role when both are zero-indexed.

text: a=kor seta anakne i=sam ta arpa=an
translation: As for my dog, it went right beside me.
note: Constructed to illustrate anakne topic-fronting. The possessed NP a=kor seta 'my dog' is marked as topic; subsequent clauses maintain reference by zero anaphora, with the dog as subject (=4.S on intransitives) and the narrator tracked by 4.O.

text: oka=an a p tane poro=an wa inkar=an
gloss: exist=4.S PFV NMLZ now grow.up=4.S CONJ look.around=4.S
translation: [We] had been living — and now I had grown up and looked around.
note: Constructed to illustrate the a p scene-boundary construction. The fourth-person suffix =an indexes the protagonist-narrator throughout both episodes; a p closes the preceding episode; tane 'now' opens the following one. Based on the pattern described by Bugaeva (2022).

text: imi anak neun oka yakka pirka korka e=kewtumu a=ramosma wa ne
gloss: clothes TOP how exist even.if good but 2SG.POSS=heart 4.A=please CONJ COP
translation: The clothes, whatever they are like, are fine; your heart is what pleased me.
note: anak after a bare NP (imi 'clothes'); the topic phrase is separated from its comment by the adversative korka 'but'.

text: ku=nu hi anak k=eramuan pe ne korka tasa itak anak k=eranpewtek
gloss: 1SG.A=hear NMLZ TOP 1SG.S=know NMLZ COP but reply speech TOP 1SG.S=not.know
translation: The question I understand, but the answer I don't know.
note: Two anak-marked phrases in explicit contrast; each heads a separate predicate clause.

text: wakka anak ku=ku rusuy ka somo ki korka sake ku=ku rusuy wa
gloss: water TOP 1SG.A=drink DES even NEG do but sake 1SG.A=drink DES FIN
translation: I don't want to drink water, but I do want to drink sake.
note: First contrastive member (wakka) is topic-marked; the second (sake) is not. The particle ka reinforces the negation on the first member with a scalar 'not even' reading.

text: kani anakne Sikot ta k=an menoko ka somo ne kusu
gloss: 1SG TOP Chitose LOC 1SG.S=be woman even NEG COP because
translation: As for me, I am not even a woman from Chitose — (so …).
note: The free 1SG pronoun kani hosts anakne; the clitic ku= could not. The clause is a reason clause; its continuation is implicit in context.

text: a=kor seta anakne i=oyakke oma ka somo ki p ne kusu i=sam ta ukasuy ipe=an
gloss: 4.A=have dog TOP 4.O=go.far go even NEG do NMLZ COP because 4.O=vicinity LOC together eat=4.S
translation: My dog never went far from me, so we ate together beside each other.
place: Kawakamu Matsuko (川上まつ子), uwepeker (AA研アイヌ語資料)
note: anakne attaches to the possessed NP a=kor seta 'my dog'; the topic discourse-tracks the dog across the following clauses. ka reinforces the negation on the embedded predicate.

text: cis patek a=ki kor an=an pe ne ru-we ne a p
gloss: cry only 4.A=do while exist=4.S NMLZ COP track-POSS COP PFV NMLZ
translation: (She) was doing nothing but crying, and yet …
note: patek follows a VP (cis 'cry'); ki-support is required before the sequential connective kor.

translation: There was neither a dog nor anything at all.
note: Both seta 'dog' and nep (indefinite 'thing/what') are marked with ka; doubled ka under negation yields total exclusion.

translation: I am the one who ate it.
note: The agent of ku=e 'I eat' provides the focused argument: the question implied is 'who ate it?' and kani 'I' is the copular predicate supplying the answer. The nominalizer pe leaves the VP with an unfilled object slot (arity +1 after the agent is indexed by ku=), creating the relative-clause gap that the focused predicate nominal fills.

translation: What one eats is fish.
note: Here the embedded clause a=e 'one eats (it)' is transitively saturated by the fourth-person agent a= and an implicit third-person object. The nominalizer pe then heads the NP 'the thing one eats', which is predicated as identical to cep 'fish': predicate-nominal focus. The same structure allows a proposition to be asserted as established fact when no explicit contrastive focus is intended.

text: ku=nu hi anak k=eramuan pe ne korka tasa itak anak k=eranpewtek
gloss: 1SG.A=hear NMLZ TOP 1SG.A=understand NMLZ COP CONJ reply speech TOP 1SG.A=not.know
translation: The question I heard I understand, but how to reply I do not know.
