note: Both topic-marked NPs are nominalized clauses: hi nominalizes the VP ku=nu 'I heard (it)' and pe ne predicates the resulting proposition as understood fact. The second clause, tasa itak anak k=eranpewtek, contrasts it with the topic 'the reply', which lacks an explicit pe ne because the bare VP k=eranpewtek closes the sentence. The two anak forms are contrastive, not merely thematic; see topic-marking-anakne for the anak system.

text: tap a=ye katu Piratur sekor a=ye hawe ne
gloss: now 4.A=say manner-POSS Piratur QUOT 4.A=say voice-POSS COP
translation: The current way of calling it is called Piratur.
note: The formal noun katu 'manner of' (affiliative of kat) nominalizes the VP tap a=ye 'one currently says/calls it', forming the topic 'the current manner of calling it'. The naming cleft Piratur sekor a=ye hawe ne then predicates that the word (hawe, affiliative of haw 'voice') of saying it is 'Piratur'. The choice of hawe over p highlights the auditory/linguistic character of the name.

text: hemanta ne kusu ene siran hi an
gloss: why COP because thus appear NMLZ exist
translation: Why has the situation come to be like this?
note: The wh-word hemanta ('why/for what reason') forces the existential an in place of the copula ne after the formal noun hi. The structure hemanta ne kusu is 'why/for what reason', and ene siran 'appearing thus' is the embedded VP. Content questions with a formal-noun tail systematically use NMLZ an (not NMLZ ne).

translation: Would that I were a bird!
note: The emphatic particle ta 'こそ' scopes over the copular predication ku=ne 'I am/become', expressing a counterfactual wish. The concordant SFP oka may follow: cikap ta ku=ne oka! The pair is paired in the oral text with rera ta ku=ne 'would that I were the wind!', a traditional couplet form.

translation: That alone is precisely what worries me.
note: Two focus particles stack: patek 'only/nothing but' restricts the domain, and tasi 'precisely' adds the emphatic-concord trigger. The concordant final particle nek closes the clause in the asserted-emphasis reading '〜のだよ'. The combination patek … tasi … nek expresses both exhaustive focus (nothing but that) and assured assertion (and that is precisely so).

text: a=kor seta anakne i=oyakke oma ka somo ki p ne kusu i=sam ta ukasuy ipe=an
gloss: 4.A=have dog TOP 4.O=leave approach even NEG do NMLZ COP PURP 4.O=side LOC together eat=4.S
translation: My dog, as for it, never left my side, so it ate with me.
place: 川上まつ子, AA研アイヌ語資料, 沙流
note: The possessed subject a=kor seta 'my dog' is fronted and marked with anakne; the complex predicate 'never even approached leaving me' follows with the result clause.

text: ku=nukar seta anakne ney ta ne yakka a=nukar seta ne noyne siran
gloss: 1SG.A=see dog TOP where LOC COP even 4.A=see dog COP seem exist
translation: The dog I saw looked like a dog you would see anywhere.
place: 丸野和子, アイヌタイムズ, 沙流・千歳
note: A relative-clause head (ku=nukar seta 'the dog I saw') is fronted and marked with anakne before the comment clause.

text: Seta anakne a=kor ikor ne kusu onne wa isam pakno pirkano kasi a=oyki kuni p ne na
gloss: dog TOP 4.A=have treasure COP PURP die.old CONJ absent until well properly 4.A=care COMP NMLZ COP FIN
translation: Dogs are our treasure, so one must care for them well until they die of old age.
place: 神崎雅好, アイヌタイムズ, 沙流・千歳
note: A bare lexical noun seta 'dog' heads a generic statement under anakne topic marking.

translation: To my wife I gave the sweets (not to anyone else).
note: Constructed to illustrate IO fronting with the allative postposition orun under contrastive stress, as described in Refsing (1986, §13.4.3) for Shizunai. In neutral order the IO ku=macihi would appear without orun.

text: he=tuk-pa pa a=mat-ne-po-utar-i a=po-utar-i ki pa pe ne kusu
gloss: body=grow-PL PFV 4.A=wife-COP-child-ASS-POSS 4.A=child-ASS-POSS do PFV NMLZ COP PURP
translation: They all grew up — the daughters and the children — because the children did so.
place: Bugaeva 2022 ch.1 ex.19, NINJAL corpus K8109171UP.296
note: The verb phrase he=tuk-pa pa 'grew (plural, perfective)' precedes the two dislocated subject NPs a=matnepoutari (daughters) and a=poutari (sons/children); the light verb ki re-predicates them in an afterthought clause. Translation follows Bugaeva 2022.

translation: Do come again, won't you.
note: The plural suppletive stem arki is required by yan even for a single addressee. hani stacks after yan to add the gentle admonitive 'won't you / I hope you will'. The cluster yan hani contracts to yanani in the Chitose speech-stream (Nakagawa 2024: 333).

translation: Let us go.
note: The fourth-person intransitive suffix =an on the plural suppletive stem paye; ro adds hortative force. Constructed for illustration; functionally equivalent expressions with ro are documented in Nakagawa 2024: 333.

translation: Should I come too, I wonder.
note: The fourth-person S suffix =an on the singular stem ek; so converts the predicate into a soliloquy deliberation. Nakagawa 2024: 334 gives the meaning as 独語の意志 (self-directed volition).

translation: There are plenty of fine cushions here, you know.
note: Nakagawa ex. 583. na follows the existential predicate and signals that the speaker expects the hearer to act on the information (sit down, use the cushions). The existential an is a 3rd-person (zero-marked) predication.

text: wen huci ka somo ne wa
gloss: bad old.woman even NEG COP SOFT
translation: She is no pauper of an old woman.
note: Nakagawa ex. 582, first clause of a pair (the second is pirka huci ne wa 'she is a fine old woman'). wa softens the emphatic negation ka somo ne; the exchange is in dialogue. Fukuda 1961: §21 notes that the particle carries a feel comparable to the Tokyo-female / Hokkaido-unisex Japanese「わ」, without claiming it is female-restricted in Ainu — see §register-gender.

text: k=onaha or-o ta ku=teskar kusu ne na hani
gloss: 1SG.POSS=father place-POSS LOC 1SG.A=report PURP COP FIN ADM
translation: I am going to report this to my father, you know.
note: Satō ex. = Nakagawa 2024: 333. na hani on a purposive declarative; neither clause is an imperative, demonstrating that hani attaches regardless of illocutionary mode. or-o is the possessed form (or-POSS) of the relational noun or 'place, location of'.

translation: If only I were a bird!
note: Nakagawa ex. 560 (= Tamura 1988b: 33; the Fukuda 1961: §12.2 citation gives the form with oka explicit). The emphatic ta triggers the counterfactual wish reading; the concordant oka is here present but may be omitted in Saru. The couplet continues rera ta ku=ne ('if only I were the wind!').

translation: About that alone am I truly troubled.
note: Nakagawa ex. 594 (source: Chiba University Ainu materials 2015: 160). The emphatic tasi triggers the concordant nek; patek 'only' restricts scope. The 4th-person A prefix a= tracks the narrator/speaker in the oral-literature register.

translation: The sound of his coming thundered on.
note: Satō ex. (oral-literature register). The bare concept form hum (not possessed humi) appears before konna. Satō classifies konna/kan provisionally as a 強調の助詞 (emphatic 副助詞) but flags its grammatical status as 'unclear'; the appearance of the concept form rather than the possessed form before konna is unexplained — the same nouns take possessed forms when functioning as formal-noun evidential heads. See formal-defective-nouns for the possessed/concept-form alternation.

text: an epitta paye=an kusu ne na
gloss: one throughout go.PL=4.S PURP COP FIN
translation: I plan to go [there] travelling the whole night.
place: Kawakami Matsuko, 'isoytak dokowa 2', ILCAA Ainu materials (Saru)
note: na closes the quoted declarative clause inside sekor hawean '(she) said'. The sequence kusu ne na (purpose + copula + na) is common in discourse: the assertive-appeal force of na urges the hearer to acknowledge the speaker's stated intention.

translation: Is it all right now?
place: Oda Suteno, 'reyep kamuy', ILCAA Ainu materials (Shizunai)
note: Nakagawa 2024: 304, ex. (corpus Shizunai). The bare formal noun ru-we (no copula) combines with the Q-副助詞 he and the existential an, realising the reduced polar-Q frame ruwe he an (Nakagawa 2024: 409e). This illustrates the sentence-type switch at the evidential tail: copula ne (declarative) is replaced by existential an and the Q-particle he.

translation: Did you understand?
note: Bare formal noun hawe without following ne or an. Adding ne yields a declarative ('you understood'); adding an would open a content question requiring a wh-word.

translation: May we board the boat?
note: Nakagawa 2024: 409b. The bare ruwe without ne or an marks the polar question. yakka 'even if' frames the conditional premise of a permission request.

translation: Is it good now?
place: 織田ステノ 'reyep kamuy', AA研アイヌ語資料 (静内)
note: Combined polar-Q frame ruwe he an. ILCAA Ainu materials; narrator 織田ステノ, document 'reyep kamuy' (静内 dialect).

translation: Is it OK if I (rather than you) kill it?
note: Nakagawa 2024: 409d. he follows the conditional clause a=rayke ciki 'if I kill it'; the focus of the question is the conditional premise, not the final predicate pirka 'good'.

translation: At the time of the famine?
note: Nakagawa 2024: 409d. he scopes the locative phrase keman hi ta 'at the time of the famine' as a fragment confirmation request.

translation: Why aren't you eating?
note: Nakagawa ex. 855. The Saru wh-adverb hnta (= hunak 'where'; used here adverbially as 'why') plus the reason marker kusu stay in the adjunct slot; he marks the reason cluster as the focal unknown.

translation: Are you well?
note: Minimal polar question with sentence-final Q-particle ya. In practice, bare-verb questions with ya alone are often felt as too direct; a formal-noun frame (strategy b or e) is common in polite speech.

text: taan pe nep tap an a
gloss: this thing what just exist Q
translation: What is this?
note: Nakagawa ex. 879 (citing Takahashi via Nakagawa 2024: 412). The Q-particle a (post-consonant allomorph of ya) closes the Tokachi content-question frame nep tap an; taan pe 'this thing' is the topic.

text: hemanta ne kusu ene sir-an hi an
gloss: what COP because like.this appearance-exist NMLZ exist
translation: Why is it like this?
note: Nakagawa ex. 856. The wh-expression hemanta ne kusu 'what because = why' stays in the clause-initial adjunct position; sir-an is the impersonal 'it is so' (sir 'appearance' + an 'exist'); hi an is the expanded content-question frame (formal noun + existential).

translation: Are you going tomorrow or the day after?
note: The NP-disjunction nisatta hene oyasim hene 'tomorrow or the day after' follows Nakagawa 2024: 323–324 (ex. 534); the polar-Q framing by rising intonation is constructed here. In natural speech ya or a final he may close the sentence instead.

translation: Yes, I heard it.
note: Nakagawa ex. 794. The formal noun ruwe is retained in the affirmative answer; the final particle un (a soft-affirmation sentence-final particle, not the existential verb) closes the clause in a confirmatory register.

translation: Fire grandmother, protect me and [let me return] safely.
place: 川上まつ子, AA研「menokoyukar 神謡 4」[aa-irc/011#3]
note: Attested from Kawakami Matsuko's menoko yukar performance (AA研音声資料). The fire deity (huci ape, lit. 'fire grandmother') is invoked as the intermediary deity, consistent with the prayer-address convention that routes all divine communication through the fire deity. The first-person object prefix en= and the conjunctive wa show the embedded prayer within the narrative frame. The word apunno 'safely, without incident' closes the petition. This is a genuine attested example of women's verse (menoko yukar) in the elevated register, with the characteristic deity-address morphology.

text: pirka p poronno k=eunkeray wa. iyairaykere.
translation: You gave me many good things — thank you.
place: 新井田セイノ, アイヌ語鵡川方言日本語‐アイヌ語辞典 [chiba-mukawa/0#322]
note: Attested formula of formal thanks on receiving gifts, from a Mukawa speaker recorded in the Mukawa dictionary corpus. The corpus form iyairaykere is the Mukawa shape of iyayiraykere (the causative-derived 'make (one) grateful'; on the proposed i=yairayke-re analysis see the causative chapter). The clause pairs a k=eunkeray 'I received' acknowledgement with the gratitude interjection, evidencing the use of the formal thanks formula in the gift-receiving situation described above.

text: hinna sekor a=ye hi ta makanak iki=an pe ne yaka anime ani a=nukáre easkay kusu néno a=ki kuni i=nisuk ruwe ne
gloss: hinna QUOT 4.A=say thing TOP hand.palm.up do=1SG.INTR thing COP DISJ animation INS 4.A=see can.CONJ because so 4.A=do IMP 1SG.O=ask-POSS REP COP
translation: When one says 'hinna', the hands move up and down with the palms up; since this can also be shown in animation, I asked them to do it that way.
place: 横山裕之, アイヌタイムズ「ゴールデンカムイ oruspe」[ainu-times/068/0#44]
note: Attested from Yokoyama Hiroyuki's talk on the anime adaptation of Golden Kamuy. The fourth-person a= marks the narrative-protagonist convention (the speaker narrates his own request in the fourth person, consistent with oral-narrative person-marking). The quotative sekor frames the word hinna as a cited form. The instrumental ani introduces the animation as the medium of depiction. This example confirms the palm-up hand gesture as part of the hinna complex in modern revitalization practice.

text: mak raymik hawe ne raymik=an ruwe ne a p oraun
gloss: how raymik way COP raymik=4.S REP COP CONJ thing after
translation: However she performed the women's greeting (raymik), having done the greeting, and then …
place: 貝澤とぅるしの口演 ウエペケㇾ「パㇱクㇽトノ ヤニ アコㇿ」[biratori/004/010#70]
note: Attested use of raymik as a woman's formal greeting in connected oral narrative. The fourth-person intransitive suffix =an marks the narrative-protagonist convention (the female narrator refers to herself in the fourth person). The reduplicated framing raymik hawe ne raymik=an mirrors the conventionalised, formulaic character of the ritual speech-act, consistent with the sex-differentiated greeting complex described above.

text: an=utári unukar=an ciki, irankarapte ani ukoitak=an hine, ukomina=an kane a=utúrenteke a=kisma kane okay=an.
gloss: 4.A=kin meet=4.S CONJ irankarapte INS talk.together=4.S CONJ laugh.together=4.S CONJ 4.A=both.hands 4.A=grasp CONJ exist.PL=4.S
translation: When we met, we said 'irankarapte' to each other, we talked and laughed together, and we were together gripping each other's both hands firmly.
place: 松本成美, アイヌタイムズ 39号「irankarapte」[ainu-times/039/0#3]
note: Attestation of the revitalization-era, gender-neutral use of the irankarapte greeting. Matsumoto Narumi describes a mixed community gathering where the formula mediates mutual address. The narrator self-references with the fourth-person paradigm — the Kushiro form an= (=an elsewhere in Hokkaido dialects) appears on the verb suffixes and as the prefix on utári 'kin/companions', carrying the logophoric/indirection convention characteristic of composed first-person prose (see the fourth-person chapter). The lexical item utúrenteke 'both hands of…' is the possessed form of urentek 'both hands' (Tamura 1996: s.v. urenteke(he)); kisma 'to grasp, hold' (Tamura 1996: s.v.) supplies the firm-handshake sense of the J translation. The construction shows irankarapte deployed as the exchange medium (ani) of a reciprocal talk verb (ukoitak 'to talk together'), consistent with its function as a greeting formula rather than a fixed prayer phrase.

text: sonno ku=pewre or ta ku=nu yukar ne ru-we ne
gloss: truly 1SG.S=be.young place LOC 1SG.A=hear epic COP track-POSS COP
translation: Truly, it is the epic I heard when I was young.
note: Nakagawa ex. 1. The sentential adverb sonno scopes over the whole predication. ku=pewre or ta is a temporal locative nominalization ('at the time of my being young'); ku=nu takes the 1SG.A prefix because nu 'hear' is transitive; the evidential ru-we ne closes the clause.

translation: Get well quickly!
note: Shibatani ex. 13 area. The -no adverbial tunas-no 'quickly' modifies the inchoative imperative pirka 'become well/healthy'. Property verbs serve directly as imperatives, exploiting the stative-to-inchoative polysemy common to Ainu intransitive verbs.

text: yaykata ka k=e hike, iyotta keraan wa
gloss: oneself also 1SG.A=eat but most be.delicious CONJ
translation: I ate some myself too, but it was the most delicious —
note: The superlative degree adverb iyotta 'most of all' immediately precedes the property predicate keraan 'be delicious', exactly as the analysis predicts: [iyotta] [property-verb], with no comparative morphology on the predicate itself. The concessive connective hike ('but') and the narrative first-person k=e 'I ate' frame the superlative in connected speech; the trailing wa is a clause-linking conjunctive. The intensifier earkinne 'very' is likewise attested modifying a predicate in the same narrator's corpus (earkinne pon yuk k=érampokiwen 'I felt great pity for the small deer', [aa-irc/003#83]).

translation: This fish is bigger than me.
note: Illustrates the akkari comparison construction: [subject-NP] [standard-O=akkari] [property-verb]. The standard 'me' is encoded by the 1SG.O prefix en= on akkari rather than by a postposition or case particle on a separate NP. With a noun standard: tan cep seta akkari poro 'This fish is bigger than a dog', with seta 'dog' as bare antecedent without any marking.

translation: …after I said that, and then, …
place: 川上まつ子, isoytak 独話2 (AA研アイヌ語資料 音声資料); aa-irc/004#133
note: orano follows the conditional–temporal particle akusu directly, at the boundary of a completed quotative frame and the next episode. The Saru narrator's spoken monologue shows this stacking as a routine narrative device.

translation: Now — after that — I set off.
note: Constructed minimal form. In attested narrative, tane typically follows a clause-final nominalizer p or a perfective auxiliary a closing an episode, and the shift in time reference is anchored to the new episode that follows.

translation: She was surprised herself that she had become pregnant, and as for that, …
place: 川上まつ子, uwepeker 民話20 (AA研アイヌ語資料 音声資料); aa-irc/030#82
note: newaanpe resumes the nominalized proposition (honkor hi 'the fact of becoming pregnant') as the topic NP of the next clause. The APPL prefix e- on oyamokte marks that the surprise is directed at the preceding fact; the REFL yay- marks the subject as co-referential with the surprisee.

translation: We ate dog and bird.
note: newa marks the first NP (seta 'dog'); the second conjunct (cikap 'bird') follows directly. Saru and Chitose speakers would use bare juxtaposition (seta cikap ci=e) in the same context.

translation: Both drink and eat.
note: Each listed verbal predicate receives usa; the construction is closed by the light verb ki 'do'. In western Hokkaido (including Saru/Chitose), usa does not function as a coordination particle.

translation: Yes.
note: Assent particle responding to a proposition. Homophonous with the transitive verb e 'eat (something)', which is distinguished by its syntactic position and person-marking behaviour.

translation: Yes? / Coming.
note: Response to being called by name or address; distinct from the propositional assent e.

translation: Greetings!
note: Pan-Hokkaido greeting formula. Morphologically opaque when treated as an interjection; a proposed decomposition is discussed below.

translation: Thanks!
note: Light informal acknowledgment in Saru and Chitose. Less formal than hinna or iyayiraykere.

translation: Hurry!
note: Standalone directive interjection. The initial h is absent in some eastern Hokkaido varieties (etak).

translation: Come quickly!
note: Adverbial use of hetak before the imperative ek 'come'; a boundary case between the interjection and adverb classes. The 2SG imperative of ek is the bare stem.

translation: They eat intestines.
note: Reduplicative noun kankan as a direct object. The 4th-person transitive agent a= marks unspecified human participants. Constructed to illustrate the argument-noun status of reduplicative mimetics.

translation: (Someone) goes slowly.
note: Manner adverb moyre in the preverbal arity-zero slot. Constructed to illustrate the adverbial integration position available to mimetic words.

translation: It makes a rattling/pattering sound.
note: Ideophonic use of kaukau in the sekor ki light-verb frame. Constructed to illustrate the depictive quotative integration strategy.

text: oyna ne ciki yukar-i ne ciki
gloss: oyna COP COND yukar-POSS COP COND
translation: whether it be an oyna or a yukar
place: 川上まつ子, AA研「uwepeker 民話8(その1)」[aa-irc/006#301]
note: A prose narration passage in which the narrator uses oyna and yukar in a generic conditional frame. The possessed form yukar-i marks the noun in predicative position before ne; both genre terms appear as interchangeable labels for sung epic here.

text: ipinu pa katu ka a=erampewtek no yukar he oyna he ki pa kor
gloss: hear PFV but FOC 4=know.NEG COND yukar DISJ oyna DISJ do PFV CONJ
translation: I did not know whether they were listening secretly, but I heard them doing yukar or oyna.
place: 川上まつ子, AA研「uwepeker 民話8(その2)」[aa-irc/007#149]
note: The disjunctive particle he…he… ('or…or…') coordinates the two genre terms, treating them as interchangeable alternatives in the narrator's uncertainty. The fourth-person a= on erampewtek 'know' indexes the narrative protagonist. The light verb ki 'do' takes the genre nouns as its complement, showing that yukar and oyna function as activity nouns (cf. ukooyna, ukoyukara 'do oyna/yukar reciprocally' in aa-irc/007#136).

translation: Let me tell one kamuy yukar.
note: The sentence-final particle so marks deliberative or hortative intent. ku= is the 1SG A-series prefix on the verb ye 'tell, say'.

text: uwepeker ku=ye kusu ne a korka
translation: I will tell a uwepeker, but…
place: 川上まつ子, AA研「uwepeker 民話20」[aa-irc/029#0]
note: The narrator announces the genre with the 1SG agent prefix ku= on ye 'say'. The fourth-person a= in ne a korka marks the narrative voice that follows. Contrast the Shizunai narrator Oda Suteno's shorter frame takne uwepeker ku=ye 'I will tell a short uwepeker' (aa-irc/026#0).

translation: I came. (hero's voice, singular)
note: In elegant narrative (atomte itak), the fourth-person suffix =an combines with the singular verb root ek 'come.SG'. In conversational Saru/Chitose this combination is ungrammatical; the everyday first-person singular would be k=ek 'I come'. The singular + 4.S combination is a diagnostic of the elegant register (Satō 2008: 263).

text: somo itak=an hi ne sekor haw-e-an=an kor
gloss: NEG speak=4.S NMLZ COP QUOT voice-POSS-exist=4.S while
translation: Saying, 'One does not speak.'
place: Kawakamii Matsuko, isoytak 独話1, ILCAA Ainu materials aa-irc/003#57
note: The intransitive haw-e-an=an follows sekor; the quoted string ends with the formal noun hi plus the copula ne. The 4th-person suffix =an inside the quote and on the reporting verb haw-e-an=an signals that the quoted speaker is other than the current narrator — a semi-direct shift treated in §3.

text: asinuma arpa=an kusu ne sekor haw-e-an
translation: She said, 'I [self] will go.'
place: Tamura 1972: 377 ex. 9a, as cited in Bugaeva 2008: 38
note: The quoted speaker is a third party. The pronoun asinuma 'self' and the suffix =an mark the quoted speaker's 1st person via the 4th-person form — the semi-direct shift. A self-quotation by the same narrator would retain the 1SG prefix k= inside the quote.

translation: I said, 'I will go.'
note: Self-quotation retains the 1SG prefix k= (reduced form of ku= before a vowel-initial stem) inside the quote. The reporting verb ku=haw-e-an marks the narrator as the 1SG subject of the intransitive hawean. Contrast the preceding example, where the same quoted content attributed to a third party takes asinuma arpa=an.

text: inne topaha i=kesanpa wa arki haw-e as
gloss: large herd 4.O=chase CONJ come.PL voice-POSS arise
translation: There arose the sound of a large herd chasing me and coming.
note: hawe as marks hearsay: the narrator reports a perceived event as ambient sound/speech rather than a specific attributed utterance. The 4th-person object i= references the narrator in the oral-narrative first person (cf. §5).

text: tap a=ye katu Piratur sekor a=ye haw-e ne
gloss: now 4.A=say manner Piratur QUOT 4.A=say voice-POSS COP
translation: The current way of calling it is 'Piratur' — that is what is said.
note: The sekor a=ye frame attributes the name; the outer hawe ne predicates the whole naming as conventionally/verbally reported fact. The 4th-person agent a= is used throughout because the name-givers are indefinite.

translation: (He was) about to sing a yukar.
place: 遠島タネランケ, Abuta yukar [center/015/0#544]; Satō 2009
note: The verb sakehawki 'sing/recite a yukar' combined with the prospective anki 'about to' — a single lexical item encoding the act of sung epic performance, distinct from prose narration verbs (ye, tuytak). Attested in an Abuta (eastern Iburi) yukar published by Satō (2009).

translation: hum-pakpak (the sakehe of the thunder-god)
place: Kaizawa Turushino 貝澤とぅるしの, Biratori; kamuy yukar 'フㇺ パㇰパㇰ（雷の神が自叙する神謡）'
note: The narrator's own metalinguistic comment (biratori/001/004#170): humihiruy だわ。sakehe. 'it's a loud sound — that's the sakehe.' Onomatopoeia of thunder's cracking/pattering.

translation: [HANCIKIKI] — we made sake
place: Nabezawa Nepuki 鍋澤ねぷき, Biratori; kamuy yukar 'ハンチキキ（スズメの酒盛り）'
note: The sakehe hancikiki precedes a narrative line that opens with the homophonous common noun sakehe 'sake (beverage)'. The refrain and the narrative vocabulary coincide accidentally.

kana: menokoyukar って sakekoye するんだけども sakehe 言わないで uwepeker に言うの。
translation: A menoko yukar is told with the refrain (sakekoye); but when one does not say the sakehe, one tells it as a uwepeker (prose tale).
place: 川上まつ子, AA研「menokoyukar 神謡6（節なし）」[aa-irc/019#0]
note: A metalinguistic (code-switched) statement in which the narrator names the criterion that separates sung verse from prose: presence versus absence of the sakehe refrain. The same narrator adds (aa-irc/019#66) that 'the sakehe is long, the uwepeker is short' — the refrain is also a length-diagnostic. The m/g lines gloss only the Ainu words embedded in the Japanese-metalanguage frame shown in the ain surface line.

translation: the near chief
note: First line of an attested couplet (Endō 2022: ch.10 §4, ex.18). The parallel second line substitutes tuyma 'far' for hanke 'near' while the head noun nispa 'chief, lord' is constant.

translation: the far chief
note: Second line. The pair hanke 'near' // tuyma 'far' is itself a fixed word-pair; together the two lines designate the full social field — all chiefs, proximal and distal.

translation: untie the beginning of the message
place: Nabesawa Nepki, Kamuy Yukar Okikurmi Hepere (No-o) [biratori/014/002#132]
note: First line of an attested kamuy-yukar couplet. sonko 'message' is constant across both lines; atpa 'beginning' occupies the substitutable slot, contrasted with sarkes 'end' in the parallel line. The logophoric a= indexes the narrating deity.

translation: hang up the end of the message
place: Nabesawa Nepki, Kamuy Yukar Okikurmi Hepere (No-o) [biratori/014/002#133]
note: Second line. The parallel structure mirrors line 1 exactly: sonko constant, sarkes 'end' replaces atpa 'beginning', atte 'hang up' replaces pita 'untie'. The paired antonymic slot-filling (beginning//end, untie//hang) is the canonical couplet pattern described above.

translation: two shining ones
note: First line of a tricola (Nakagawa 1995: 45; cited in Endō 2022: ch.10 §4, ex.16). Describes embroidery beauty. The second parallel line replaces tu 'two' with re 'three'; the third line supplies the predicate kotuytuyke 'crossed over'.

translation: three shining ones
note: Second line. With tu // re functioning as a 'many' doublet rather than an exact count, the pair together means 'many shining ones'. A third line, kotuytuyke 'crossed over', closes the verse unit.

translation: I arrived at Ukurmem today.
note: Everyday (yayan-itak) pattern: locative marked by the particle ta. After Satō 2008: 263.

text: kamuy menoko uni-hi tane anakne a=ko-sirepa na
gloss: goddess woman house-POSS today TOP 4.A=APPL-arrive FIN
translation: Now I arrived at the goddess's house.
note: Elegant (atomte-itak) pattern: the locative goal is marked by the applicative prefix ko- on the verb in place of the particle ta. The fourth-person prefix a= marks the hero-narrator. After Satō 2008: 263, ex. 20.

text: ar retar kamuy a=tura wa ek=an a=rayke wa ek=an ruwe ne na
gloss: entirely be.white god 4.A=COMIT CONJ come.SG=4.S 4.A=kill CONJ come.SG=4.S track-POSS COP FIN
translation: I brought the pure-white kamuy-bear back with me and killed it, I tell you.
place: Kaizawa Turushino, カムイユカㇻ『ハラトンナ』白熊神 [biratori/003/006#149]
note: Attested number-agreement override in kamuy yukar verse: the singular stem ek combines with the fourth-person suffix =an (ek=an, twice) for the hero-narrator, where everyday Saru/Chitose would block the combination and require the plural stem (arki=an). The clause closes with the narrative evidential ruwe ne na, as is typical of verse narration.

translation: Let me tell one divine epic.
note: Speaker's framing utterance uses everyday first person ku=. Inside the narration, the hero-narrator switches to the fourth-person a=/=an. From the reading-text frame in Satō 2008, chapter 21 (千歳).

translation: [My] father and mother were water-deities, and …
place: 川上まつ子口演 uwepeker 民話 9 [aa-irc/009#136]
note: Attested use of the elegant possessed kin-noun forms onaha 'father' and unuhu 'mother' with the fourth-person possessive a= (the oral-narrative person-marking convention). The narrator dignifies her parents by naming them wakkauskamuy 'water-deities'. The example confirms onaha/unuhu as the literary-register kin terms in connected ritual narration, in contrast to the dialectally unstable colloquial hapo.

text: iresu kamuy, páse kamuy, k=onkami na
translation: O raising-deity, O reverent-deity, I pray.
place: 神崎雅好, Ainu Times no. 30 [ainu-times/030/1#11]
note: Attested prayer formula by Kanzaki Masayoshi. The relational epithet iresu kamuy 'the deity who raised [me]' (i- indefinite-object + resu 'raise') is used in the deity-address slot, instantiating the i-resu kamuy / i-resu huci prayer-only substitution described above rather than the everyday ape huci. The honorific páse kamuy 'reverent/weighty deity' is the intensifying epithet that accompanies the prayer register. The first-person agent prefix ku= surfaces as k= by prevocalic reduction before the vowel-initial onkami, and the final na closes the prayer as a ceremonial assertion. The same speaker's longer prayer (ainu-times/030/1#1) opens iresu kamuy, mosir kor húci ... , preserving the further prayer-only epithet mosir kor huci 'grandmother who rules the land'.

translation: I reverently worship.
place: 鍋沢モトゾウ (Motoanrek), Monbetsu; prayer text ex. 13 in Endō (2022) §2.3
note: Double applicative stacking (e- + ko-) on the worship verb, a morphological hallmark of the prayer register. The 1SG prefix ku= surfaces as k= through prevocalic reduction before the e- applicative. The full form in the prayer text also includes the pase- 'weighty/reverent' prefix; only the onkami clause is reproduced here.

text: néno a=numke kuni arikiki utar opitta ramossi wano k=éyayrayke ruwe tapan na.
gloss: so 4.A=choose COMP work.hard people all heart ABL 1SG.A=be.grateful track DEM.PROX FIN
translation: So I am grateful from the heart to everyone who worked hard so that [the landscape] would be chosen — this is a recognized fact.
place: 浜田隆史, アイヌタイムズ 42号「平取町重要文化的景観 nea=numke」[ainu-times/042/1#6]
note: Attested use of the ceremonial assertion frame ruwe tapan na in composed public prose. The frame closes a declaration of gratitude: the speaker presents the sentiment as an established, recognized fact (ruwe 'track/evidential fact' + tapan 'this' + na) rather than a bare assertion, matching the ceremonial assertive-present reading described above. The fourth-person a= on numke and the complementizer kuni embed the purpose of the collective effort; ramossi wano 'from the heart' intensifies the gratitude verb éyayrayke.

translation: (Thank you — said by a woman while performing raymik.)
note: hinna (lower-Saru hunna) is the gendered women's expression of thanks for received food or gifts, accompanied by the raymik gesture (stroking below the nose with the index finger). The male counterpart is the gesture onkami (bowing with both hands joined), unmarked for a parallel verbal formula. The degree form hioy'oy (< hinna hinna) signals a lighter acknowledgment. Source: nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-26 (asserted); consistent with the gendered-genre patterns documented in Endō (2022) §2.

translation: Expressing thanks (saying hinna), they went home all the way.
place: 織田ステノ, アイヌ語アーカイブ「村長の息子と貧乏人の娘」(1988) [nam-archive/oda-minwa/28#1383]
note: Attested narrative use of hinna in a Shizunai tale told by Oda Steno: hinna ki 'to perform/say hinna (to express thanks)' with the conjunctive kane accompanying the departure; the NAM archive J translation renders the clause as 感謝をしながらずっと帰っていきました. This corroborates the documentation of hinna as a gendered deferential-acknowledgment act (Tamura 1996 s.v. iyayraykere notes hinna as the midstream-and-upstream women's thanks form accompanying raymik), here embedded in a narrative clause rather than uttered as a bare interjection. The plural return verb hosippa indexes the departing party.

text: atuy kor kamuy a=ne hine an=an ru-we ne
gloss: sea have god 4.A=COP CONJ exist=4.S track-POSS COP
translation: I am the god who holds the sea.
note: Hirosawa ex. 16. A sea-deity self-identifies at the opening of an uwepeker: ruwe ne closes the introduction of the narrator's identity as discourse-new information, cast in the fourth-person logophoric frame (a=ne, an=an).

translation: (she) was crying
place: Abuta/Iburi yukar, narrator 遠島タンケ (Tōshima Tanke), l. 46; Satō 2009: §2.2.1
note: Cited from Satō's aspectual analysis of the Abuta yukar text. kor okay encodes a durative background state — the weeping frames the main-line action, not as a storyline event.

text: yaykeste=an wa tan uske ta ek=an wa an=an ruwe ne korka
gloss: wander.about=4.S CONJ DEM place LOC come=4.S CONJ exist=4.S track-POSS COP but
translation: I wandered about and came to this place and have been living here, but …
note: The narrative 'I' is indexed by the fourth-person =an throughout: ek=an pairs the singular verb ek 'come' with the 4th-person ending, and an=an ruwe ne closes the clause as narrative-default. The everyday 1SG ku= never appears; the protagonist speaks of herself in the non-everyday logophoric frame.

text: sekor kane hawean hawe as ruwe ne akusu ora
gloss: QUOT CONJ say voice-POSS exist track-POSS COP CONJ CONJ
translation: … a voice said so, and then …
place: Kimura Kimi, ウエペケㇾ『チナナサパ』ホッチャリの頭 [biratori/020/002#48]
note: Attested double evidentiality in a Saru uwepeker. The inner reportative hawe as (voice-POSS + existential, 'a voice is heard saying …') is embedded under the outer inferential ruwe ne (track-POSS + copula), which ratifies the character's hearsay report as narrator-level established fact; the sequence is then chained onward with the sequential connectives akusu ora 'and then'. This is the pattern Dal Corso (2018: 331–333) describes as the narrator ratifying a character's indirect source as shared narrative knowledge.

text: aysirkamuy epirma hawe ne nankor ruwe ne
gloss: ghost teach voice-POSS COP probably track-POSS COP
translation: … it was probably the ghosts (of your parents) who told you so.
place: Nabesawa Nepuki, ウエペケㇾ『アアチャハ イレス』私の叔父に育てられた [biratori/016/010#164]
note: Attested low-reliability indirect frame: the inner reportative hawe ne (voice-POSS + copula) is combined with the epistemic nankor 'probably' and then wrapped in the outer ruwe ne, so the narrator presents an uncertain attribution — the uncle's conjecture that the dead parents' spirits themselves did the telling — as shared narrative fact. The clause is the close of a quoted utterance (the following line resumes with sekor a=aca hawean 'so my uncle said').

translation: fish
note: Reconstructed pre-form: PA */ti-ʔe-p/ (Alonso de la Fuente 2022, Table 18), decomposed as the medial/4th-person prefix *ti-, the verb *ʔe 'eat', and the nominalizer *-p — 'what all eat'. Common Ainu */ciʔep/ gives Horobetsu ciʔep (glottal retained), Saru cep (glottal lost), ‹SA› Raiciska ceh (p debuccalized). Triple-corroborated: Alonso 2022 Table 18, morpheme-db curated decomposition (confidence 1.0), and community discussion (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2023-12-06).

translation: (Pre-PA reconstructed form) 'the thing that all eat'
note: The etymological decomposition underlying Saru cep. The prefix ci= descends from the pre-grammaticalized medial/resultative morpheme *ti=; -p is the nominalizer productive elsewhere in the grammar. See Xr internal-reconstruction-and-grammaticalization-pathways for the full grammaticalization pathway.

translation: (someone's) eye; the affiliative/possessed form of sik
note: Constructed to illustrate the possessed form of sik 'eye'. The base retains its coda consonant k unchanged; the h is the onset of the grammaticalized suffix hi 'thing, place'. The connecting vowel matches the base's final vowel (here i), yielding sik-i-hi. The Sakhalin Raiciska form is likewise sik-ihi, showing the same k — compare the surface citation form sis (§2 below), where the coda has been debuccalized.

translation: (one's) hand (affiliative/possessed form)
note: Affiliative form of tek 'hand'. In the Janhunen–Alonso analysis, -ehe = lost base-final vowel e + noun hi 'thing'. The SA cognate shows tek-ihi (vowel i by analogy): Janhunen (2020, via Alonso 2022 §2.1).

translation: be pregnant
note: Morphological illustration. The suffix -kor 'have' derives possessive stative verbs from body-part nouns. Alonso (2022 Table 16, §175); mdb decomposition conf. 0.85.

translation: fish (lit. 'the thing eaten [by all]')
note: Morphological reconstruction. Pre-PA *ti=(ʔ)e pe > PA */ti-ʔe-p/ > CA */ciʔep/ > Saru cep (glottal stop lost), Horobetsu ciʔep (glottal stop retained as an archaism), SA ceh (final stop debuccalized). Triple-corroborated: Alonso (2022 §4 / Table 18); mdb curated decomposition (ci=, e 'eat', -p NMLZ; conf. 1.0); community analysis (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-06). The prefix ci= is glossed RES (resultative/inclusive) following Alonso 2022; a community alternative (nukopoli, 2023-12-21) proposes middle-voice for ci= here, parallel to the ci= discussed in the anticausative chapter.

translation: I give it to you.
note: Saru-Chitose prefix-only transitive person marking: the portmanteau eci= is the sole marker for all first-person-A–second-person-O combinations. Horobetsu uses the circumfix e=kore=as; Ishikari e=kore=an. After Nakagawa & Fukazawa (2022: §4.1).

translation: (He) looked toward his wife's head.
note: Horobetsu allative un. Nakagawa & Fukazawa (2022: ex. 4), from a Chiri-lineage Horobetsu text.

text: nean nupuri or en oman kor
gloss: that mountain LOC ALLAT go CONJ
translation: when (we) went toward that mountain
note: Tokachi allative en. Nakagawa & Fukazawa (2022: ex. 5), from Sawai 1995: 61.

translation: wooden spatula
note: Standard accent type: open σ1 forces accent to σ2. Accent mark (´) marks the onset of the high-pitch domain. Comparative form from Nakagawa & Fukazawa 2022 §3.1.

translation: wooden spatula
note: Irregular accent type: open σ1 and σ2 force accent to σ3. Same lexeme as the Saru form, differing only in accent position. Data from Nakagawa & Fukazawa 2022 §3.1.

text: nean nupuri or en oman kor
gloss: that mountain place ALLAT go while
translation: when (they) went toward that mountain
place: Sawai 1995: 61, cited as example 5 in Nakagawa & Fukazawa 2022
note: Tokachi allative en. The locative noun or 'place' takes the allative en as a postposition; the verb oman 'go' is not suppletively plural here.

translation: looking toward (at) my wife's head
place: Y. Chiri 2004: 40, cited as example 4 in Nakagawa & Fukazawa 2022
note: Horobetsu allative un, contrasting with Tokachi en. The affiliative suffixes -ihi and -ha mark inalienable possession on wife and head respectively.

translation: I ate fish.
note: The Saru coda -p in cep 'fish' (PA *ciʔep, Alonso de la Fuente 2022 Table 18) corresponds to Sakhalin Raiciska ceh. The Horobetsu dialect retains the Common Ainu form ciʔep with the glottal break.

translation: the eye (of —)
note: Sakhalin Raiciska affiliative (possessed) form. The independent SA form is sis (debuccalised from *sik, then h becomes s before i), but the affiliative suffix -ihi attaches to the underlying stem /sik-/, restoring the base /k/. Demonstrates that the debuccalisation is a surface phonological process leaving the lexical representation intact.

translation: I want to smoke (tobacco).
place: 新井田セイノ, アイヌ語鵡川方言日本語‐アイヌ語辞典 [chiba-mukawa/0#3048]
note: tampaku (< Japanese tabako), corpus frequency 49 tokens (rank 1968). A nativized early loan with full phonological repair (b → mp).

text: kes to an kor sihainin orowa peko umma koraci a=nepkire
gloss: every day exist while manager from cattle horse like 4.A=work-CAUS
translation: Every day I was made to work like cattle and horses by the manager.
place: 小松哲郎, アイヌタイムズ「Tamamusi Sadayû」[ainu-times/017/2#14]
note: peko (cattle) and umma (horse) are early Japanese animal loans; sihainin (支配人 'manager, overseer') is a later administrative loan. 4.A marks an indefinite/impersonal agent with the narrator as implicit object of the causative.

translation: the raccoon-dog lord, dispatched with a written order
place: 織田ステノ, AA研アイヌ語資料 uwepeker Moyuk [aa-irc/018#71]
note: kampi in the administrative sense 'written order'; tono (< 殿 'lord') titles a supernatural figure cast in a bureaucratic role. an= is the 4.A prefix in Shizunai dialect.

text: terebi sinbun or ta zeikin uk wa umma hok kur oruspe a=nu ruwe ne
gloss: television newspaper place LOC tax take CONJ horse buy person news 4.A=hear track-POSS COP
translation: On television and in the newspapers, one hears the story of a person who took tax money and quietly bought a horse.
place: 浜田隆史, アイヌタイムズ「zeikin oruspe」[ainu-times/017/5#5] (excerpt)
note: Modern loans terebi (TV), sinbun (newspaper), zeikin (tax) retain Japanese phonological form without repair. The early loan umma (horse) is fully nativized. ruwe ne is the inferential evidential treated in the evidential chapters.

translation: The stream flows downstream.
note: Constructed illustration of nay as a geographic common noun. The motion verb san 'go down toward the sea/shore' takes nay as its subject; the construction shows nay as a free noun in an active predication. The san direction also underlies the panke/penke 'downstream/upstream' spatial terms that feed Hokkaido toponym patterns.

translation: tip of the land; headland, cape
note: Constructed illustration of the compound underlying Shiretoko 知床 (Shibatani 1990 §1). sir 'land, visible landscape' combines with etok 'tip, head' to form a compound place name; the Japanese reflex preserves the Ainu compound structure.

translation: (Proto-Ainu) thing that holds bitterness; ancestor of sikerpe 'Amur cork-tree fruit'
note: Constructed illustration of the reconstructed proto-form *siw kor pe per Ochiai (2026: 196). The attested Saru form sikerpe reflects w-deletion and regressive vowel assimilation (o → e). This is an analytical construction, not a form found in any attested Ainu text.

translation: He is a headman.
note: Constructed to illustrate the morphological integration of the Wanderwort kotan. The compound kotan-kor-kur (settlement-have-person) is attested throughout the Hokkaido oral-literature corpus; the third person takes zero marking, leaving the copula ne bare.

translation: (They) make a sail.
note: Constructed minimal context. kaya is the Hokkaido reflex of the Nivkh loanword; the Sakhalin cognate covered fish-skin garments as well (Batchelor 1938: 241).

translation: I have salt.
note: The form sippo 'salt' has no recoverable Ainu morpheme segmentation — diagnostic of a loanword. Contrast the fully transparent cep 'fish' (< ci=e-p), whose internal structure was reconstructed by Alonso de la Fuente (2022: Table 18).

translation: my elder brother
note: The 1SG possessor prefix ku= and the affiliative suffix -ihi co-occur; the possessed form yup-ihi suppresses the final vowel o of the citation form yupo. Third-person possessor is zero-marked: yup-ihi alone = 'his/her elder brother'.

translation: his/her eye (possessed form)
note: Third-person possessor is zero; the affiliative suffix -ihi appears after consonant-final stems. Contrast tek-e 'his/her hand', where the shorter -e allomorph follows the stem-final k.

translation: my hand
note: The 1SG possessor prefix ku= combines with the affiliative suffix -e on the body-part noun tek 'hand'.

translation: The weather is good.
note: S-incorporation of the natural-phenomenon noun sir 'land, appearance, weather' into the intransitive stative verb pirka 'be good'. The incorporated noun fills the S slot; no independent subject NP appears.

translation: I am by the river.
note: The locative noun or 'place' takes the river NP pet as its possessor; the postposition ta marks static location. The possessor relation is adnominal: pet is 'the river's place'. First-person S is marked by the intransitive suffix =an on the existential verb.

text: teeta Shiranuka kotan or ta, ekasi utar usa húci utar usa uykari ko, kanna kanna ne tuytak ye hawe ne.
gloss: long.ago Shiranuka village place LOC elder ASS various grandmother ASS various gather COND again again ANAPH tuytak say talk COP
translation: Long ago in Shiranuka village, whenever the elders and the grandmothers gathered, this legend was told again and again.
place: 松本成美 (Matsumo Narumi), Ainu Times no. 31 (Kushiro) [ainu-times/031/1#2]
note: A Kushiro-dialect speaker uses tuytak, the eastern term for the prose folktale, in a narrative-metalinguistic frame, directly evidencing the geographic distribution claim above. kanna kanna 'again and again' modifies the telling; the anaphoric ne picks out the legend ('this legend', translation この伝説) told as tuytak. The conditional ko ('when[e]ver they gathered') is the eastern form noted in the conditional-clause chapter.

text: uwepeker anak sunke hawe ka somo ne
gloss: uwepeker TOP lie talk also NEG COP
translation: Uwepeker is not false talk at all.
place: 大須賀るえ子 (Osuka Rieko), Shiraoi; アイヌ語ラジオ講座テキスト 10
note: A metalinguistic comment on genre: the speaker denies that uwepeker belongs with sunke itak ('lying/false talk'). The predicate hawe ka somo ne ('is also not talk [of that kind]') frames the negation over the noun phrase sunke hawe. hawe = voice/word/talk.

text: pananpe an penanpe an hine sir-an pe ne ru-we ne hike
gloss: Pananpe exist Penanpe exist CONJ appearance-exist thing COP track-POSS COP although
translation: There were Pananpe and Penanpe, and…
note: Standard Pananpe–Penanpe opening. The third-person existential frame (no fourth-person a= prefix) contrasts with the first-person fourth-person narration of human prose tales. Hirosawa cites the underlying Tamura audio materials; ruwe ne predicates the simultaneous existence of the two characters as established narrative fact.

text: a=ne ruwe ne sekor amameponcikappo isoytak
translation: […and so] I was [one of them] — thus Little Sparrow told the tale.
place: 川上まつ子 (Kawakami Matsuko), uwepeker '民話15' (ILCAA Ainu materials 022:109)
note: Canonical closing formula. The fourth-person copula a=ne (narrator-as-protagonist 'I am') is wrapped in the quotative sekor, and the verb of narration isoytak then names the fourth-person protagonist amameponcikappo ('Little Sparrow'), disclosing the identity of the first-person narrator. ruwe ne predicates the whole disclosure as established fact.

translation: I gave my child away.
place: 川上まつ子 (Kawakamimatsuko), ILCAA Ainu materials (AA研アイヌ語資料)
note: Fragment from a human prose tale. The fourth-person prefix a= marks both the possessive relation ('my child') and the transitive subject ('I gave'). Everyday first-person narration would require ku= for both roles; the prose-tale convention substitutes a= throughout.

translation: (hancikiki!) — [we] brewed sake.
place: 鍋澤ねぷき (Nabezawa Nepuki), 平取町アイヌ口承文芸, 'カムイユカㇻ ハンチキキ（スズメの酒盛り）'
note: The sakehe hancikiki is the fixed refrain for this sparrow-sake-party kamuy yukar. It precedes the narrative phrase sake-he ci=kar 'we brewed sake'; here sake-he uses the possessed form of sake as an ordinary noun ('the sake'), homophonous with the genre term sakehe 'refrain'. The first-person ci= (1PL.EXCL) marks the deity/group of characters.

translation: I come.
note: Everyday Saru/Chitose: 1SG subject on the singular suppletive stem ek.

translation: I come. (verse; hero-narrator)
note: Verse register (atomte-itak): the fourth-person intransitive suffix =an appears with the singular stem ek. In prose =an is restricted to plural stems (arki=an 'we come.PL'); the singular + =an combination is a diagnostic of the verse register (Satō 2008: 263).

translation: Today I arrived at Ukurmem.
note: Everyday (yayan-itak): the locative goal is marked by the free particle ta.

text: kamuy menoko uni-hi tane anakne a=ko-sirepa na
gloss: divine woman house-POSS today TOP 4.A=APPL-arrive FIN
translation: Now I arrived at the goddess's house.
note: Verse register (atomte-itak): the goal is marked by the applicative prefix ko- on the verb, in place of a particle. The fourth-person a= indexes the hero-narrator. This is Satō's illustrative contrast ex. 20.

translation: I offer worship (this is a fact).
note: Constructed to illustrate the 1SG prefix in prayer speech; the ruwe tapan na frame marks formal/ceremonial assertion — see §ruwe-tapan below.

text: tu ray onkami re ray onkami
translation: [She] worshipped greatly, twice and three times.
place: 川上まつ子, AA研「uwepeker 民話8(その1)」[aa-irc/006#164]
note: The fourth-person a= is zero-marked here (null allomorph in narrative prose). The numeral-adverb frame tu…re… ('twice…thrice…') with ray (intensifier) is the standard formulaic expression of repeated ritual action. Contrast the 1SG ku= in prayer proper (§person-marking).

text: kamuy menoko uni-hi tane anakne a=ko-sirepa na
gloss: god woman house-POSS now TOP 4.A=APPL-arrive FIN
translation: Now I arrived at the divine woman's house.
note: Satō 2008 ex. 20 (Chitose): elegant-register example contrasting with the colloquial particle-marked form. The goal applicative ko- incorporates the locative relation that would be marked by ta in everyday speech. Here the fourth-person a= marks the (narrative) first person, illustrating the register's applicative morphology in a verse context; in prayer proper, ku- would replace a= (see §person-marking).

text: ko-onkami a ko-onkami a ayne ora
translation: Having worshipped [the deity] again and again, finally…
place: 川上まつ子, AA研「uwepeker 民話8(その2)」[aa-irc/007#276]
note: The goal applicative ko- marks the deity as the target of worship; the fourth-person a= indexes the narrative protagonist. The verb reduplication (ko-onkami a ko-onkami a) is the standard iterative-intensive frame in ritual narrative, paralleling the 'twice and three times' pattern in §person-marking.

text: sonno yayrayke kewtum ku=kor wa ku=onkami ru-we tapan na
gloss: truly be.grateful heart 1SG.A=have CONJ 1SG.A=worship track-POSS DEM.PROX FIN
kana: sonno yayrayke kewtum ku=kor wa ku=onkamuy ruwe tapan na
translation: Truly with a grateful heart I offer worship — this is a fact.
note: The source text has ku=onkamuy, a form with final -y not found in Saru/Chitose documentation of onkami; it may reflect Samani dialect phonology or a different stem shape. Morphemic line normalised to onkami; the ain line gives the source form. ruwe tapan na is the ceremonial assertion frame.

translation: Older sister, are you there?
note: Polar question via bare ruwe (without ne). The argument of an is zero-marked (3rd person, the sister inside the house). The same formula with an explicit 2SG.S prefix appears later in the same exchange (see §3 below).

translation: Come on in, please.
note: o is a non-lexical interjection (Japanese sā 'well then' equivalent). ya in ASA functions as the imperative softener yan of other dialects; the footnote in the source makes this explicit.

original: サポ、トテクノ エアン ルウェ？
translation: Sister, have you been well?
note: e= is the 2SG.S prefix (intransitive subject), marking the addressee as the sole argument of an. totekno (in good health, well) is an adverb modifying the predicate. The polar-question ruwe frame is the same as in §2.

original: トテクノ クアン ワ。
translation: I am well.
note: ku= is the 1SG.S prefix, mirroring the 2SG.S e= of the question. The clause-linking particle wa (CONJ) closes the turn without a following clause; in conversational Ainu, a wa-final utterance signals a complete turn while leaving the chain formally open (see Nakagawa 2024: 345).

text: numan poronno upas as kusu tanto sonno merayke na
gloss: last.night much snow fall because today truly be.cold FIN
original: ヌマン、ポロンノ ウバシ アシ クス タント ソンノ メライケ ナ。
translation: Because there was a lot of snow last night, today is truly cold.
note: The causal clause (numan … kusu) provides the reason; the main clause (tanto … na) asserts the result. as 'stand/fall' is the standard verb for snowfall (upas as = snow falls). The sentence-final particle na is a soft assertion marker.

original: ソンノ メライケアン。
translation: It really is cold.
note: merayke=an: the 4th-person intransitive suffix =an attaches to the property verb, yielding a general-experiencer reading ('it is cold out'). Compare merayke na above, where the subject is 3rd-person zero-marked.

original: ニサッタ シリピリカ ナンコンナー。
translation: Tomorrow will probably be fine.
note: nankor encodes inference-based assertion (INFR): the speaker has no direct evidence about tomorrow's weather and reasons from current conditions. The Katakana ナンコンナー represents the ASA sandhi form nankor + na → nankornā.

translation: There is a bowl here.
note: SA teeta 'here' carries the phonemic long vowel ee; the Saru cognate locative is ta (short). 'an is the singular existential; the suppletive plural form 'okay appears in (2).

gloss: DEM lake above-LOC bird many exist.PL
translation: There are many birds on that lake.
note: 'okay is the suppletive plural existential (singular 'an). kaa is the position noun 'above (in contact)' in the elderly register, taking the locative suffix -ta. SA enforces strict grammatical number agreement; the singular 'an would be ungrammatical with a plural subject here.

translation: This is not a dog.
note: SA analytic negation: the focus particle ka is followed by the negative predicate hannehka (< han- NEG + copula root), with the copula nee optionally omitted. Hokkaido Saru uses somo ne (NEG COP) instead, an entirely distinct form.

translation: Everyone came together.
note: 'ariki is the suppletive plural stem of 'come' (singular 'eh); =hci is the SA third-person plural subject suffix cliticized to the verb. HK uses the cognate suppletive plural stem arki, but has no suffix cognate to =hci in this position.

translation: Grandmother sang while crying and had me listen.
note: 'en= is the SA first-person singular object prefix (1SG.O), cognate with HK en=. The verb yuukara 'recite oral literature' is the SA cognate of HK yukar; the long initial vowel yuu- in SA corresponds to the short yu- of the HK form, consistent with the SA length–accent correspondence discussed in the preceding section.

translation: I kill (something).
note: Illustrating the three boundary symbols: = separates the person marker ku= from the stem (an orthographic convention, not a clitic analysis); - separates the verb root ray from the CAUS suffix. The portmanteau gloss 1SG.A joins two atoms with the dot, expressing person (1SG) and role (A) from a single morpheme.
